Non-uniform transformations of matrices find numerous practical applications in various fields such as data security, artificial intelligence, and computational biology. Specifically, the problem of varying row and column sums in binary matrices, with constraints on non-negative integer values, has significant implications. A binary matrix transformation can be viewed as a form of image processing, where the matrix is "blurred" into a lower resolution representation, analogous to the Gaussian filter in traditional image processing techniques. Furthermore, this type of transformation has significant connections to the coverage problems in computational biology, where the aim is to ensure that a particular area of a matrix is "covered" by a series of overlapping queries. A key aspect of these problems is achieving a predetermined level of coverage in the matrix. Researchers have previously proposed various sampling algorithms to achieve a margin-based binary matrix transformation, defined as the difference between row and column sums. A margin-based binary matrix sampling algorithm utilizes a random sampling method to obtain a scaled version of the matrix, where each element is independently selected with a probability proportional to the absolute value of the element in the original matrix, resulting in a transformed matrix with the desired sampling probability. Our findings show that this algorithm achieves a margin that is within a constant factor of the optimal margin, with an exponential time complexity in the worst case scenario, contrasting with previous non-uniform sampling algorithms which have been shown to have polynomial time complexities. Our analysis indicates that a general sampling algorithm for binary matrices may face a time complexity of O(n^3) with the number of rows in the matrix. Our work also demonstrates the applicability of fixed margin binary matrix sampling in the coverage problems of computational biology, where the proposed sampling algorithm achieves a time complexity of O(n^2) with the number of rows in the matrix. Our research reveals that a parametric sowing process enlivens silent modes within a microresonator optical frequency comb by generating an up-conversion mechanism, allowing for the exploration of the mode spectrum and its application to characterization of the microresonator and its adjustment through external influences. By leveraging sowing-induced nonlinear optical interactions, we can create novel coherent light sources with adjustable wavelengths, stiffness of optical fibers, and incorporated external cavities. This technique offers promising prospects for precision spectroscopy at various atomic transitions, the development of multi-channel optical synthesizers with high stability, and the investigation of highly complex quantum systems. Moreover, parametric sowing enables the exploration of the microresonator's phase space, where we identify phenomena of chaotic dynamics and associated characteristics, including the associated noise and its influence on optical frequency comb stability. We demonstrate that by trapping a sowed mode in a loop-mirror external cavity, we can adjust the microresonator's properties, such as glycan or stiffness, using this new technique. In summary, parametric sowing provides a groundbreaking, versatile tool for microphysics research and development of advanced photonic systems. This method could also be extended to other types of microresonators, such as photonic crystal resonators and Kirsting lattice resonators, by adjusting experimental conditions, such as temperature or sol-gel treatment. Finally, we outline the future research directions in this field. Please see our main article for a more detailed description of the results. Quantization has emerged as a highly effective method for accelerating inference in deep neural networks, particularly on devices with limited resources such as GPUs and TPUs. Interestingly, previous studies have discovered that employing quantization also improved the models' generalization capabilities, a benefit typically associated with techniques such as regularization and data augmentation. In this study, we sought to uncover the underlying reasons behind this observed improvement by examining the neural tangent kernel (NTK) of binary-weight neural networks. Our analysis reveals that binary weight quantization leads to anisotropic Gaussian-like continuum models, whose eigenspectra exhibit a gap, thereby resulting in improved generalization performance. Furthermore, our findings suggest that the effectiveness of various quantization methods can be attributed to the formation of this anisotropic kernel. To validate our hypotheses, we successfully derived the NTK of binary-weight convolutional neural networks and observed correlation between the kernel's spectral gap and generalization performance in practical experiments. Our analysis provides a theoretical basis for the effectiveness of quantization in improving generalization performance. Additionally, it offers a measurable criterion for evaluating and selecting the effectiveness of different quantization strategies. We hope that our study will serve as a valuable reference for the ongoing research into quantization. The code used in this study is available at https://github.com/jindal-krishna/quantization. In systems undergoing a phase transition, quantum critical points hold a special place where the phase diagram's critical boundary intersects with the thermodynamic critical line. Typically, this quantum critical point represents an ideal scenario where information remains accessible due to the absence of a characteristic energy scale. Additionally, we've applied these changes while maintaining Miller and Sheffield's precise formulation of the relationship between the field and the evolution processes. The new formulation includes random zero sets that exhibit alpha-stable fractal properties and show asymptotic stability. We've also established that the probability of the zero sets intersecting can be expressed as a multiplicative constant, dependent on the value of alpha, under certain conditions. When alpha equals one, the interaction between the field and the SLE processes is reinterpreted as a SLE decomposition theorem that was initially developed by the author and Gwynne. The theorem describes the zero sets of two coupled fields as a single SLE process with certain stochastic obstacles. This investigation involves resolving the Navier-Stokes equations for a fluid with periodic properties and initial conditions. Given the equations' invariance with time, we conclude that any possible singularity in the solutions occurs after a certain time point. We demonstrate that, at any given time, the maximum magnitude of the velocity and pressure within the fluid can be quantitatively bounded by the Navier-Stokes equations, despite the complexity of the pressure function, which is periodic with a known length. This analysis relies heavily on the theory of Littlewood, initially developed by Littlewood in his 1949 correspondence with Atanu Ghosh and Rees in his 1987 work. We show that the maximum magnitude of the velocity can be expressed as the product of a constant, the viscosity, the reciprocal of the wavelength, and the square of the nondecaying portion of the velocity's maximum magnitude, as denoted by the symbol $\kappa^\perp$. We show that these estimates are precise and valid by constructing explicit examples that reach these parameter values. Quantum algorithms are growing in popularity but successful implementation relies on reliable, error-correcting quantum memory in the backplane, an aspect that's often overlooked in educational materials. Our research introduces a novel, traditional approach to verify quantum computations without the need for error-correcting codes. Our method leverages the low error rate of quantum computations to bound the error rate for a specific outcome, allowing us to apply a classical, high-confidence verification technique if the error rate remains within non-deviating limits. This approach offers several advantages, including simplified implementation, higher confidence levels, and compatibility with older quantum processors, including those from IBM. Our research provides an outline of this verification method and demonstrates its efficacy on a practical example using IBM's quantum experience. Additionally, we open-source a package called qcheck for easy integration with existing quantum circuits and experiments. Our study shows that, in the context of binary operations, the probability of significant errors is extremely low, and we can successfully verify quantum computations in linear time if these errors don't occur. Our research contributes to the creation of more robust quantum algorithms by incorporating classical techniques and promoting the use of traditional verification in quantum computations. Furthermore, our research serves as a model for developing other classical tools in quantum computing. Our findings also underscore the importance of reliable quantum memory for practical quantum computations and we suggest enhancing existing quantum education with our research. Under typical circumstances, in any sequence of events, the likelihood of a sequence occurring is directly linked to how recently it has occurred, with older sequences being less likely to happen again soon. This statistical pattern holds true across a variety of contexts, including the sequence of letters in words, the movement of planets, and the selection of letters in random words. However, when a sequence of events is chosen randomly from a limited set of possibilities, there is a notable exception to this general trend: the sequences that are chosen most frequently are not the ones that are closest in time or space. Additionally, we have found that, in general, the likelihood of a sequence occurring is directly proportional to the square of the distance between the sequence's start and end, offering a mathematical formula to predict the likelihood of a sequence based on its components and the likelihood of its individual parts. This finding, in turn, is tied to a mathematical representation of the sequence's structure, which can be used to predict the sequence's likelihood and offer insights into its composition. Finally, we have identified a group of words, for which the likelihood of a sequence is directly proportional to the square of the distance between the sequence's start and end, by establishing new records for the longest and shortest words that exhibit this property, as well as the words that exhibit this property most frequently. These breakthroughs utilize cutting-edge computational techniques, including a recently developed algorithm for generating random words at a specified frequency. This algorithm is notably simple and general, allowing it to be applied to a variety of contexts, including the sequence of letters in words, the movement of planets, and the selection of letters in random words. Furthermore, we have found that, in general, the likelihood of a sequence occurring is directly proportional to the sequence's length, offering a mathematical formula to predict the sequence's likelihood and explain a long-standing statistical pattern, known as the "galton board" effect. This paper proposes a novel approach to examining signal characteristics using a mathematical framework that employs the statistical properties of spectrogram level contours. Spectrogram level contours serve as effective descriptors of non-stationary signals, yet their statistical analysis presents significant challenges due to the intricate nature of spectrogram variability. This breakthrough facilitates the creation of predictive probability models and confidence intervals for spectrogram level contours, ultimately enabling the temporal segmentation of signals into distinct regions based on specified threshold values. The proposed method is demonstrated through its application to the detection of changes in audio signals and its further extension to the analysis of mass spectra for the purpose of biomarker identification. Comprehensive results illustrate the accuracy of the proposed segmentation technique compared to existing state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, this study explores the extension of this framework to multiple spectrograms, enabling the simultaneous characterization of overlapping signals in multi-channel scenarios. Additionally, this paper examines the implications of its findings for spectrogram level contour estimation and the detection of anomalies, including false detections, particularly in the context of mass spectrometry. We present a new methodical approach to identify and analyze complex network behaviors, specifically focusing on a universal and robust framework that detects travelling chimeras and synchronized groups in spiking neural networks. Traveling chimeras, characterized by distinct membrane potential states, allow for simultaneous action potential propagation and stable oscillatory activity. This approach uses an automated pipeline to identify chimeras and synchronized groups in large neuronal networks of any topology and size, tracing back their origins to initial conditions and revealing their dynamic evolution. We validate this framework using numerical simulations of various network models, observing traveling chimeras and synchronized groups in clump, wave, and spike configurations. Furthermore, we demonstrate the ability of our framework to uncover hidden patterns in clump configurations, revealing multiple chimeras and groups using different initial condition sets. We believe this method will contribute significantly to the understanding of chimeric states in complex biological and artificial networks. The associated code and documentation are publicly available for access.

By leveraging REBOUND, a highly flexible and user-friendly N-body code, this project aims to adapt and implement stochastic forces as a module, thereby expanding the scope of possible forces within the code framework. We achieve this adaptation by integrating a new module called "xFMOD" within REOUND, thereby contributing to the growth of the REOUND community. Through thorough testing, we validate the xfMOD module by cross-correlating it with established methods and exploring its effects on N-body simulations, including planetary systems, binary systems, and gravitational noise. Additionally, this project serves as a model for participatory research within the REOUND community, showcasing the potential for community members to drive innovation and improvement in the code. We hope that the xfMOD module will serve as a starting point for further development and research within the REOUND community, with applications in numerous areas of N-body astronomy. The project also offers guidance on integrating new features to REOUND and shares useful tips and resources for the community. The binary system test provides the most rigorous method for assessing gravitational models. By analyzing the extensive binary test consisting of six extensive parameters from various pulsar timing arrays and a timing array of white dwarf binaries, our research demonstrates that a single unique solution exists that satisfies all requirements. We then show how to translate this extensive binary test into the binary test framework through a dimension reduction technique. Furthermore, our findings indicate that a single unique solution exists for the latter as well. Notably, our research reveals that the extensive binary test can serve as an effective means of constraining novel gravitational theories, such as $S^2$ gravity, by applying a sum-rule approach. Based on this method, our research excludes certain parameters as potential solutions and presents confidence intervals for the remaining ones. We then demonstrate that the binary test framework can also be employed to assess additional features of $S^2$ gravity by utilizing the extensive parameters, thus providing further insight into this model. Overall, our research highlights the utility of the extensive binary test as a robust tool for evaluating novel gravitational theories in a comprehensive manner. The issue of location privacy has gained significant attention in recent years due to the potential risks involved, such as unauthorized access to sensitive information. A common approach to mitigating this risk relies on systems that supply users with location privacy solutions, but these systems frequently compromise between location privacy and navigation functionality. This study aims to address this concern by introducing an innovative method that enhances system security using a conditional normal distribution prior for location tracking. By integrating this method into the existing paradigm of sequential probability ratio tests, researchers were able to develop an algorithm combining location tracking and privacy protection. Furthermore, theoretical findings and simulations demonstrate the proposed algorithm's performance, specifically showing it attains the best possible balance between navigation accuracy and privacy security. Notably, while the new algorithm achieves optimal results in both areas, the trade-off between them deteriorates as the system's signal-to-noise ratio decreases. Interestingly, this trend also applies to the current best-in-class GPS technology used in various mobile devices. Ultimately, the novel algorithm presents a practical solution for minimizing location privacy risks while also enabling seamless navigation on mobile devices. Moreover, the research presents an interesting finding relevant to privacy protection, showing that location privacy concerns can be alleviated even in scenarios with zero signal-to-noise ratios. Fisher's mean effect size is not only a measure of average treatment impact but also an essential component of his statistical theory. We demonstrate that this concept plays a critical role in modern causal inference methods, particularly in randomization analysis and the construction of confidence intervals following p-value testing. Notably, its significance extends to non-randomized studies as well. The importance of Fisher's mean effect size is reflected in the relationship between its squared value and the variance of log-transformed p-values, a connection that holds even in the presence of irregularity. Based on this finding, we verify the applicability of the delta method in retrieving the mean effect size from the mean of log-transformed p-values. Furthermore, this result empowers the application of sample-specific confidence intervals to the mean effect size, a practice supported by asymptotic arguments as well as simulations showcasing its validity, accuracy, and computational feasibility. We explore the implications of these findings on the broader interpretation of p-values in statistical inference. The proposed method, which can be easily implemented using the provided R code, offers a flexible alternative to existing approaches such as the sample mean and quantile estimation. We draw particular inspiration from the approach of Hermon and Zhang (2020), which utilizes a general theorem to facilitate a straightforward proof of consistency in both the continuous and discrete contexts. We also offer an alternative proof based on a'switch' function, as well as an initial exploration of a hybrid approach combining functional Taylor expansions and consistency, opening the door for potential further research in this area. In the discrete case, considering a Markov chain $X$ with a transition probability matrix $P$ and a probability distribution $\pi$ that satisfies the detailed balance condition with respect to $P$, Lalley in 1996 demonstrated the existence of a Markov chain $X^{(\lambda)}$ with states $S$ such that $\pi^{(\lambda)}(x) = \pi(x)$ for all $x \in S$ and $\lim_{\lambda \to 0} \mathbb{P}(X_t = x \mid X_0 = y) = \pi^{(\lambda)}(x)$ for any initial state $y$, provided that $X$ is reversible.

In numerous studies across various healthcare settings, researchers have employed process improvement methodologies and statistical tools to analyze patient flow and service delivery strategies in emergency departments (EDs). To address the limitations of traditional statistical models in accurately capturing the dynamics of individual patient interventions, and the challenges of estimating variability in scenarios with limited data observations, an alternative method is proposed. This involves creating typical response curves for intervention durations using nonparametric kernel density estimation and conditional regression trees. Not only does this method enable researchers to incorporate clinical staff insights and knowledge, but it also allows for the incorporation of decision-makers and stakeholders in the decision-making process. This approach is demonstrated through an application in the ED of a large teaching hospital in Bogotá, Colombia. By utilizing this method, insights are gained into the patterns of treating patients with longer-staying patients, and using the obtained estimates, a queueing model is constructed to optimize the hospital's resource allocation and patient processing mechanisms. This methodology offers a versatile framework for analyzing intervention durations, and its application can contribute to improving the quality of care and operational efficiency in EDs. This research has potential applications beyond hospitals, and its methodology can be applied to a wide range of settings where real-time service processing and patient flow management are prevalent. In multi-agent systems, collaborative planning is typically reserved for advanced AI systems with high processing power, whereas simpler agents are often relegated to basic tasks. We explore the feasibility of applying standard robotic communication methods to facilitate cooperative actions among agents with limited capabilities, no prior knowledge, and no access to advanced computation. A key challenge lies in generating concise communication among the agents, as direct information exchange is often impractical. We introduce a novel distribution method that leverages binary representations and random projections to reduce information exchange, allowing standard multi-agent planners to scale down their solutions for the sake of communication. Through simulations involving large-scale scenarios, we compare the performance of existing multi-agent planners and demonstrate their compatibility with our proposed communication approach, achieving comparable results, notably up to 11 times better outcome quality in complex scenarios. The proposed approach shows great promise for enabling cooperative behaviors among simple agents with limited capabilities, paving the way for a range of applications, including search and rescue scenarios with basic robots. Additionally, the underlying communication techniques can be applied to other domains to facilitate information exchange among entities with restricted computation and communication capacities. The effectiveness of online fundraising largely depends on how well a crowd is engaged. While successful campaigns often create a positive and energetic crowd atmosphere, unsuccessful ones tend to have a less active and less positive crowd. In this study, we analyzed data from over 1,800 crowdfunding projects on multiple platforms to identify the correlation between crowd engagement metrics and the financial outcomes of campaigns. Our results reveal both platform-specific and generalizable indicators of successful crowd engagement, including higher comment rates, more diverse contributor bases, and the presence of crowd leaders. These findings can inform the development of system interventions aimed at enhancing crowd atmosphere and, ultimately, the success of campaigns. System designers may utilize these metrics as performance indicators, enabling data-driven decision-making and a systematic approach to optimizing crowd engagement. By standardizing these metrics across platforms, developers can share knowledge and best practices, ultimately creating a more unified and effective approach to managing crowds. In various industrial settings, efficiently sequencing tasks for robotic manipulation can significantly boost production efficiency and lower costs. A fast and versatile approach known as Cluster-And-Transfer (CAT) has gained prominence in addressing this challenge, by grouping tasks based on spatial proximity and then sequentially carrying out the associated tasks en bloc. Despite its advantages, the standard f2-catalogue* variant of the CAT method has a notable Drawback: tasks far from the starting point may cause disruptions to the overall schedule when prioritized first. In response, we introduce a straightforward yet effective optimization strategy to address this limitation. By modifying the f2-catalogue* method to take into account the physical layout of the tasks and promoting tasks closer to the starting point, we enhance overall efficiency and reduce disruptions. In comparison to the original f2-catalogue*, our proposed method demonstrates improved results, with a maximum 24.8% decrease in starting point deviations and up to a 14.1% improvement in schedule completion time in a variety of real-world scenarios. Additionally, we introduce a clustering approach for situations where tasks are grouped automatically, resulting in improved schedule completeness and reduced starting point deviations. Overall, our optimization strategy and associated methodology offer efficient enhancements to the standard f2-catalogue* method of the CAT technique. These results can be applied to diverse industrial settings, encompassing automated storage and handling facilities, where robotic manipulation sequencing plays a vital role in optimal operation. Graph classification has significant practical value in numerous disciplines. Despite the effectiveness of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) on classified graph data, they typically assume an abundance of labeled examples and a large amount of annotation-free source data. Nonetheless, labeled data is costly and time-consuming to obtain, whereas annotation-free source data is readily available and provides valuable insights in many scenarios. Consequently, there's a need to develop methods that make efficient use of limited labels and unannotated source data for graph classification. 

In this research, we present the concept of pseudo-labeling for GNNs, a semi-supervised method that incorporates limited labels into unannotated graphs through pseudo-labeling. We assess the efficacy of two pseudo-labeling strategies, including a strategy based on the prediction of a pre-trained model and a strategy grounded in supervised contrastive learning. We also conduct experiments on six graph datasets to evaluate the merits of our approach, comparing it to supervised and semi-supervised baseline methods. Notably, our research finds that pseudo-labeling offers superior performance to baseline semi-supervised methods in six graph datasets, while matching the performance of supervised baselines in four of these datasets. Consequently, pseudo-labeling emerges as a versatile and effective technique for semi-supervised graph classification tasks. We hypothesize that the effectiveness of pseudo-labeling could be attributed to the addition of noise to the limited labels, which may facilitate the model's ability to generalize beyond its annotated boundaries. We also identify potential avenues for further research, suggesting that pseudo-labeling could be combined with data augmentation techniques to achieve even better results. 

The code for this research is publicly available at: https://github.com/erogravl/PL-GNNs. 

In terms of contributions, this research makes the following advancements: (i) it introduces pseudo-labeling to GNNs, offering a semi-supervised solution to graph classification; (ii) it develops and evaluates two pseudo-labeling strategies, including one centered on pre-trained models and another grounded in supervised contrastive learning; (iii) it shows through extensive experimentation on six graph datasets that pseudo-labeling outperforms semi-supervised baselines and matches supervised baselines in four of these datasets; (iii) it proposes hypotheses for its effectiveness and potential avenues for further research.

This article further explores and develops the concept of chiral aspects in 2dcft within the pAQFT framework, building upon a previously published study.  It specifically investigates how these aspects relate to a massless scalar field in globally hyperbolic 2-dimensional spacetimes.  The study identifies subalgebras that contain either chiral or anti-chiral observables, constructing these explicitly and showing they are embedded in the full theory's algebra.  It also establishes that the construction of these subalgebras is robust to variations in the spacetime's geometry and extends existing results to the context of distributed quantum fields.  Finally, the article examines the possibility of extending the pAQFT construction to include fields that are defined on curved spacetimes, exploring the relation between chiral aspects and symmetries, such as U(1) global symmetry, and comparing this with the flat spacetime case.  Along the way, new results are obtained about the first chiral variation of the stress tensor's distribution in relation to the Weyl tensor.  This work provides a theoretical framework for studying chiral phenomena in 2dcft and reveals interesting and non-trivial results about the properties of these fields.

This research proposes a technique for creating robust, frequency-stable M{\o}lmer-S{\o}rensen gates within ion-trap quantum computers by leveraging the unique properties of the ion string's motion. By selecting specific pulse patterns that evenly distribute energy across multiple frequency modes, it is possible to develop a framework for designing MS gates with adjustable bandwidth and duration. The framework's application in a 21-qubit system using 13 spatial modes and 4 periodic modes has shown the ability to implement gates with large diameters (>10$\pi$ Mrad) and short durations (20$\sim$40$\mu$s, limited by heating constraints), while still maintaining low levels of gate-induced heating (0.5$\sim$3 photons per gate). The associated heat budget could be reduced by using advanced ion-cooling methods, making it possible to implement gates that are currently limited heating-free. The new technique offers a promising way to tackle the issue of wide-frequency-sweeps in quantum computation and to expand the scale of complex quantum algorithms. Additionally, it provides a valuable resource for developing quantum algorithms with flexible frequency structures and for creating practical quantum gates in specific ion species and trap designs. The research further identifies and outlines the necessary technological advancements required to reach the goal of wide-frequency-sweeps in quantum algorithms. If achieved, this paradigm could serve as a crucial building block for developing practical quantum computers with high coherence levels. The work has been partially presented at PITTPS 2021, and this document provides a detailed expansion of the associated talk. Graphical Gaussian processes offer a framework to tackle these complex dependencies, and we find that the intersection of these models aligns with the parameters of the functional Gaussian graphical model, enabling a more comprehensive understanding of this parameter space by characterizing its geometry and identifying'slices' of the space, each corresponding to unique model interpretations, such as the 'independent function process' and the 'hierarchical process'. Furthermore, we explore stochastic volatility models, and develop a new hierarchical approach to latent variable models, both of which are situated within the functional Gaussian graphical model framework. To efficiently tackle high-dimensional datasets, we introduce a variational Bayesian method for scalable parameter estimation, and demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through numerical experiments on synthetic and real-world data. Specifically, our analysis reveals that our approach outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in terms of log-likelihood metric on a well-known healthcare dataset. Current quantum compilers primarily optimize individual circuits one-off without accounting for repeating patterns within circuits. These patterns are prevalent due to the limitations of quantum algorithm design, including the duplication of similar circuits and parameterized circuits with shared components. Our work introduces a novel quantum compilation approach that systematically identifies and leverages repeating patterns in circuits to maximize compilation efficiency. We have developed predictable algorithms to identify and eliminate redundant gates within circuits, detect duplicated circuits, and share parameterized circuit subcircuits. These algorithms guarantee a constant time complexity for compiling circuits with any number of patterns. In a bilayer semiconductor system with weak coupled layers of materials with different band gaps, our analysis explores how electron-phonon interactions influence the excitons that form at the interface. By applying the Fr\"{o}hlich Hamiltonian to this model, we derive the polaron's Hamiltonian to the second order and utilize a variational method to estimate the polaron's effective mass. Our findings demonstrate that the exciton's effective mass is directly proportional to the strength of the electron-phonon interaction and varies inversely with the distance between the layers, whereas the binding energy of the exciton exhibits the opposite trend. Furthermore, our research reveals that the fraction of the polaron's wave function localized within a layer increases with the distance between the layers, albeit at a slower pace than the ratio of the effective mass to the binding energy. Our theoretical analysis offers insight into how electron-phonon interactions impact the properties of excitons in bilayer systems, thereby providing a framework for the optimization of excitonic conductors using this model as a reference. Additionally, our research may serve as a foundation for the investigation of layered 2D materials with varying band gaps. This work presents a novel, adaptable policy-driven approach designed to effectively recover from failures in sensor-based tracking and localization using radio signals. To achieve this, we develop a transfer learning-based strategy that identifies commonalities in the effects of failures on state estimates, enabling us to recover even in cases where complete data loss occurs. This method surpasses traditional approaches, which require specific knowledge of failure patterns, in both complexity and required information and facilitates the development of a portable, adaptable recovery algorithm. This algorithm can determine the cause and effect relationship of failures on state estimates without prior knowledge, enabling effective localization and tracking recovery. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through simulations of various failure scenarios in sensor-based tracking and localization systems. This approach is also adaptable to localization systems that use radio signals, as illustrated by a mobile robot localisation test. This approach is expected to effectively support the localization and tracking of mobile devices in scenarios with diverse patterns of failure. The Cotton tensor, an alternative to the Einstein tensor in general relativity, plays a significant role in describing the spacetime geometry and its links to the sources of gravity. However, the Cotton tensor has a major drawback: it implies that the divergence of the Cotton tensor is zero in the presence of sources of gravity, which contradicts the relationship between the Einstein tensors and the sources of gravity as stated by Einstein's equations. Consequently, this limitation restricts the usage of the Cotton tensor in describing irregular sources of gravity and soliton solutions. On the positive side, when considering vacuum situations, the Cotton tensor is directly linked to the Ricci tensor and, consequently, is related to the Ricci scalar through the Laplacian. Notably, this connection means that a vanishing Ricci tensor results in a Ricci scalar of zero, which indicates that the Ricci scalar may hold the underlying geometric meaning in describing vacuum situations. Furthermore, we derive novel relationships between the Ricci scalar and the Ricci tensor, contributing to a deeper comprehension of the general theory of relativity. These relationships reveal that the Ricci scalar is the spatial average of the Ricci tensor and that the divergence of the Ricci tensor is zero when the Ricci tensor is regular. We introduce a visualisation tool written in Elm that displays Coq proof strategies within an interactive diagram, showing each step and associated goals, with connections to corresponding areas in the Proof Tree Visualiser. This tool can be accessed at https://coq-psv.github.io/. This document provides an overview of the technology behind coq-psv and instructions on setting it up, in addition to a case study using the Finitary Proof Tactics library. This has several benefits, including facilitating teaching, navigating complex proofs and optimising proofs for human understanding. In the future, we plan to enhance coq-psv with the ability to load Coq vitamins, enabling visualisations of proofs tied to learning content, curriculum objectives and other pedagogical information. This could be particularly useful in lectures, seminars and other educational settings. This research is a by-product of a Proof School project, involving Cambridge University Education and Mathematics colleges, which aims to make interactive visualisations of mathematical proofs available for public use. This has strong links to the established Mathieu Descoteaux's MathProof and the newly launched ProofSchool projects. This document provides a guide for incorporating coq-psv into existing proof-based projects, in particular those involving MathProof. This is particularly relevant as there are plans to release the necessary infrastructure for integrating coq-psv and MathProof, allowing these to be integrated. This will enable users to view both visualisations side by side, as demonstrated in this document using a coq-heapq case study. This combines the interactive diagram and hierarchical structure provided by MathProof to give a comprehensive view of proofs. This technology has far reaching implications and we believe will have a significant impact when combined with other tools for teaching and learning mathematics. This could potentially enable students to better understand key mathematical concepts such as the fundamental theorem of calculus. Section 1 introduces the context and aims of the Proof School project, in particular those involving MathProof. Section 2 provides an in depth description of the technology behind coq-psv, in particular how it generates interactive diagram visualisations of Coq proofs. Section 3 provides instructions on setting up coq-psv and includes a case study using the Finitary Proof Tactics library. We demonstrate that the fourth moment of holomorphic Hecke cusp forms is finite, and establish an exact upper limit for this moment. This precise limit was previously stated by Huang in [8] for the space $S_k^{new}(N)$ with even $k$ and odd $N$. Our approach is an extension of Huang's result, and can be generalized to the space $S_k^{1-new}(N)$ as well. This generalization also yields an exact upper limit for the fourth moment of holomorphic Hecke cusp forms, which aligns with the results of Liu and Wang [20] for the space $S_k^{new}(N)$. The primary tool employed in this study is the relationship between the space of cusp forms and the metaplectic Eisenstein series, and a crucial step involves the utilization of an exact formula for the correlation function of two metaplectic Eisenstein series, as described in Theorem 3.1. This theorem is a significant refinement of Theorem 1 in [7], and can be proved by integrating the method of [7] with the results of [14], [15], [16], [17], [18], [19]. 

In this study, we also establish several auxiliary lemmas, and demonstrate that the bound $L$ in (1.3) is optimal. This optimal bound can be confirmed by constructing idempotent Hecke cusp forms with specific properties. The construction of these idempotent Hecke cusp forms involves modifying the method of [20] and [8], and can be generalized to the space $S_k^{1-new}(N)$ as well.

In interior point methods (IPMs), an efficient iteration system similar to conjugate gradient method is used to solve quadratic optimization problems or higher-order equations. This paper proposes a straightforward yet effective stopping criterion that can replace the conventional convergence test based on residual norms in IPMs, enabling inner iterations to terminate prematurely when a sufficient level of convergence is achieved without compromising optimality. We demonstrate that this new criterion has several benefits, including reduced computational costs, more predictable running times, and better resilience to irregular convergence patterns. Furthermore, it allows solving large-scale problems to be solved on standard laptops, making it suitable for solving real-world large-scale optimization problems as evidenced by our experimental results. Additionally, we have integrated this termination criterion into PyIPM, a popular open-source IPM software library. We have also tested this new criterion in Clp, another popular optimization software library that uses interior point methods. This paper presents detailed performance comparisons between PyIPM, Clp, and IPOPT to showcase the effectiveness of our proposed termination criterion. Establishing trustworthy AI systems necessitates high-quality training data. However, there's currently an acute lack of accessible, well-governed, and standardized incident database that industry and academic sectors could reference for developing training data. As a result, AI systems are and will continue to be vulnerable to similar errors that led to high-profile incidents such as racist Alexa queries and travel ban confusions in the past. A shared incident repository could support the development of more resilient AI systems. This paper proposes the establishment of a comprehensive AI Incident Repository that compiles documented instances from diverse fields and makes them publicly searchable to inform the design of training data for AI systems. By doing so, the repository can contribute to more effective AI governance and incident prevention. For instance, knowledge of hospital staff being mistaken for criminals by AI-powered surveillance systems already informs us of the significance of diverse data inputs in reducing false positives. By harnessing the repository, we can create AI systems that learn from real-world incidents rather than relying on theoretical assumptions. To facilitate the creation and maintenance of the AI Incident Repository, a subsite has been set up at https://airrepo.org/ that houses currently compiled incidents and provides a submission system for documenting new incidents. A new algorithm has been created that enables the precise calibration of quantum field theories using a technique called the renormalization group. This algorithm converts the full theory into a simplified model by eliminating less significant components while accurately reproducing the essential interactions. This process is repeated until the desired level of simplification is achieved, at which point the new model can be compared to existing ones. Currently, researchers employ complex approximation methods to achieve similar outcomes but with significant errors. We are able to eliminate errors because the algorithm operates directly with the full theory's equations rather than an simplified version. While the algorithm's computational complexity grows exponentially with the number of eliminated components, it can still be implemented in a practical form by utilizing advanced computer techniques such as gradient descent and tensor network representations. We have successfully tested this algorithm on a specific type of field theory known as Yang-Mills theory, which models subatomic particles called hadrons. We have demonstrated that the algorithm can simplify complex quantum systems into more manageable models, specifically one that hadrons have been studied against for decades called the rho approximation. We have even found a precise correction to one of the key properties of hadrons called the sigma charge, which had been targeted by researchers for over a decade using other techniques. We have shown that this correction is highly accurate, specifically to a level of 0.5%, which is comparable to current experimental uncertainties. This new algorithm has numerous applications and could be used to study a wide range of quantum systems, including other particles and complex materials called nuclei. It also has the potential to be applied to other types of field theories, such as those describing superconducting materials and exotic particles called quarks. Finally, this algorithm could be useful in studying the behavior of certain systems when their temperatures exceed their characteristic energy levels, a phenomenon known as thermal screening. Current business process management techniques rely on a single process model to guide both design and implementation, but such a model may not adequately capture the complexities of real processes, leading to model inconsistencies and implementation issues.  To address these limitations, our approach integrates a formal method to ensure process models align with their specifications, and we extend this method to accommodate constraints during runtime process execution, enabling the reparation of model discrepancies when issues arise during implementation.  Our technique is based on the acceptance of finite state automata and provides tools for defining and refining process models, as well as identifying and resolving problems during runtime process execution.  The efficacy of our approach has been demonstrated through experiments involving actual case studies from clinical treatment protocols and publication management processes.  We are now developing methods to transmit model specifications to process engines and are exploring the automatic generation of model repair strategies.  Future research will focus on improving the efficiency of our approach, particularly when dealing with large process models.  Ultimately, our long-term goal is to create a versatile language for managing process specifications, including designing, implementing, and reparing processes with inconsistencies.  The core of this language is grounded in finite state automata.  This research is significant because it addresses the fundamental challenge of ensuring process model correctness and provides a novel, automata-based language for designing and refining process models, as well as identifying and resolving issues during runtime process execution. Quipper is a domain-specific language designed for static hardware or emulated hardware execution, used to create creating quantum circuits and implementing algorithms within them. Due to the inherent complexity and fragility of quantum systems, the development of reliable software is crucial for successful operation. Quipper's static type system helps in compiling quantum circuits efficiently and identifying potential errors before runtime. Although Quipper's static analysis provides a high level of safety, it has limitations when it comes to validating the overall correctness of quantum algorithms. This study involves enhancing Quipper with a functional logic extension, allowing for the specification and verification of quantum algorithms through a combination of functional and relational reasoning about machine-level Quipmer instructions. An example is provided to demonstrate how this extension facilitates verifying the correctness of quantum algorithms at different levels, from high-level circuits to low-level machine code. Specifically, this work involves developing a semantics for Quipper-M, which models the execution of Quipmer programs on actual hardware using memory for storage. It also involves creating corresponding verification and correctness proofs for a specific quantum algorithm using the ZQF framework's machine semantics, relational reasoning, and functional logic principles. This research contributes to advancing hardware-dependent quantum software semantics, enabling future verification and correctness proofs for quantum algorithms across different hardware configurations. Additionally, this work provides a new approach to quantum programming, leveraging the quipper-m's ability to model actual hardware execution and the ZQF framework's functional logic, which integrates well-known quantum algorithms with the functional logic framework, making it easier to reason about quantum software. This project also makes available a public repository with the implemented prototypes of quipper-m's semantics, verification tools, and the used example at the following link: https://github.com/charleskgr/quipper-m-semantics. Beyond a threshold, the maximum's probability distribution transforms from a Gaussian to a Weibull form, where a power-law exponent emerges. This exponent exhibits critical behavior, shifting between two forms of scaling, and can be mapped to a critical point on an equilibrium line in a renormalization group study of the matrix model. Utilizing this mapping, we identify the critical point and associated equilibrium behavior, revealing two types of scaling for the maximum's distribution. One form of scaling corresponds to a traditional critical behavior, while the other resembles a 'dream team' scenario, offering potential applications in the context of extreme events. multivariate analysis; however, its practical implementation is often hindered by
the difficulty in defining a depth function that is consistent with at least two
of its original dimensions. To overcome this limitation, our approach involves
using a point process that operates in a higher-dimensional space and then
utilizing a transformation to reduce the dimensionality back to the original space
while preserving the functionality of the depth function. Specifically, we
apply the isometric log-ratio transformation to a spatial point process that is
based on depth-based attractive interactions, resulting in a point process that
can effectively capture patterns of clustering in data. Furthermore, our
results also demonstrate the ability of this depth function to provide insight
into the underlying structure of the data by identifying groups of related
points. The proposed method is then tested on a variety of synthetic datasets and
shown to outperform alternative dimensionality reduction techniques. Finally, we
also illustrate its applicability to the analysis of a real-world dataset
consisting of locations of bird sightings in the Amazon rainforest. Monte Carlo simulations for lattice field theories rely heavily on Markov Chain Monte Carlo algorithms. These algorithms demand a reliable implementation to ensure scientific validity, yet theirs often lacks. The process of verifying an implementation's accuracy is termed'standardization'. This note aims to introduce the concept of standardization by examining the differences between various methods for solving the lattice fermion matrix, highlighting the advantages and disadvantages of each. It explores the criteria necessary to establish a reliable implementation and suggests a course of action for those seeking to standardize their own methods. Specifically, we focus on the bulk fermion mass regime and use a ferromagnetic lattice model as a simplified example to illustrate key concepts. We thoroughly investigate the bulk fermion mass regime, evaluating the impact of finite lattice effects. To facilitate this comparison, we create analytical predictions for key physical characteristics, incorporating the effects of irreducible fermion mass and lattice anisotropy. These predictions are based on mean field theory and the next-order high-temperature expansions. We comply with the principles of the Lattice Baryon Collation by maintaining transparency in our methods and making all code used in this study publicly accessible. We strongly encourage others to do the same. We advocate for a collective effort to establish a comprehensive set of standardized algorithms for lattice quantum field theories. These algorithms can be used for benchmarking and quality control, promoting consistency in published results. Ultimately, we strive to make the process of producing reliable numerical evidence more accessible and transparent. The likelihood of word appearances and inter-word spacings is found to be significantly influenced by the frequency of surrounding words. This discovery motivates our development of two novel approaches for structured text recognition. The first method, WordFavor, leverages contextual word probability to prioritize recognition results that align with regular expression-based word patterns. The High-Dimensional Ranking Lasso (HDR Lasso) is an important problem with extensive applications in data analysis and machine learning. It involves selecting key variables from a large dataset, denoted as $\mathcal{S}$, that directly correlates with target variables, using an l1-regularized ranking loss function. The HDR Lasso problem can be transformed into a sparse optimization issue by incorporating constraints on the l1-norm of $\mathcal{S}$, making it a sparse optimization problem with a continuous objective function and constrained variable $\mathcal{S}$. However, the original problem exhibits difficulties such as variable dependence, non-smoothness, and sparse optimization complexity, but these challenges can be overcome by leveraging the Adapt-Sie algorithm. This algorithm utilizes adaptive sieving to simplify the variable domain and stems from a blockwise coordinate descent method. The Adapt-Sie algorithm comprises three main components: (i) problem reformulation via Lagrange multipliers; (ii) variable pruning via Lagrange multiplier thresholding; and (iii) selected variable update via blockwise coordinate descent. The Adapt-Sie algorithm has been successfully applied to various sparse optimization problems and has exhibited superior performance and scalability on high-dimensional datasets compared to state-of-the-art methods. Consequently, the Adapt-Sie algorithm has shown great potential in solving the HDR Lasso problem and has been extensively validated on numerous real-world datasets, demonstrating its capacity to efficiently select valuable variables even in extremely large datasets. Moreover, the Adapt-Sie algorithm has been successfully implemented in an open-source software framework, AHS, and is now freely accessible for public use. These overlooked effects are essentially landfills for waste generated by the environmental benefits that AI is supposed to provide in the first place. Specifically, our article offers practical advice to AI researchers on creating environmentally friendly and sustainable technologies. We present these recommendations not only to mitigate the negative consequences of existing AI solutions, but also to guide future developments toward more sustainable and eco-friendly technologies. In the long run, our investigation seeks to contribute to developing artificial general intelligence that considers the environmental implications of its actions and decisions. We hope that our article will inspire a broader discussion on the environmental dimensions of AI technologies and promote eco-friendly and sustainable AI development. Over the past ten years, the approach of using multi-level verification systems to tackle complex verification problems has gained significant traction. These complex problems often arise in areas like software testing and biochemistry, and the multi-faceted nature of their verification process makes them particularly challenging. The concept of "stacking issues" has been introduced to describe problems requiring multiple layers of proof, and a key characteristic of such problems is the occurrence of verification conflicts, or contradictions arising within a proof structure as new information is added. Prior research identified a core set of stacking issues, and proposed a solution involving the application of kernelization to verify whether a given instance can be resolved through proof modification. In this paper, we explore kernelization in the context of stacking issues, and present new results demonstrating the computability of parameterized kernel sizes for two distinct parameterizations, as well as a parameterized kernel for one specific type of stacking issue, thereby resolving an open question initially posed by Bauland et al. in 2008. Furthermore, this research yields efficient kernel sizes for various problem instances, and the resulting kernels exhibit substantial reductions in size compared to the original problem instances, thereby providing a significant improvement. Specifically, we can derive kernel sizes with a linear or near-linear scale for verification problems involving regular expressions, context-free languages, and simple programs. Moreover, this research reveals that a parameterized kernel size of $O(n^{3.34})$ can be computed for the regular expression model, and even smaller kernel sizes of $O(n^{1.29})$ can be obtained under specific assumptions. Similarly, this parameterized kernel size of $O(n^{3.34})$ can also be obtained for the context-free model, and this result further demonstrates that a parameterized kernel size of $O(n)$ can be computed for the simple program model. Consequently, this research offers a parameterized kernel size that is merely $O(n)$ for a problem previously considered to be "difficult" in the context of program verification. Specifically, this result has been successfully applied in the verification of nested loops in C and Verilog programming languages. Furthermore, this research has been successfully tested on verification problems arising from the analysis of software systems, the study of RNA structures, the examination of proof sequences, the investigation of regular expressions, the analysis of context-free double pushdown systems, and the examination of simple programs. Additionally, this research has been successfully applied in the verification of program snippets that incorporate complex control flow mechanisms, such as recursion and jumps. In a scenario of global uncertainty, individuals tend to rely on available information and form opinions based on pre-existing beliefs, as evidenced by the persistence of structural inequalities across generations, despite shifting societal attitudes. As a result, opinions and actions become linked to established social hierarchies, and individuals with higher social standing and access to information exert greater influence over their decisions. This study develops a model combining opinion dynamics and a theory of structural equilibrium to illustrate how opinions and social structures interconnect. The proposed framework is then used to investigate the dynamics of opinions and actions in a society with a established social structure and a history of inequality, and the resulting analysis shows that diverse groups of individuals with varying social standing and information access can coexist, and that actions within each group become predictable and consistent due to the unique perspectives and values associated with each group's social class. Ultimately, this proposed framework is shown to be capable of emulating empirical observations and providing a potential explanation for the observed patterns of actions and opinions. We'll review contemporary developments in Chern-Simons matter theories, a type of chiral three-dimensional gauge theory, whose non-supersymmetric versions may hold key insights into universal relationships between gauge theories. Notably, recent breakthroughs in supersymmetric frameworks have revealed novel duality patterns, prompting speculation that similar connections might exist in non-supersymmetric contexts. Although non-supersymmetric dualities are inherently more fragile than their supersymmetric counterparts due to anomalies, research has shown that certain dualities can still hold in regimes with vanishing 't Hooft anomalies. This hope for non-supersymmetric dualities to mirror supersymmetric dualities under certain anomalies is the primary focus of this review. Following an introductory overview of Chern-Simons matter theories and gauge theory dualities, we'll delve into specific examples of chiral gauge theories that are thought to be dual to each other. We'll then examine how these dualities can be used to tackle intricate problems in quantum field theories, such as phase transitions and semimetals. Finally, we'll discuss the current state of research in non-supersymmetric dualities and possible future areas of investigation.

A linear complementary set of group codes is a collection of group codes with identical ranks and cyclic codes, whose direct sum equals the entire group algebra. We establish a fundamental property: any linear group code with a complementary group code achieves this linear complementary set property. Additionally, we present two distinct methods to construct such linear complementary sets. Firstly, we prove that for a finite field of Q elements, it is possible to find a linear group code of rank r to exponent q-1 in the group algebra G(algebraic over k), where G has order q^n, and a complementary group code of rank r when q is an odd number. Secondly, we demonstrate that for any finite principal ideal field of degree m to q-1, it is possible to find a linear group code of rank r to exponent q-1 in the group algebra G(algebraic over k) and a complementary group code of rank r. These results validate two conjectures proposed by Chen et al in 2021. Our work also finds an alternative proof to a theorem initially proven by Chen et al. Our findings enhance the current known bounds: for a finite field of Q elements, we can find linear group codes of rank r to exponent r to (q^(1/n)) m, and a complementary group code of rank r when r is a multiple of 2 and m is a multiple of 2; otherwise, a complementary group code of rank r can be found when r is a multiple of 2. These results are best-case scenarios that match the theoretical upper bounds. Our work also broadens the definition and linear complementary group codes properties to finite principal ideal fields and provides the equivalent results. Finally, a demonstration is provided showing that group codes can be used to build linear complementary group codes of rank 1 in the group algebra G(algebraic over k). We then present an example of such a code in the group algebra Q8(algebraic over k), where k is a finite principal ideal field of Q elements. Our work also finds an alternative proof to a theorem initially proven by Chen et al in 2021. Our findings enhance the current known bounds: for a finite field of Q elements, we can find linear group codes of rank 1 to exponent 1 to (q^(1/n)) m, and a complementary group code of rank 1 when r is a multiple of 2 and m is a multiple of 2; otherwise, a complementary group code of rank 1 can be found when r is a multiple of 2.

In graph-based modeling, the assignment problem is a critical task that can be defined as finding the optimal configuration of variable values that minimize a designated objective function, such as entropy or mean squared error. This objective function is often dependent on the model parameters and can be simplified using a function representation that captures the relationship between variables, allowing for more efficient computation of the assignment. This abstract represents the core concept of a novel approach that uses a function representation to quickly compute the mean squared error and other objectives, enabling a global search optimization method that evaluates all possible assignments, resulting in exact solutions for small problems and near-optimal solutions for larger ones. The sample consisted of 383 type 1 and 173 type 2 Active Galactic Nuclei from the SDSS catalog, each with narrow-band imaging of the surrounding host galaxy in u-g-r colors. By applying principal component analysis to these colors, we identified a primary mode of variation associated with the host galaxy's luminosity, as well as secondary and tertiary modes linked to the nucleus and dust emission. Notably, Seyfert galaxies tended to display more negative principal component scores than Quasars, indicating greater variability in nucleus-related modes. Additionally, type 2 Active Galactic Nuclei were found to score more negatively than type 1 Active Galactic Nuclei in the nucleus-related dimension, suggesting a role of dust in obscuring the nuclear emission. We observed a correlation between active galactic nucleus inclination angle and host galaxy mass-to-dynamical mass ratio, using the broad-line region's velocity decomposition and the host galaxy's spectral energy distribution to estimate inclination angle and mass-to-dynamical mass ratio, respectively. This association implies a closer relationship between active galactic nuclei and their surrounding host galaxies. Our study's findings are consistent with the hypothesis that active galactic nuclei draw material and energy from their surrounding interstellar medium, ultimately feeding back into the environment. This hertzprung-russell diagram like structure of active galactic nuclei offers a framework for understanding active galactic nuclei as dynamic components of a larger host galaxy context. This context may also be relevant to the microwave background anisotropy and the active galactic nuclei population at very large redshifts. Deep neural network training for computer vision tasks can benefit from pre-training techniques, especially when limited data is available. A common approach involves initially training a model to estimate depth from a single image, then utilizing the resulting weights as a starting point for segmentation tasks. Despite depth estimation's significance in this context, the process is often overlooked due to the assumption that classification tasks serve this purpose better. Nonetheless, we argue that depth estimation provides more relevant features for segmentation and propose an alternative solution where both strategies are simultaneously harnessed to estimate segmentation masks through a multi-task approach. We demonstrate the efficacy of this method by comparing it against the standard practice of pre-training classification models and show that depth-based pre-training yields better results in the absence of sufficient data. Additionally, we investigate the impact of varying training objectives and image synthesis techniques on the model's performance, revealing that a straightforward approach tends to perform better than more complex methods that divide tasks, multi-task training, and domain randomization. Consequently, we present a simple yet effective model that surpasses the state-of-the-art in semantic segmentation without domain adaptation, outperforming established baselines by a significant margin. The associated code can be found at https://github.com/asharakeh/depth_for_segmentation.

Generating coherent and interesting stories about time-series data has been a challenging task. Existing methods typically assume access to labeled data or require significant input from human narrators, including written summaries, selected segments, and preferred formats (e.g., narratives, anecdotes). Our goal is to create a narrative generator that can work with unlabeled data from various domains while using a narrators' inputs to tailor the stories. We began by analyzing over 120,000 narrations from the Anecdotes dataset and discovered four key components: (1) selecting relevant time-series segments, (2) describing their temporal relationships, (3) attributing temporal characteristics, and (4) narrating the story. We then leveraged these insights to develop TCube, a neural model that can create coherent stories using unsupervised time-series data. TCube achieves state-of-the-art results on Anecdotes, outperforming previous methods by 14% in narrative quality, according to automated metrics. Additionally, TCube enables personalized story generation when provided with human inputs, such as annotated segments, summarizations, or temporal relationships, which can be particularly useful in various real-world applications. Our source code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/asharakeh/TCube.

Developers often require additional resources from external platforms to supplement their knowledge, with many turning to Stack Overflow for solutions to their programming challenges. Understanding which external links are shared on Stack Overflow can aid in optimizing search engines for programmers, helping to identify relevant information on the internet related to commonly encountered programming issues. This study analyzes the prevalence of frequently shared external links on Stack Overflow, examining how often these links are referenced in questions and answers across different tags and platforms. Our investigation used a sample of 160,673 questions gathered through a random sampling of 20 different tags, with each sample containing at least 1,000 questions per tag. We then analyzed the shared links using a frequency distribution approach, focusing on the top 10 most frequently mentioned external links for each sample. After aggregating the results, we applied a correlation ranking method to identify common patterns across all samples. Our analysis shows that external links to well-known platforms such as GitHub, Wikipedia, and JavaScript Documentation are frequently referenced in Stack Overflow, with links to official documentation being the most commonly shared type. Interestingly, the top-ranked GitHub resources on Stack Overflow are primarily related to configuration, API, and README files. Our findings provide valuable insights for search engines, suggesting that prioritizing the indexing of these official documentation types and GitHub resources would be beneficial in optimizing their results for programmers, given their high frequency of sharing on Stack Overflow. Future work could further validate these findings through user surveys to verify that the shared links on Stack Overflow are indeed useful for resolving common programming challenges. Additionally, exploring the propagation of these frequently shared resources across other online platforms could further elucidate their origins and spread. On a broader scope, this study contributes to research in the computational spread of information, illustrating how online communities can shape the dissemination of digital information through their collective sharing behaviors. Ultimately, this digital information can then be leveraged by search engines to develop more informed searching strategies that take into account the social sharing behaviors of programmers. The data used for this study can be accessed through a public GitHub repository. The Stack Overflow data was obtained through a Dataset package, while the sampled data was shared via ZIP files. Our analysis is available on GitHub, with our study itself being published under the CC-BY license. The related research was conducted under the umbrella of activities covered by the permission.

Medical professionals need comprehensive information about patients to make informed decisions, but current technology struggles to obtain this data due to varying report writing styles. Traditional natural language processing methods rely on extensive datasets from a specific domain to learn and adapt, but such datasets are rare. A novel approach, domain generalization, enables learning universal patterns across different domains by training from multiple sources and ignoring domain-specific characteristics. Our research applies this method to extract symptoms and symptoms-related information from unstructured medical notes, demonstrating promising results with significant accuracy improvements, from 72.8% to 80.6%, 75.1% to 80.9%, and 70.4% to 76.1% in terms of F1-score, precision, and F1-score averaging recall and precision, respectively, using three large medical datasets. These results position our work as a pioneering achievement in the domain generalization field, particularly in the clinical natural language processing domain. Automated driving systems rely heavily on advanced driving techniques like steering bygone methods which are often plagued by slow convergence and inconsistent performance. This has led to a growing interest in Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) which offers a promising approach to developing high-quality automated driving systems. The core idea being that an intelligent agent can learn to navigate complex environments by interacting with their surroundings and adjusting their actions based on reward feedback. This results in self-learning controllers that adapt seamlessly to changing environments. However, implementing DRL effectively poses significant technical challenges which we aim to address in this study. The main contribution of this research is a novel DRL-based steering model which leverages an innovative combination of the Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) algorithm and a custom multi-step Markov Decision Process (MDP) model. This model enhances training efficiency by utilizing information from past experiences and offers a notable improvement in performance over state-of-the-art benchmarks. Moreover, we introduce a groundbreaking technique for sampling experience from driving videos that significantly boosts the model's generalizability. The efficacy of this model was evaluated in the Unity driving simulation platform and the results show notable improvements in performance and generalizability when compared to state-of-the-art benchmarks. Moreover, we demonstrate that the model is highly resilient to disruptions and adversarial attacks. Recent breakthroughs in neuromorphic hardware technology enable the development of energy-efficient spiking neural networks (SPNNs) capable of capturing task-specific computational patterns. However, accurately replicating deep convolutional neural networks (DCNNs) within SPNNs remains a significant challenge due to current deep neural networks' complex structures, which are beyond the feasible capabilities of current neuromorphic systems. To overcome this limitation, we present a novel deep SPNN architecture based on a multi-level hierarchical design, featuring localized full connection layers within the early stages to effectively capture low-level feature data. By combining reversible operations and an energy-efficient quantization technique, our approach achieves significant energy savings without compromising accuracy. Notably, the proposed network outperforms state-of-the-art SPNNs while reducing the parameter count by 81.12%. Furthermore, our results demonstrate a substantial energy saving of up to 87.16% while maintaining near-equal accuracy compared to the baseline DCNN model. To facilitate the deployment of our spiking model on real neuromorphic hardware, we also provide detailed instructions on converting the design to fit available VLSI chip constraints. Our work will likely inspire future research within this emerging field, paving the way for the development of highly efficient SPNNs capable of accurately replicating DCNNs. We analyze how temperature affects the mass-radius relationship of quark stars aligned in the same spin direction, in addition to the impact of a strong magnetic field, for various values of the magnetic field and the strange quark mass. Our findings show that as temperature increases, the mass-radius curve of the quark star shifts towards a more compact state, with the radius decreasing as the temperature rises. Introducing a strong magnetic field also alters the mass-radius relationship, resulting in a more pronounced effect when the magnetic field and temperature are at their highest levels. Furthermore, a higher strange quark mass leads to a more noticeable change in the mass-radius relationship due to temperature and magnetic field fluctuations. To gain deeper insights, we examine how temperature and magnetic field influence key thermodynamic properties, such as the adiabatic index, entropy per baryon, and heat capacity, revealing significant variations in these properties at high temperatures and strong magnetic fields. To summarize, our research highlights the substantial effects of temperature, magnetic field, and strange quark mass on the thermodynamic properties and mass-radius relationship of spin-aligned quark stars. These findings could provide valuable input for the investigation of exotic states of matter in compact objects using astrophysical methods.
