A new task-based computing paradigm is emerging, driven by decentralized networks of interconnected devices, including smartphones, tablets, TVs, and various types of embedded systems, which are increasingly accessible through web browsers on devices with sufficient processing capabilities. To take advantage of this opportunity, we was introduced Pando, a volunteer computing platform that leverages existing resources on devices to execute computationally intensive tasks. Unlike traditional peer-to-peer applications, Pando utilizes a novel approach based on remote procedure calls to facilitate interaction between a client's browser and a server, while also ensuring security through client-side assessment of worker integrity. Our current implementation demonstrates the feasibility of running compute-intensive applications on a diverse range of devices via a visual representation, showcasing the execution of parallel code on multiple browser instances and remote devices. Notably, the project's primary focus is on supporting scientific research and promoting the development of sustainable grids for volunteer computing purposes. To achieve this goal, we made available a set of useful functionality to the community, which can be accessed via a GitHub repository that contains the detailed documentation and source code required to contribute to the project. Furthermore, we successfully completed a series of benchmarks to evaluate the platform's performance across a wide spectrum of scenarios. Our experiments, which are outlined in a companion paper, highlight the potential of Pando to sustainably deploy compute-intensive applications on a large scale. Results show that the platform can significantly reduce deployment times and energy consumption by leveraging the collective power of diverse devices. In particular, our experiments demonstrate that Pando can deploy tasks up to 2.55 times faster than BOINC, the industry standard for volunteer computing, while also achieving energy savings of up to 10 times using equivalent resources. In particular, our analysis reveals that Pando's performance is primarily affected by the architecture of the client's browser and the available storage capacity, traits that are outside of the developer's control. Nonetheless, our study also uncovers several optimization strategies that could further enhance the platform's efficiency and open up new avenues for research in related areas. In conclusion, Pando is a groundbreaking initiative that empowers developers to create innovative applications, showcasing the immense potential of volunteer computing to sustainably leverage the collective computing power of diverse devices. Our analysis highlights numerous opportunities and challenges that could shape the future of this paradigm, while also demonstrating the feasibility of successfully deploying compute-intensive applications on a large scale using only standard web browsers. Machine learning models have become ubiquitous in science and industry but often struggle with a key interpretation challenge: understanding how inputs are combined to generate outputs. In particular, models like random forests and gradient boosted trees present a daunting interpretation task due to their intricate structure and massive numbers of trained trees, featuring numerous learned features and complex feature interactions. To tackle this issue, we introduce the attribution graph, a novel, simplified representation that clarifies how inputs contribute to outputs, taking into account various correlations between attributes. Furthermore, we develop a method to automatically identify key attribute connections and remove insignificant ones, effectively decomposing complex models into more manageable components. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach on multiple datasets and make our code available for public use. We believe this approach will contribute to better, more transparent decision-making in various applications. In federated learning, multiple parties collaborate on training a joint model by sharing local parameters across network segments. However, concerns arise over data owners' parameter updates being intercepted and manipulated by malicious entities during this process. To address this issue, we propose the concept of federated training within Trusted Execution Environments (TEEs), an approach we call flatee. Using TEEs, data owners train the model within a secure environment, and the FED average algorithm is executed within another to prevent malicious interference. We test this approach with PyTorch, a popular machine learning framework, and demonstrate its effectiveness through a real-world example involving horizontal federated training across vertical data partitions in MySQL. This framework offers data privacy protection and serves as a building block for more complex federated training applications. We gather and share key findings from our development process, including benchmarks and best practices, to aid other developers in incorporating TEEs into their workflows. This includes the benefits of utilizing MySQL for vertical data partitions and running multiple Batches of iterations within a single UE to boost overall performance. We believe our work has the potential to expand the reach of federated learning into data environments protected by TEEs, a previously underexplored area within the field of FL. Using Thistle, a Linux-based UE, we evaluate the performance of training a ResNet50 model using synthetic CIFAR10 data owned by 10 distinct entities and demonstrate that training in TEEs offers comparable results to training outside of it. This achievement marks a significant breakthrough in bringing FL into TEEs and shows that our approach has the potential to securely and efficiently protect sensitive data while training joint models. We will make our code available to the public so that other researchers can build upon our findings and explore the capabilities of flatee and TEEs in future developments. We test several scenarios, including multi-UAE training and multi-node communication, and uncover the performance limitations of training FL models within TEEs, primarily caused by network latency and data transfer delays. This research sheds light on the trade-offs between security and performance, and we identify key areas for improvement, including enhancing communication efficiency between multiple UEs and exploring alternative algorithms that could alleviate performance bottlenecks. Ultimately, our research opens the door for future research within this area by identifying potential challenges and highlighting areas that require further investigation. We propose several potential areas for future research, including the development of new FL algorithms tailored to TEE environments and investigations into the practical implications of employing FL within real-world data environments. The growing demand for embedded systems in various applications drives the need for efficient evaluation of embedded operators. We propose a novel approach for automated operator evaluation on embedded devices, primarily targeting development tasks. This method enables developers to swiftly assess and refine operators without the need to set up elaborate test environments, thus improving the productivity of embedded software development. For instance, when evaluating a JPEG decoder, instead of simply measuring decoding time, our approach allows developers to assess and compare different implementation options in terms of image quality metrics, such as peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR), with values ranging from 10 to 40. This measure provides valuable insight into each implementation variant and facilitates more accurate qualitative comparisons. We demonstrate the efficacy of this approach by evaluating several embedded image and video decoder implementations using various metrics. These evaluations show that, despite identical input and output, metric values can differ significantly between evaluations, emphasizing the importance of reliance on reliable and trustworthy measurement tools. All evaluation code, including the used image and video files, is openly accessible on GitHub for reproducibility purposes. Due to its cross-platform capabilities, this approach can be applied in a wide range of development contexts, extending beyond embedded systems to general programming tasks. Nonetheless, its primary intended application remains embedded system development. We identify two primary benefits of this approach, namely enhanced productivity and increased trust in evaluation results, with the latter stemming from process transparency, verifiable measurements, and full visibility of evaluation processes. We highlight several areas for further research and present open questions for the compiler, programming system, and decoder communities to address. Finally, we outline the potential for integration of our approach within existing embedded development tools and evaluate its compatibility with widely used development tools, including Keil, IAR, GCC, Eclipse, and Arm Mbed. This includes a step-by-step guide for seamless integration within Mbed. Compilation results for evaluating decoder implementations using various metrics are also provided. In particular, we demonstrate how to utilize the Mbed online platform for evaluating several decoder implementations under the same conditions, including metric PSNR with values ranging from 10 to 40. This illustrates the extensive potential of our approach for advanced evaluations in real-world embedded development tasks. All code for this paper is openly accessible on GitHub for reproducibility purposes. It includes a separate branch for Mbed compiler evaluation, showcasing its compatibility and efficiency in real-world development tasks. We eagerly look forward to addressing the presented research questions and contributing to further innovations in embedded system development. This research introduces Timeloops, a component that automatically generates system call policies for containerized microservices based on dynamic analysis. Containing a microservice within a container isolates it from system resources, but does not necessarily prevent malicious activities if system calls are not properly restricted. We present a learning framework in which a microservice's system call policy is discovered through dynamic analysis, effectively shielding sensitive system areas from access risks. We examine the efficacy of Timeloops in a benchmark test consisting of seven microservices from diverse domains, utilizing Linux namespaces and seccomp to shape a microservice's system call environment and define allowed call policies. We assess the reliability of Timeloops using various evaluation methods that analyze system call policies from different perspectives, including similarity, validity, and adaptability. We compare the system call policies learned by Timeloops with those created by security experts to determine similarities in different domains, highlighting the importance of verifying system call policies. We test the robustness of Timeloops in handling unexpected system calls and evaluate its performance using different benchmark microservices. We demonstrate that Timeloops effectively learns system call policies for microservices in various domains and can be an invaluable assistance to system administrators in managing and hardening containerized microservices. However, a thorough validation of system call policies is also necessary to ensure seamless operation and security of the system. Early research suggested that imposing strict non-sigmoidal mappings on neural networks could hinder their performance. Conversely, studies in Hadamard spaces and related theories imply that linear classifiers may be insufficient in curvilinear environments. This contradiction prompted an investigation into linear classification in more general, commodity space forms. Despite initial expectations, the research revealed that linear classification is indeed achievable in these spaces, with the outcome not necessarily dependent on the dimensionality of the data. Notably, a key discovery involved the creation of a metric-compatible partition in any commodity space, allowing for independent distance calculations within each partition set. Furthermore, the research established conditions under which linear classification becomes both necessary and sufficient. Although these findings may seem contradictory to existing theories, they actually provide a unified explanation for the outcomes of previous studies in Hadamard spaces. The research also identified new applications and hypotheses for future exploration. A comprehensive open-source library, including implementations of the proposed concepts, has been made available. In the vicinity of a supermassive black hole at the center of a galaxy, the black hole's gravitational influence grows gradually as the distance from its center decreases. Researchers have found that stars in this region can be organized into specific patterns, such as nearly circular orbits at farther distances and more elliptical orbits at closer distances. A 1970 study initially established that these stars are arranged in a specific order, with stars on more circular orbits appearing at greater distances, and this pattern becomes more distinct as the stars' orbital eccentricities decrease. Later studies built on this work, using new mathematical techniques and computer simulations to further analyze these arrangements. These studies used various mathematical tools, including special types of mathematics, to study the arrangements under different conditions. Notably, one study used computer simulations to explore the arrangements in a galaxy's disk-like shape, and it discovered that the arrangements change based on the direction from the black hole. Another study used computer simulations to explore the arrangements in a galaxy's plane, and it discovered that nearby stars can disrupt and shape the arrangements. A different study used computer simulations to explore the arrangements when the stars' motions are not symmetrical. Despite these advancements, recent work revisiting the original findings shows that previous studies were incorrect in certain assumptions and uses new mathematical techniques to rectify these errors. This work examines the arrangements using different mathematical approaches and finds that the arrangements are complex and difficult to break down into simpler components, requiring new and innovative mathematical strategies. As a result, the problem of understanding these arrangements remains complex and in need of further analysis. Based on recent work, future research should focus on using new mathematical approaches, such as topology and other forms of high-level mathematics, to study the arrangements. Additionally, future research should utilize computer simulations to explore these arrangements under different real-world conditions. It is hypothesized that utilizing these high-level mathematical approaches will provide new insights into the arrangements. Specifically, using these high-level mathematical approaches will allow researchers to make new connections between the ideas and other areas of study. To test this hypothesis, we propose a research project that utilizes these high-level mathematical approaches and explores these arrangements under different real-world conditions through computer simulations. This project will specifically investigate how the ideas can be applied to study other phenomena in astronomy. To do this, we will use various high-level mathematical approaches to study the arrangements and make new connections between the ideas and other areas of study. At the same time, we will also conduct a thorough examination of the arrangements using computer simulations, focusing on their behavior under different real-world conditions

This paper introduces a cutting-edge approach called sequential decision-making with learning, encompassing random model predictive control and adaptive cruise control. We begin with an overview of control theories such as reinforcement learning, adaptive control, and predictive control, highlighting random model predictive control as a innovative strategy. To illustrate its utility, we develop an adaptive cruise system utilizing random predictive control, incorporating learning techniques. Our approach results in reduced computational costs, eliminating the need for sparse parameterization and model simplification. Moreover, RMPCs can employ learned policies without the constraints of linear system models, demonstrating its efficacy in complex, high-dimensional systems. We showcase the performance of this method in an adaptive cruise setting, comparing its outcomes to those of traditional methods. Notably, RMPCs enable the deployment of learned policies from various reinforcement learning techniques, ultimately enhancing system safety with constraints-based control. This innovative method presents a novel solution for high-stakes, real-world autonomous driving systems, offering a promising future direction for autonomous vehicle development. We anticipate that RMPCs will serve as a bridge between autonomous vehicle systems and the deployment of learning methods, ultimately facilitating the adoption of this technology in life-critical systems. This paper explores a versatile method called compressive independent component analysis (CICA) that incorporates elements of compressive sensing and independent component analysis to analyze high-dimensional data with numerous sources and constraints on coherence. CICA is demonstrated to be effective in various scenarios, including a dimensional reduction technique that retains important features, a super-resolution method that estimates source statistics from sampled data, and a sparse component analysis (SCA) method that extracts individual signals through dictionary learning. To achieve these goals, CICA is shown to be a viable and efficient solution for analyzing data with restricted access to sources and samples. Furthermore, SCA is differentiated from existing methods and a theoretical guarantee is provided for its performance. Experimental results are presented to verify the efficacy of CICA and SCA in multiple applications. Additionally, a related method called compressive independent component analysis with constraints (CICAcon) is proposed, allowing for the inclusion of existing knowledge and learnable constraints to enhance the recovery of independent signals. We're examining a specific model known as the abelian quantum double, which is a lattice gauge theory built over a compact abelian group $G$. This theory features a set of unitaries called fluxes, associated with compact objects called plaquettes in the 2D plane, along with unitary transformations, linked to loops in the 2D plane, that act on the group $G$. The region-specific algebras formed from these fluxes and transformations share similarities with von Neumann algebras. These algebras, along with their morphisms, construct a category called $\mathcal{C}_{G,x}$. Our work focuses on evaluating the size of the morphism set within this category, denoted by $\text{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}_{G,x}}(I,\tilde{I})$, for two types of objects in the category: identity regions $I$ and regions $\tilde{I}$ shaped like a disk, all occurring in the abelian quantum double context. This investigation uses unitary couplings, which couple the group $G$ to its dual $\hat{G}$ via a map $\hat{F}$. Notably, the set of morphisms between these regions is shown to be equivalent to a group called the unitary quantum group $U_{G,x}\rtimes \text{Spin}^{+}G$. This result presents an interesting connection between the unitary quantum group and the abelian quantum double, which can be further applied to the study of topological orders. These studies aim to better understand the intrinsic properties of quantum double models, as well as other chiral topological orders, using algebraic and categorical techniques to analyze their underlying structure as a category. This work builds upon previous research, such as a study on the entire algebra of the abelian quantum double, using similar techniques to examine the size of the morphism set. This investigation also explores the category for more complex regions, such as a cylinder and a torus, using deformation techniques to examine the effects of deforming these regions and calculating the size of the morphism set for different shapes. These results present an interesting comparison with the findings for other chiral topological models, such as the free boson and free fermion models. These studies aim to clarify a disputed claim that the size of the morphism set for these topological orders is determined by the homotopy group of the region's 2-dimensional space. This investigation also examines the connections between these topological orders

This study presents a method to remotely control the movement of the LDV's laser beam, enabling a more efficient and widespread sampling of the two-dimensional space, using an automated and high-precision sample collection system. The research includes the implementation of a mathematical algorithm that allows the LDV to collect data from a two-dimensional grid, using the probe's limited capability to detect the velocity of particles within a specific zone. The study also showcases its results of which demonstrate the probe's ability to measure velocities in a fully two-dimensional space, rather than just a narrow section, successfully collecting over a hundred data points per second in a completely automated manner. In a test, the system's ability to collect data in both a grid and a rotating pattern was verified, showing its potential to be used in the study of turbulent flows and other complex systems where the LDV's high-resolution measurements are essential. The development of this automated system marks an important breakthrough in the high-resolution measurement of the velocity fields of turbulent flows and promises to contribute significantly to our understanding of these complex systems. We examine the spectra of theories that employ disjunction and existence operators, analyzing their dual relations and examining the implications of these relations for theory consistency. The dual relation in such theories behaves differently than in typical first-order logic, leading to inconsistencies when attempting to apply certain logic rules. Additionally, we demonstrate that the dual relation cannot be represented as a correspondence between models, and we discuss its comparison to other dual relations in the context of first-order logic. Finally, we investigate whether the introduction of quantifier operators could yield a meaningful dual relation. Specifically, we consider theories that include universal quantification and propose a novel definition for the dual relation in these theories. This definition maintains consistency and allows the treatment of model theory and algebraic theories equally. Furthermore, we highlight how this dual relation can be utilized to reconstruct various categories of first-order logic and algebra. Specifically, we show that the spectra of theories that include universal quantification can be utilized to define a category that is equivalent to the initial theory, and we identify specific cases in which this approach encompasses dependent type theory and algebraic varieties. Finally, we suggest potential areas for further research in this field. Rather than providing a comprehensive proof of a significant mathematical concept, this memo aims to provide an accessible introduction to the subject and its relationship to existing research in dependent type theory and algebraic varieties. The concept of utilizing an electrostatic or magnetic lens with a programmable phase disc has been proposed as a means to program the phase of electron beams in transmission electron microscopy. Investigating the potential of this idea to correct optical aberrations in a TEM is crucial for optimizing electron microscopy's capabilities. Through simulations based on the wave optics approach, we examine the effectiveness of implementing an electrostatic deflector with a programmable phase disc within the TEM. By modeling the phase disc as a series of rectangular barriers and using S-matrix theory to calculate electron wave transmission, we explore the interaction between beam phase and S-flag coefficients. These coefficients can be adjusted to achieve specific phase shifts, facilitating the implementation of an aberration corrector. However, our findings indicate that a phase-disc-based corrector may not be an efficient solution for the TEM, due to the constraints of available coil windings, which significantly limit its potential for correcting severe fifth-order astigmatism. Nevertheless, the concept of utilizing a programmable phase disc remains valuable for other applications where its unique characteristics can be fully utilized. One such possibility is its integration into an electron microscope-based spatial light modulator to explore new possibilities for optimizing electron microscopy and other wave-imaging techniques. Moreover, its innovative phase-disc design could be adapted into a TEM objective lens, even without programmability, to improve its stochastic aberration properties and serve as a crucial component in stochastic phase retrieval and other cutting-edge imaging methods. Ultimately, this study confirms that utilizing a phase-disc-based lens for aberration correction in the TEM is not feasible, but rather a stepping stone to more promising technologies. On the other hand, its advanced design could still contribute to optimizing existing imaging technologies and facilitate novel applications. Additionally, its findings can be utilized as a useful guide in evaluating the potential of similar concepts, such as wavefront control in scanning microscopes, and propose alternative solutions for realizing aberration correction. To achieve this, our study employs not only wave optics simulations but also analytical modeling based on the weak-scattering approximation, revealing that while certain concepts, such as phase-disc-based modulation of electron waves, hold promise, others may struggle with efficiently modulating sufficient electron waves to achieve effective beam control. Through this comprehensive analysis, this report provides a detailed assessment of the possibilities and limitations of wavefront control, leading to accurate predictions and recommendations for future research. Continuous conversation speech synthesis has remained challenging due to variations in speaking styles and contexts. Current systems are typically confined to their training data and fail to adapt to new situations, which is a critical shortcoming. Our proposed method, MaskedDialog, addresses this limitation by leveraging a masking technique to generate unseen conversation segments by learning from the properties of spoken language, particularly the relationship between spoken words and their surrounding context. To further enhance our model's performance, we developed a custom objective function, the Conformance Conformance Penalty ( CCP), which measures the adherence to spoken language characteristics based on spoken words, their adjacent context, and the speaker's overall conversation context. Our findings indicate that atomic translations along the mirror's normal axis can stimulate electromagnetic radiation, albeit this effect is substantially diminished by the mirror's slenderness. Conversely, atomic movements perpendicular to the mirror give rise to particle-like waves emitting radiation over a broad spectrum, with photon statistics exhibiting non-classical behavior and Poincaré symmetry in momentum space. Notably, the non-classical behavior persists even when the atom is in close proximity to the mirror's edge. In the relatively under-studied region of a star cluster called Westerlund 2 in the constellation of Norma, a large group of large stars, including red supergiants and yellow hypergiants, has been discovered. Utilizing data from the VISTA survey of the Magellanic Clouds, the team identified 94 potential red supergiant stars and 15 yellow hypergiants within a 150 parsec area around Westerlund 2. Notably, these luminous stars are not concentrated around the cluster's center but instead spread out across a vast area. The presence of 23 paired stars, potentially linked to binary systems, was also detected, including 6 pairs that display striking spectral features. The abundance of these large stars in this particular area suggests that the cluster is relatively young, estimated to be around 1 million years old, and in a stage of pre-main-sequence cluster development. However, the presence of multiple large stars also raises questions about whether these stars originated within the cluster due to supernovae explosions that formed them. Further analysis using the cluster's Turn-Off point revealed that these large stars are inconsistent with the expected distribution based on their mass. The most effective way to explain these findings is through binary interactions that can create these massive stars through mass transfer and/or runaway collisions. Improving text readability in scanned historical documents is essential, yet difficult due to various distortion types during the scanning process, including perspective distortion, which alters the document's shape, making further analysis challenging. Albeit perspective distortion is the most visible, other distortion types such as bias, scaling, and shear distortions also exist, although they are harder to recognize. In an attempt to overcome these challenges, a new text enhancement framework is proposed, aiming to rectify all distortion types and enhance text readability through an adversarial multi-task network. The framework consists of a text recognition module, an adversarial generator module, and a discriminator module, working together to refine captured images and improve text readability through an adversarial process. The proposed framework is tested using the IIIT Delhi CDIP dataset and achieves notable results, outperforming existing methods in text readability and perspective correction. Moreover, the framework demonstrates the ability to utilize deep learning models effectively in text enhancement tasks. As a result, the framework contributes to the development of more efficient text extraction algorithms in historical documents captured from various angles. Indonesia's vast and diverse population necessitates ID document extraction for various legal and unofficial purposes, such as opening social media accounts. Despite the importance of this task, existing solutions fail to account for the nation's most widely used ID cards, the Kartu Tanda Penduduk (KTP). This study presents a novel approach that leverages the integration of Optical Character Recognition (OCR) and Natural Language Processing (NLP) to accurately extract key information from KTPs. Our proprietary OCR-free method utilizes NLP to pinpoint and extract vital details from scanned or photographed KTP images. Additionally, we developed an analysis of the extracted information to validate its accuracy and consistency. This study showcases the efficacy of NLP-based extraction over traditional OCR techniques, demonstrating a 97% success rate in extracting information from KTP images without OCR. Furthermore, we developed an innovative 12-step analytical framework to verify the extracted information, showcasing the capabilities of NLP to supplement OCR techniques. This research has significant implications for both official and unofficial purposes in Indonesia, including verifying user information for social media platforms. The proposed solution can be readily applied to other countries with extensive and diverse populations, including Mexico, Brazil, and India, using similar NLP techniques. The source code for this project has been made publicly available on GitHub at https://github.id/ID-KTP-Extractor. Furthermore, a web-based application demonstrating the proposed solution has been deployed on Heroku at https://id-card-extractor.herokuapp.com. Colorizing black and white images has become a fully inverse problem that can reconstruct a roughly accurate color image from grayscale data assuming the sRGB color space and a specific color profile. However, fully inverse problems often yield low-resolution output images due to the limited information in grayscale data. In the case of vintage astronomical photographs, not only are they grayscale but they also frequently suffer from noise, degradation, and variability in exposure and field of view. These issues make the fully inverse problem approach more challenging for applying color to astronomical images. To tackle these limitations, we have developed a generative adversarial network (GAN) model that takes grayscale images as input and produces a high-resolution colorized image in the AB color space commonly used in astronomy. By incorporating techniques like residual learning, batch normalization, and Leaky ReLU, we achieved a low reconstruction error rate of 1.14 and a high PSNR of 34.08 for our colorized images. By comparing our method with other output enhancement techniques, we found that PsnrEnhance and FSR produced the lowest PSNR and Sam 2.0 the highest Sam score while Colorize the lowest Sam score. These results demonstrate that our GAN-based approach is the most effective at colorizing and enhancing astronomical images. To verify the performance of our model, we tested it on well-known astronomical images and obtained a 90% subjective approval rate from professional astronomers. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first application of GANs to vintage astronomical photographs. We have released the open-source code for this project at https://github.com/LePhanTran/Astronomical_PCA_Colorization. We propose a novel approach to determining the architecture of a neural network, drawing on the universal estimation theorem. This method enables us to calculate an optimal activation function for each layer of the network, thereby maximizing its non-linearity, in much the same way that the Jacobian is used to maximize non-linearity in traditional optimization techniques. Unlike conventional methods that rely on trial and error or gradient-based backpropagation, this approach allows us to isolate complexities in different layers, thereby reducing overfitting by controlling the overall complexity of the network. Furthermore, we have found that the proposed method performs consistently better than existing architectures, and excels in a wide range of complex prediction tasks. Notably, we have observed significant improvements in tasks such as image classification and language modeling. In addition to its superior performance, the new method is also highly scalable and can be used to analyze and optimize very large neural networks that are beyond the scope of conventional methods. In total, we have evaluated the proposed approach on 32 different datasets, and consistently found that it outperforms existing architectures. In particular, we have found that the proposed method can achieve up to 25.5% better performance in tasks such as image classification, and as much as 30.0% better performance in language modeling tasks. In contrast to conventional wisdom that additional layers result in better performance when applied to tasks such as image classification, we have found that the proposed method can achieve similar or better performance using fewer layers, thereby reducing computational costs. Specifically, we have observed that a 2-layer neural network using the proposed method can achieve similar or better performance in image classification tasks when compared to a 4-layer neural network using conventional methods. In total, we have evaluated the proposed approach on over 40 different datasets, and consistently found that it outperforms existing architectures while reducing computational costs. In particular, we have observed that a 2-layer neural network using the proposed method can achieve up to 30.0% better performance in tasks such as language modeling, and as much as 25.0% better performance in image classification tasks while reducing computational costs by over 2x when compared to a 4-layer neural network using conventional methods. We are developing a cognitive artificial intelligence (AI) framework called CogAI, which enables large-scale cooperative learning between human and robots in complex, big-data environments. This cooperation involves both agents learning from each other's experiences. CogAI consists of three layers: strategic decision-making, interactive learning, and external data analysis. The first layer uses machine learning to make informed decisions based on past experiences, the second layer applies reinforcement learning to adjust strategies through trial and error, and the third layer uses deep learning to annotate and classify environmental data in real-time. This annotation process improves both agents' understanding of their environment by learning from each other's feedback, ultimately enhancing CogAI's ability to make informed decisions and overcome obstacles. We are currently implementing this system using standardized technologies such as ROS, Kubernetes, and Kubernetes Persistent Volumes, which enables us to access CogAI from anywhere and use external tools to support decision-making. This approach combines AI-powered decision-making with human input from various external sources, including cognitive computing services, to create a collaborative learning environment. In this paper, we outline our high-level strategy for multi-agent cooperative learning and describe the key components of CogAI. We also present preliminary results of our implementation, which demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in complex, large-scale, high-mobility scenarios. We will continue to develop CogAI to address challenges in human-robot collaboration, such as autonomous decision-making, robot navigation, and feature extraction using computer vision and machine learning. For instance, we are planning to apply deep learning techniques to analyze environmental features and develop robotic navigation strategies based on learned patterns and predictions. This research is part of a broader effort to advance cognitive computing and create a collaborative learning environment that extends beyond robots to include other devices, such as drones, vehicles, and sensory equipment. In the future, we will leverage this approach to develop more sophisticated robotic systems that can learn and adapt in a variety of challenging environments. For example, we will demonstrate a drone swarm that can autonomously navigate and coordinate their mobility in a large-scale, outdoor setting, which will be presented in a companion video. A new bias-corrected estimator has been created for the mean of the absolute differences between a median-regressed variable and the median of another variable, under specific model assumptions. This proposal addresses the challenge of performing median regression analysis with a non-parametric approach, which often suffers from biased results. Unlike existing bias-reduced estimators that assume a parametric model, this novel estimator can operate in the absence of specific parameter values, such as the slope and covariance matrix. Instead, it relies on consistent estimates of these parameters, such as those obtained from a within-group estimator like the within-groups least squares method. The asymptotic correctness and efficient rate of convergence of the proposed estimator have been established, along with a recommendation for its use in practice, including the choice of bandwidth. A series of numerical experiments have been conducted to evaluate its performance under different scenarios. Finally, this proposal is further demonstrated through an analysis of real-world data from the Consumer Expenditure, Microcode 5-Level Balance Survey conducted by the Bureau of Labor Statistics. The results show that the proposed estimator can provide a more accurate representation of data when examined through absolute deviations around the median of expenditure levels. The associated computer code for this study is available online via the repository GitHub: https://github.com/yangchunli bias_reduced_mrd. The task of Relation Extraction aims to extract information about relationships linking two entities, which is a crucial task for constructing knowledge graphs from unstructured text. Traditionally, models focused solely on extracting relation information have struggled to leverage the vast knowledge graphs datasets available, limiting their effectiveness. In contrast, models trained on knowledge graphs data can improve Relation Extraction by cross-training, as demonstrated in various studies. To optimize cross-training, this paper introduces a novel task, Knowledge Graph Link Prediction, and proposes a dual-training approach, where models are simultaneously trained on both Relation Extraction and Knowledge Graph Link Prediction to maximize performance. Evaluations on five datasets have shown a significant enhancement in models' abilities, achieving state-of-the-art results in nearly all cases, and providing actionable insights into the best practices for dual-training in future research. The source code and generated knowledge graphs are available on GitHub at this link: https://github.com/alec-1992/KGLP. Experimental evidence on additional datasets confirms the validity of the proposed approach, underscoring the potential for wide application in various NLP tasks. While recurrent neural networks have shown excellence in modeling complex sequential data, their widespread adoption has been hindered by difficulties such as vanishing gradients and grammatization instability. Our proposed Modulated Recurrent Activation module, a variant of the recurrent neural network, aims to improve local functional representation by incorporating multi-scale features and flexible modulation of contractive transformations. By incorporating an inverse gain mechanism and utilizing a dynamic contraction matrix, we can bypass traditional constraints like the Eliott limit and the Lipschitz constraint, enabling more agile modeling of sequential data with variable lengths. Our innovative design of the Modulated Recurrent Activation module has several key benefits, including enhanced performance, improved generalizability, and the ability to generate synthetic data that mimics real-world distributions. Ultimately, our detailed analysis demonstrates that the Modulated Recurrent Activation module can serve as a valuable building block for a variety of machine learning applications. Specifically, we utilized the Modulated Recurrent Activation module to develop novel sequence generation, classification, and denoising models, all of which outperformed existing benchmarks. Our work has also been accompanied by a comprehensive open-source repository that enables other researchers to access and utilize our code, data, and experimental protocols. Additionally, our pre-trained models can be downloaded at https://www.astro.iutmontp.edu/~shawnmikel14/modulated-recurrent-activation-models. A detailed description of our data can be found at https://github.com/shawnmikel14/modulated-recurrent-activation-data. Our understanding of how high-resolution virtual reality (VR) affects perception is limited, particularly with regard to the concept of shadow aspect. This study explores the notion of shadow aspect in relation to VR, examining its application to the analysis of perceptual alterations in immersive environments. The proposed framework is grounded in the ideas of Maurice Merleau-Ponty and Jean Baudrillard, and involves applying the principles of hyperreality to the context of VR experiences. By examining how hyperreality influences user perceptions and interactions with VR, this framework seeks to contribute to the development of more immersive and interactive digital environments that better reflect the complexities of human experience. The full text of this paper has been published in the proceedings of the 2021 International Conference on Philosophy, Technology, and Society, hosted by the University of Maine. The authors would like to express their gratitude to the organizers for providing the opportunity to present their work. The current version of this paper has been updated to reflect the discussions that took place during the conference.

High-mass binaries are considered the primary source of runaway stars and massive runaways.  Studies of stellar core formations have shown that binary creation is influenced by cores' angular momentum, mass, and magnetic properties.  Most research has focused on cores with fixed properties, neglecting the dynamic processes of core formations.  This study employs two numerical tools to simulate mass growth in rotating cores and binary creation, taking into account a control simulation without magnetic effects for comparison.  The results show that increasing systems' mass leads to a shift from unequal mass binaries to equal mass binaries, in contrast to a study using cores with fixed properties which showed a decline in equal mass binaries with rising mass.  The binary creation efficiency also increases with total mass in systems both with and without magnetic effects, although magnetic effects impede binary creation in this system.  Binary properties show little correlation in terms of mass ratio, semimajor axis, and magnetic effects, with most binaries falling into the mass ratio range of 0.1 to 0.5.  The system's efficiency in creating binaries is unaffected by magnetic effects or core mass loss.  Magnetic effects have little impact on binary creation and do not alter core's rotation rates.  Binary creation in this system is completed at a stage that precedes the creation of third system members, which requires additional dynamic processes.  Future research should be focused on mass accumulation in stellar cores, as their formation dynamics have a notable impact on the resulting binary systems.  The study also lays the groundwork for investigating runaway star creation, with the binary creation process already showing some similarities. This research outlines advancements made to the M-ar-K-Rapid ICA algorithm to improve its effectiveness in solving independent component analysis problems. Initially based on the fastICA method, the modification involved incorporating the optimization techniques of adaptive regularization and multi-stochastic gradient descent to enhance its convergence and reliability. Extensive evaluations using the ANI repository of synthetic data and the DIPCO dataset containing real EEG signals revealed that the modified algorithm outperformed the original fastICA in over 90% of cases, while also demonstrating greater stability and performance consistency. Furthermore, comparisons with other state-of-the-art algorithms from the BISA repository confirmed that the modified M-ar-K-Rapid ICA algorithm consistently produced better results. Interestingly, our analysis also showed that the original fastICA, although less effective, still demonstrated better performance when used to analyze real EEG data compared to other top-performing algorithms from the BISA repository. Building on these findings, we validated the efficacy of our modification by successfully separating mixed EEG signals into individual channels using the modified M-ar-K-Rapid ICA algorithm. Specifically, we applied the algorithm to a set of six signals, which it accurately separated in under 10 milliseconds, thus verifying its potential for in-depth brain signal processing applications. Given its improved performance, stability, and rapid processing capabilities, we propose the modified M-ar-K-Rapid ICA algorithm as an efficient solution for ICA problems in fields such as neuroscience and bioinformatics. With further optimization, this algorithm may also be suitable for real-time ICA applications in clinical and industrial settings. To confirm these results and facilitate future reproducibility efforts, we publicly hosted the modified M-ar-K-Rapid ICA algorithm on GitHub under an open-source BP license agreement. We have also made the ANI repository of synthetic data and the DIPCO dataset containing real EEG signals available for download on our GitHub page for further research and validation. Additionally, we documented our method in an academic report filed with the IEEE Data Port repository under the reference "RP-2022-ICT001". We would like to express our gratitude to Dr. Peter Tino for his guidance and support throughout this research project, as well as the ANI repository authors who made their data available for download. We also appreciate the feedback and suggestions from Dr. Piotr Wojciechowski and other reviewers who helped improve the quality of this research. We hope that our results will contribute positively to the fields of ICA and signal processing. Please feel free to contact us via our email addresses for any further discussion or collaboration opportunities.

This discovery indicates that the domain's class does not depend on its equivalent class $\mathcal{E}(\sigma)$. Additionally, we derive a condition for domains that belong to the class $\mathcal{E}(\sigma)$, given a finite number of points. This leads to a new infinite family of domain separations, where each separation is associated with a distinct value of $\sigma$. If we assume the continuity hypothesis, we find a set of real numbers $(\sigma_i)_{i\geq 1)$ such that the associated domains are in class $\mathcal{E}(\sigma_i)$, allowing us to explore the properties of such a sequence. In computer science, program verification relies on formal methods to confirm that programs produce accurate outputs for all possible inputs, based on predefined specifications. However, these specifications often fail to account for the program's actual purpose, due to the challenge of formalizing natural language into verifiable code. To address this issue, we introduce a new method, called Framework, which enables the efficient creation of specifications from a program's high-level description, allowing for the reuse of existing specifications through framework composition. Framework consists of two primary components: (1) template specifications, created using a formal language with provenance, and (2) specifications of framework frameworks, which can be composed to produce new specifications. To facilitate this process, we also develop a Framework Studio, consisting of (1) a specification editor and (2) a reasoner, which uses dependency analysis to guide the verification of composed specifications. Ultimately, our approach successfully verifies complex programs, including a custom sorting algorithm and a public key encryption system, utilizing Framework specifications composed from multiple templates. Additionally, we demonstrate the versatility of Framework by showcasing its application in verifying existing proof frameworks, including Isabelle/HOL and Coq, using Framework. Furthermore, we show that Framework can be used to create efficient and efficient specifications for complex algorithms, including a custom sorting algorithm and a public key encryption system, using Framework specifications composed from multiple templates. To evaluate Framework, we performed a set of experiments, comparing its performance to Isabelle/HOL and Coq, demonstrating its versatility and efficiency in verifying a range of complex algorithms. In particular, we found that Framework outperformed Isabelle/HOL and Coq in verifying each of the following algorithms: (i) custom sorting algorithm, (ii) public key encryption system, and plain Newton's method, verifying over 1000 lines of code in each case. These results highlight the effectiveness and efficiency of Framework in supporting a wide range of complex algorithm verification. To facilitate this evaluation, we also developed a set of tools, including (1) a specification generator and (2) a verification launcher, allowing Framework to easily be applied to verifying existing proof frameworks and verifying new algorithms. In particular, we show that Framework can be used to verify (i) custom sorting algorithm, (ii) public key encryption system, and plain Newton's method, verifying over 1000 lines of code in each case. These results illustrate the versatility and efficiency of Framework in supporting a wide range of complex algorithm verification. To conclude, we believe that Framework provides an innovative and efficient approach to formal method tools

Incidents such as accidents, fires, and riots generate considerable online attention in the form of social media posts, with users often providing location and time information via hashtags. We have developed an approach to process and analyze social media incident reports in real-time, enabling the identification of incidents across multiple locations at the same time. This is because users may post updates about the same incident from different locations by switching between accounts or devices. Our method involves accurately estimating the incident location and time, filtering out redundant and duplicate reports, and grouping relevant posts together. We evaluated this approach using a dataset of Sydney New Year's Eve tweets and found that it enabled the detection of incidents across 15 distinct locations with less than 10 minutes latency. This capability has several practical applications, including instantaneously identifying incidents such as riots, terrorist attacks, and natural disasters reported on social media and verifying users' safety following events such as earthquakes and hurricanes. Furthermore, this approach can be used to improve location estimation accuracy by resolving ambiguities caused by users switching between accounts or devices. It can also be employed in applications such as traffic monitoring, air quality analysis, and environmental pollution by detecting incidents such as smog and traffic jams on social media. Additionally, this methodology can be used to select relevant photos for incident-related posts by grouping Incive-related tweets together and reducing latency. We plan to make the code for this approach publicly available. It will be implemented as a cloud-based service enabling users to input query locations, times, and topics and retrieve associated tweets in real-time. This service will offer multiple deployment options, including a web interface, streaming APIs, and SDKs for integration with other applications. With its real-time capabilities, this approach outperforms existing methods in several areas, including micro-blogging, photo sharing, and location-based social networking. It has several novel features such as real-time incident detection, low latency, and instantaneously identifying incidents, which set it apart from other methods in this area. More broadly, this research contributes to the emerging field of instant analytics that enables rapid processing and analysis of rapidly evolving events on social media. It has far-reaching applications in breaking news, trending topics, and real-time research, and can be applied to various domains such as news, events, and social media. We evaluated the performance of this approach using metrics such as precision, recall, F1 score, latency, and incident detection across multiple locations. The results show that our method outperforms state-of-the-art techniques in precision, recall, F1 score, latency, and incident detection

Currently available statistical tools such as the power spectrum and bispectrum show limitations in capturing certain cosmological properties and non-Gaussian patterns that can be identified through the cross-correlation of cosmic microwave background (CMB) data with large-scale structure (LSS) surveys. To address this constraint and enable a more comprehensive exploration of the LSS-CMB cross-correlation at a smaller scale, we have developed an automated and rapid approach to examine potential distortions in the CMB bispectrum. This innovative method utilizes a pre-computed bispectrum database to compare observed distortions with those predicted using cosmological models at a faster rate than possible through standard analytical methods. A key advantage of this approach is that it allows for a more straightforward evaluation of model assumptions against observed data, without the need for time-consuming computational simulations. We have successfully applied our method in a search for a previously identified non-Gaussian distortion effect known as the "alignment effect" in the cross-correlation data shared by Planck and DES datasets. Although our analysis of these specific datasets did not yield statistically significant evidence for the alignment effect at a $2\sigma$ confidence level, our method's speed and adaptability make it suitable for use in analyses involving a wider range of datasets, such as those involving other LSS surveys like DESI and LSST. Furthermore, our method's versatility allows for its potential application in various observational constraints such as those derived from quasars via QSO-CMB cross-correlation and those expected from future galaxy surveys, enabling researchers to better understand the properties of these cosmological objects. To fast-track future analyses, we have made our code and bispectrum database publicly available at a designated repository. We are open to collaborations that can further enhance our method, taking into account multiple approaches such as using machine learning algorithms and future improvements in computational speed through GPU utilization. We look forward to the joint efforts of fast and creative researchers worldwide. To this effect, we are proposing two specific research directions that can accelerate our method: utilizing machine learning algorithms to develop more streamlined models that can be directly compared with observed data, and exploiting the speed-enhancing capabilities offered by modern GPU architectures to accelerate our analysis routine. We believe that by harnessing these innovative possibilities, we can significantly enhance our method and make it an even more efficient and powerful tool in the hands of researchers. We look forward to the exciting advancements that can be achieved through these efforts. Recent research has examined the reliability of machine learning models against malicious attacks, involving an adversary who provides labeled data while hiding its true origin to deceive the model into ignoring opposing inputs. We explore a novel framework that utilizes Bayesian uncertainty measurement to quantify adversarial influence and maintains model reliability in the face of potential deception. Through verification, we establish that Bayesian posterior convergence and consistent training data contribute to detecting an adversarial attack. Furthermore, we derive conditions for detecting high-entropy inputs and develop a method to identify multiple simultaneous attacks. We also propose an algorithmic approach to remove adversarial influence and recover the genuine data, using a wave-like process known as the wave gradient algorithm. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework through experiments involving digital image classification. We successfully removed adversarial influence in complex images and recovered the underlying patterns, outperforming traditional non-robust Bayesian models. Additionally, we created an adversarial training program to enhance the robustness of Bayesian models, yielding superior outcomes compared to state-of-the-art adversarial training methods. Our work provides a comprehensive approach to maintaining reliable machine learning models in the presence of malicious attacks and recovering the underlying data while removing adversarial influence. We publicly release the code for this research at https://github.com/steveninman/BayAdversarial.

In early 2020, China experienced an unprecedented coronavirus outbreak coinciding with the Lunar New Year, a major holiday characterized by significant travel among the nation's 1.4 billion people. This context fostered the rapid dissemination of rumors regarding the epidemic, which spread rapidly online. This study aims to analyze the propagation dynamics of these rumors within China, particularly in major metropolises, by leveraging a novel dataset comprising 590 verified rumors collected from popular social media platforms Baidu Tieba and Baidu Zhidao. A proprietary dissemination mechanism is proposed to categorize these rumors into four types, based on their online discussion threads, and evaluate their spread across different regions, tempo, and impact using spatiotemporal rumour propagation curves. The analytical framework allows for comparative assessments of rumour dissemination in major Chinese cities, including Beijing, Shanghai, Shenzhen, and Chengdu, and reveals distinct patterns observed in online forums, particularly in Tieba discussions, which show a notable increase in rumour propagation in smaller cities. Furthermore, this study employs spatial analysis and heat maps to identify popular rumour themes and gauge their spread across Chinese provinces, revealing that north-eastern provinces experienced the highest rumour propagation rates. Notably, Tieba forums exhibited higher rumour dissemination than Zhidao forums, and rumour propagation in major cities surpassed that in smaller towns. The COVID-19 pandemic provided a unique backdrop to this research, allowing us to quantify the impact of public health crises on online misinformation. Ultimately, this study offers a framework for disseminating and assessing the spread of rumours, particularly in the context of public health emergencies. Various strategies are proposed to mitigate the rapid dissemination of rumours in China, centred around the swift action of social media platforms, fact-checking initiatives, and public awareness campaigns led by government agencies and key opinion leaders. Given their success in containing the pandemic, these measures could be replicated to address similar crises in the future. It might be useful for understanding the spread of misinformation in public health crises and similar events in the future. Additionally, the research code is available on a public repository. In a practical scenario involving pixel classification from hyperspectral images, reducing the number of spectral dimensions can lead to improved computational efficiency and effectiveness. However, this decrease also results in incomplete spectral data and subsequently affects classification performance. To minimize classification errors when limited spectral data is utilized, an optimal approach must be implemented. Various methods exist for dimensionality reduction in such images, including Principal Component Analysis (PCA), which is widely used due to its simplicity and effectiveness. Our study examines the impacts of reducing spectral dimensions using PCA on classification accuracy when using built-in hyperspectral image classification methods in ENVI/IDL. Different dataset sizes were tested to evaluate the interactions between dimensionality reduction and classification methods, and our results show that PCA's effect on accuracy varies depending on the dataset and method employed. When a dataset is relatively small and limited spectral data is used, certain classification methods are insensitive to dimensionality reduction. Our findings provide guidance on the suitable application of dimensionality reduction techniques to minimize classification errors when limited spectral data is utilized. Additionally, our research demonstrates the potential for kernel methods to be used with large datasets and spectral data to achieve the most favorable results. Our work contributes to the ongoing research in remote sensing dimensionality reduction, and our analysis serves as a reference for practitioners seeking to reduce dimensional spectral data while minimizing classification errors. Finally, our codes and associated datasets are available for download at https://github.com/Azahray/HRPI-DDR. This repository can be accessed by the public for their use and benefit.

Recent advancements in natural language understanding have been fueled by sizeable pre-trained language models, including T5 and RoBERTa. However, these models have been found to unnecessarily incorporate vocabulary and learn unnecessary contexts, hindering their general applicability and effectiveness in tasks with limited data. This study presents a novel method of model reduction by leveraging the inherent hierarchical structure of language, enabling it to identify and prioritize crucial words and phrasal units. Our approach adapts an existing pruning technique, incorporating additional hierarchical language insights to effectively remove secondary words and phrasal components. Hierarchical language understanding is implemented through the establishment of word and phrase-level knowledge graphs, incorporating concepts from NLP and NLU. Our model reduction approach is then applied and evaluated on four distinct natural language tasks: machine translation, question-answering, sentiment analysis, and text classification, using a recently introduced tool that enables the efficient model reduction process. Notably, our models achieved a level of performance comparable to that of the base model, demonstrating state-of-the-art results in all evaluated tasks. Additionally, our reduced language models exhibited a remarkable reduction in size, spanning from 15% reduction in the case of T5 to as much as 85% reduction in the case of RoBERTa. Our reduced models also displayed a notable increase in their inference speed, achieving a notable acceleration of 30% in the case of T5 and as much as 60% in the case of RoBERTa. Our model reduction approach has been made openly available for the benefit of the NLP community at https://github.com/psardes/pruning. Furthermore, the open-source tool enabling the efficient model reduction process has been jointly developed by Google and Facebook researchers, details of which can be found in our companion paper. Our model reduction approach has been successfully applied and evaluated on six distinct BERT-based models, achieving reductions in model size spanning from 15% reduction in the case of BERT to as much as 70% reduction in the case of BART. Notably, our reduced models also achieved a notable increase in their inference speed, achieving a notable acceleration of 30% in the case of BERT and as much as 50% in the case of BART. A widely employed method for refining protein structures with high accuracy involves readjusting atomic positions based on the analysis of NMR data in a process called molecular dynamics refinement, yet it fails to account for the atomic electronic environment. A new way to improve protein structures has been developed, involving the adjustment of protein coordinates using quantum-mechanical calculations of amide proton chemical shifts, allowing for the direct comparison of predicted and experimentally measured values. This new approach has been successfully tested on a set of 18 high-resolution protein structures and has shown notable agreement between predicted and actual results for 25 commonly occurring amide proton environments. The development of this method has enabled the validation of refined protein structures using quantum-based predictions of amide proton shifts, thereby providing more accurate electronic information. The validation process has also revealed the validity of empirical chemical shift prediction methods that are commonly used for protein structure refinement, thereby confirming their reliability. These libraries can be accessed through the CS-REFINE web server, where the quantum-based chemical shift refinement method can also be applied. The establishment of this new electronic shift refinement tool is expected to contribute to the improvement and validation of protein structures, thereby advancing our understanding of protein function and biology. Recent advancements in deep learning have led to breakthroughs in classification tasks, driven largely by the wide availability of labeled data. Nonetheless, collecting ample labeled data remains a daunting task for many sectors due to time constraints, domain expertise requirements, or secrecy concerns. In response, researchers have explored the realm of learning with limited or no labels, while others have examined the impact of loss function choices on supervision levels in data-efficient deep learning methods. Despite their existence, the influence of loss function modification remains understudied in these contexts. We investigate the effect of modifying the loss function in supervised classification tasks, focusing on three areas: binary classification with imbalanced data, multiclass classification with ordered responses, and multiclass classification with mixed frequencies. Our analysis reveals that certain loss function modifications demonstrate superior performance on various metrics, including accuracy, balanced accuracy, and the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve. Notably, our findings also indicate that these models exhibit enhanced robustness against perturbations and adversarial attacks. We open-source our code on GitHub, inviting others to build upon our research. We also propose an optimization strategy to mitigate the vanishing gradient problem commonly encountered in gradient penalty methods, enabling the efficient training of high-performance models. We demonstrate the emergence of min-max local optima in the loss landscape, along with the identification of a first-order stationary point. Our research paves the way for further innovation in future research. Additionally, we address potential challenges in deploying our approach, such as the data dependency inherent in gradient penalty methods, and suggest possible avenues for their mitigation. We also analyze the known adversarial examples under our loss function modification, focusing on binary classification with imbalanced data, and explore their potential application in medical diagnostics. We gather and show annotated adversarial examples, highlighting their correspondence with positive classification errors, negative classification errors, or both. Our research contributes to the ongoing discourse on adversarial examples, revealing new insights into their underlying mechanics. Furthermore, we examine the relationship between loss function modification and data augmentation, examining the effect of these techniques on supervision levels in data-efficient deep learning methods. Our analysis links loss function modification to data augmentation via their shared dependence on balance parameters, enabling the development of future research opportunities. We also delve into the connections between loss function modification, knowledge graph embedding, and graph representation learning, focusing on the balance parameters that govern these techniques. Our research reveals common ground among these distinct areas, paving the way for potential collaborations and advancements. Lastly, we reflect on our research findings, noting their broader implications and areas for further exploration.

This diagrammatic form can be iteratively decomposed into simpler components, known as parquet blocks, which capture the underlying geometric relationships within the original Hamiltonian. This framework provides a general approach that can be applied to both classical and quantum systems, and reveals a clear distinction between the underlying geometry of interactions and the observed phenomena in various parquet approximations. Through this viewpoint, a hamiltonian perspective on the parquet approximation is established, which can be used to derive a self-consistent approximation by minimizing the free energy. While this approach converges to a reasonable solution in non-interacting systems, it converges to an incorrect fixed point in the strongly interacting system studied as an example. Despite this issue, the framework can still be used to derive a correct approximation by applying a new definition of the parquet block, in which the geometric constraints are taken into account. This modification can be applied to both classical and quantum systems, and results in a correct description of the systems within the approximation, as demonstrated by testing it on a non-interacting Fermi gas model. The hamiltonian perspective offers a valuable tool for developing parquet approximations, in which the underlying geometric constraints are explicitly taken into account. While this approach may lead to incorrect results for some systems if the standard definition of the parquet block is applied, it can also be used to derive a correct approximation by applying a new definition that accounts for these constraints. This framework can potentially be applied to a wide range of systems, including both classical and quantum systems with complex interactions, and may result in a new class of parquet approximations that can accurately describe the underlying geometric constraints in these systems. Using advanced $ab ~initio$ methods that account for exciton effects, we investigate the lattice and electronic structure of $\bf TiSe_2$ in its normal and trigonal structures. Our results show that exciton interaction plays a crucial role in determining the trigonal structure's stability, a finding that contrasts with previous $ab ~initio$ studies. Additionally, we demonstrate that incorporating exciton effects into phonon frequencies via density functional theory reveals strong correlations with exciton formation energies and the Born-Huang expansion's assumptions. This alignment of phonon modes with exciton states facilitates the creation of a phonon distribution at high temperatures, supporting the concept of exciton liquefaction in $\bf TiSe_2$ above 1000 K. This approach presents an innovative method for exploring the excitonic liquid state in materials. Furthermore, we propose that incorporating exciton effects into the self-energy correction for electron number density and electron scattering rate could lead to the emergence of a Fermi liquid state in $\bf TiSe_2$ at lower temperatures, a phenomenon that requires further experimental verification. Our study provides a theoretical framework that could be applied to other materials, such as $\bf Ta$_2$O$_5$, to better understand their excitonic properties. This approach can potentially identify candidate materials for the realization of excitonic superconductivity. Finally, we acknowledge that our calculations of trigonal structure stability and exciton properties are sensitive to specific method assumptions and approximations, highlighting the need for continued advancements in $ab ~initio$ techniques that can provide a more precise description of these phenomena. Under normal conditions, this phenomenon involves ordinary Cooper pairs losing this characteristic as the light's orientation is adjusted. However, researchers have recently discovered that in certain types of superconductors called doped semiconductors with a peculiar electronic property called spin-orbit coupling, ordinary Cooper pairs exhibit unusual magnetic behavior. Building on earlier studies of another type of superconductor called a nematic superconductor, where pairs of electrons that have an unusual magnetic property called triangular spin polarization exhibit unusual magnetic behavior, we have found that this phenomenon can be seen in another category of superconductor called a nematic superconductor. Utilizing a advanced computational tool that accounts for the complex relationships between magnetic fields and electronic properties, known as the BAGT model, we have simulated the magnetic behavior of a compound called IrTe2 when exposed to a magnetic field and polarized light in a certain orientation. Our study provides the first evidence that this phenomenon can occur in another category of superconductor called a nematic superconductor. We propose a versatile framework called Minimax Engaged Learning (MEL), an adaptive method that reallocates computational resources between data labeling and model training in accordance with dynamic resource constraints. MEL is derived from a game theoretical model, specifically a minimax approach, where the labelling strategy is minimized and the model training strategy is manipulated to maximize labelled data utilization. By engaging in an iterative game of data labeling and model training, MEL leverages the output of each step to optimize both processes in subsequent iterations. Notably, MEL offers two primary benefits: 1) adaptive computational efficiency allows models to be trained with limited computational resources, effectively utilizing the available capacity to mimic full computational resources; 2) enhanced generalization performance is achieved by expanding the training dataset through repeated iterations of data labeling and model training. MEL's effectiveness is demonstrated through the integration of Adversarial Training and Multi-task training techniques. Furthermore, the framework can be applied across various machine learning setups, including classification, object detection, and semantic segmentation, on benchmark datasets such as MNIST, CIFAR-10, PASCAL VOC 2012, and the BDD100K dataset. Specifically, MEL has been successfully implemented on a NVIDIA T4 GPU with 70MB RAM, a NVIDIA Tegra X1 automotive SoC with 512MB RAM, and a Google Pixel 4 smartphone with 6GB RAM. The source code for MEL is publicly available on GitHub. The research presents a novel approach to machine learning, demonstrating that adaptive computational resources can be effectively managed to enhance model generalization. While the framework has notable performance enhancements, further research is required to fully integrate game theory into machine learning. From a theoretical standpoint, the application of game theory in machine learning holds significant promise for enhancing model generalization, albeit with potential complications arising from the non-convexity of the model parameter space. Notwithstanding these challenges, the minimax paradigm offers an attractive solution, specifically in adversarial training, while presenting uncertainties in multi-task training. The integration of game theory with deep learning, specifically the use of reinforcement learning for model training, presents notable difficulties, primarily stemming from the efficient computation of game equilibrium. Nonetheless, the research in this area is an active area of research, and our findings contribute to this research by demonstrating that deep learning can be effectively modeled as a minimax game, while presenting novel solutions, specifically in the application of Adversarial Training and Multi-task training.
