We introduce a groundbreaking dataset for weather classification, comprising 132,600 images, each accurately labeled with detailed weather conditions drawn from a comprehensive dataset. This collection spans 73 unique weather types, derived from a combination of precise weather descriptions and more general, high-level weather categories. Current weather forecasting systems often employ coarse-grained weather descriptions but struggle with the more specific types. Our multi-class weather classification framework can be applied in both video and image prediction scenarios and holds vast potential for various applications across computer vision. We conduct a thorough evaluation of numerous Convolutional Neural Network architectures, including a meta-hyperparameter search utilizing Google Cloud's AI Platform, to identify the optimal model and configuration. Our analysis further examines the effect of training on large datasets and the utilization of image enhancement techniques to improve the performance of our weather classification system. Ultimately, we demonstrate a highly accurate weather classification model, achieving a remarkable top-1 accuracy of 58.16% across all weather types, with specific classes reaching as high as 82.19% top-1 accuracy. Our framework, dataset, and source code are openly available for public use. This work holds the potential to empower computer vision-based weather forecasting and enables the seamless integration of weather and computer vision disciplines. Experimental evaluations have shown a substantial improvement in accuracy with our dataset and model, outperforming existing approaches by a notable margin. Notably, our open-source dataset and model aim to facilitate further research and advancements in the multi-class weather classification domain. Our weather classification model and dataset can be accessed via the following GitHub repository: https://github.com/jayramki/WeatherClassifcation and Google Cloud AI Platform Datasets: https://cloud.google.com.ai-platform/datasets/create. Additionally, our models and results are hosted on GitHub under the repository: https://github.com/jayramki/WeatherClassifcation-models. Our weather classification model has been deployed on Google Cloud, with the ID 'weather-classification-161017-154015'. This cloud deployment can be accessed via the link: https://google-cloud-ai-platform-161017-154015.cloud.google.com/. The overwhelming scientific consensus that human activities are causing climate change has yet to translate into corresponding public opinion. A pressing question arises: what happens when societal norms conflict with scientific findings? This study proposes a framework to analyze the interplay between distinct social norms. Our results reveal three distinct clusters of countries, characterized by varying levels of institutional and economic adherence to the scientific consensus. Furthermore, a novel agent-based model demonstrates that these three categories can also be attributed to differences in public opinion dynamics. Ultimately, this research underscores the significance of distinct social norms in shaping individual behaviors and societal trends. Additionally, this work contributes to the body of literature examining the relationship between social norms and climate change behavior. Several implementation strategies are suggested to mitigate the discrepancies between the scientific and social consensus, with a focus on fostering a culture of environmental responsibility that complements economic prosperity. Finally, this study highlights the value of employing multi-faceted approaches to address the complex issue of climate change behavior. Key Implementation Suggestions are provided at the end of this abstract and in the conclusion. Building on the framework and analysis presented in this research, we propose various implementation strategies to bridge the gaps between the scientific and social norms. These implementation strategies can be summarized as follows: (i) Climate Change Education: Integrating climate change into school curricula can help bridge the gap between the scientific and social norms, particularly among younger generations. (ii) Public Engagement Campaigns: Effectively communicating the findings of climate change can aid in closing the gap between the scientific and social norms, with a focus on leveraging trusted messengers and accessible information to the general public. (iii) Corporate Social Responsibility: Encouraging businesses to promote their environmental efforts can aid in closing the gap between the scientific and social norms, with a focus on showcasing their eco-friendly practices. (iv) Policy Incentives: Offering incentives to individuals and businesses that adopt environmentally responsible behaviors can aid in closing the gap between the scientific and social norms, with a focus on standardizing these incentives across different domains. (v) Cultural Change: Empowering climate leaders and promoting their pro-environmental practices can aid in closing the gap between the scientific and social norms, with a focus on fostering a culture of environmental responsibility. Finally, this study highlights the value of examining distinct social norms in addressing the complex issue of climate change behavior. Building on the framework and analysis presented in this research, various implementation strategies can be utilized to bridge the gaps between the scientific and social norms, with a focus on cultivating a culture of environmental responsibility that complements economic prosperity.

We examine the use of the Koopman operator theory for modeling and controlling soft grippers that use rheological materials in their actuators. To develop an efficient model, we first develop a simplified model of the dynamics of a single DOF system using the Extended Koopman operator framework, which results in a linear constant coefficient system after conversion back to original space. This model is effective in generating control signals for a modular gripper's extended finger, allowing it to track a target trajectory within specified tolerance levels. Furthermore, we successfully apply the developed model to a multi-fingered gripper consisting of three DOFs, whereupon we develop an optimal control algorithm to regulate the extension of the fingers in a synchronized manner. As part of our research, we also created a virtual 3D environment using Unity to visualize and test the models and control algorithms. Moreover, we successfully verified the validity of the proposed models and control strategies through experimental testing of both the single DOF and multi-fingered grippers. To further streamline the modeling and control process, we developed a LabVIEW-based interface for quickly setting up and running experiments within the proposed framework. Overall, the research outcomes demonstrate that the Koopman operator framework presents a versatile approach for modeling and controlling the complex and non-linear dynamics of soft grippers, as well as other soft robotic systems and related applications. One of the fundamental techniques in machine learning is stochastic gradient descent, however its original algorithm has limitations, especially when working with large datasets and multi-dimensional data. In response, researchers developed the mini-batch gradient descent method, yet it still poses challenges when dealing with small datasets and complex dimensional spaces. Consequently, researchers created the mini-batch gradient method, but it necessitates frequent parameter adjustments, inhibits convergence of certain algorithms, and can result in suboptimal solutions. In an effort to address these issues, researchers have been exploring alternative methods such as online learning, evolutionary algorithms, and evolutionary gradient descent, yet these methods often struggle to compete performance-wise with traditional methods. Despite these challenges, it has been observed that evolutionary algorithms, due to their information-sharing mechanisms, can outperform gradient-based methods in specific tasks. Inspired by this insight, we introduced the Organic Gradient Descent algorithm, a hybrid approach that combines the strengths of information-sharing and gradient-based methods. In OGCD, we utilize information-sharing to update parameters and retain the characteristics of existing methods, and have empirically demonstrated its superiority to state-of-the-art methods across a range of benchmark datasets. Notably, OGCD has been shown to surpass state-of-the-art methods for hyperspectral image classification by accurately identifying features in dimensionally high spaces. In addition, OGCD has been successfully applied to classification and regression tasks, and has outperformed competing methods in 119 evaluations across 32 diverse datasets. OGCD's exceptional performance can be attributed to its capacity for exploring diverse spaces, robust generalization, and efficient convergence, and its source code has been publicly released for validation. In order to validate OGCD's efficacy, we conducted extensive evaluations across a range of benchmark datasets, and have provided in-depth analysis to facilitate future research and knowledge-sharing. Furthermore, we have identified potential applications and research avenues based on OGCD's impressive results. Specifically, we have explored the potential for OGCD to be applied in deep learning, its capacity for addressing issues in dimensionally high spaces, and its promise for improving evolutionary optimization methods. In summary, OGCD is a novel, generalized algorithm that surpasses state-of-the-art methods, and has been demonstrated to be effective, generalized, and efficiently converge across a range of diverse tasks and dimensional spaces. In clinical settings, doctors gather different types of data such as patient demographics and test results to inform treatment decisions, but due to technical issues some related information is missed, leading to incomplete knowledge about patients.  By incorporating electronic health records (EHRs), which include all the data collected, a more comprehensive understanding of patients can be gained.  However, using only EHRs may not provide a complete picture, as they do not include information gathered through more traditional methods such as doctor-patient conversations.  Our research addresses the issue of incomplete knowledge by integrating different data types, specifically clinical data from EHRs and unstructured conversation notes, with a view to improving lung cancer prognosis by incorporating both clinical and social factors.  For this purpose, a deep learning model called GRU-based Attention for Diagnosis (GAD), is developed to combine multiple sources of information in a more effective manner. Building upon existing knowledge in NLP, this paper provides an in-depth overview of reinforcement learning-based training data creation, including relevant theoretical and methodological contributions and empirical observations. Furthermore, future research avenues are also explored to facilitate continued progress in this area. The authors present their work in this domain on the Authentic Language State Description (ALSD) framework, which aims to create realistic and applicable language models using RL. The corresponding Lie algebra $\mathfrak{h}_R(\Omega)$ represents a class of finite-dimensional Lie algebras derived from the derivative operators on polynomial vectors with coefficients from $R$ and subgroups from $\Omega$. This paper investigates the properties of vacuum modules for $\mathfrak{h}_R(\Omega)$ and establishes a significant connection to the tensor products of one-dimensional subalgebras, resulting in a decomposition of the algebraic limit of tensor products of subalgebras by its truncated versions. As a consequence, the study yields a classification of finite-dimensional modules for $\mathfrak{h}_R(\Omega)$ that are relatively simple, or 'irreducible'. Additionally, the investigation confirms a long-standing conjecture regarding the existence of vacuum modules for Lie algebras in this class, known as 'type A', first proposed by V. Ginzburg and Y. Tange. The associated central elements for such modules in this study are referred to as 'creation-annihilation' operators and are denoted by $E_\chi$ for a given character $\chi$ in the algebra's characters $\hat{\frak R}$. For characters that can be rationalized to elements in the group $\Omega$, the study demonstrates that the corresponding subalgebra acts by zero on a specific 'vacant module' for each $\omega$ in $\Omega$, and that these modules are isomorphic when their algebras are connected. The creation-annihilation operators for characters that cannot be rationalized to elements in the group $\Omega$ do not, however, act by zero on a 'vacant module'. Social media monitoring through sentiment analysis on platforms like Twitter enables
organizations and individuals to track the public's emotions towards them and their rivals.
As a result, analyzing public sentiment has become both crucial and difficult to accomplish.
In this project, we gathered and annotated seven days' worth of Twitter data, which included
140 hand-labeled sentences from different domains, such as sports, arts, music, and more.
We used an LSTM model to classify sentiment on a scale of seven levels, but due to
limited training data and high class variability, our results were hindered. We also explored
other sentiment analysis techniques and compared them to an LSTM model. Ultimately, we
conducted an in-depth error examination to gain deeper insight into our model's performance. 
The full code is available on GitHub for public access at https://github.com/AdityaSoni21/TSE.

Recent breakthroughs in large language models have transformed the chatbot industry, enabling the creation of sophisticated conversation systems. This paper presents a new approach to developing open-domain conversation systems that can engage in dynamic conversations according to various roles. Each role defines a chatbot's personality, thereby determining its response style and topic preferences. By leveraging the flexibility of role-based chatbots, we can deploy a single model to accommodate multiple roles, reducing the need for model duplication and simplifying development. Additionally, our method facilitates easy role switching and domain shifting, enhancing the model's versatility. We tested our approach with three roles and demonstrated its effectiveness through extensive evaluation. Furthermore, our chatbot design inspired the creation of a role-defined open-domain conversation dataset, which is now available on GitHub for the benefit of the research community. This dataset provides a framework for evaluating open-domain conversation systems with customizable roles and can be used to develop more advanced chatbots. Furthermore, we conducted a comparative analysis of our model's performance using the newly created dataset and found that our approach outperformed other state-of-the-art open-domain conversation systems in various evaluation metrics. The source code for our model and dataset can be accessed on GitHub at the following link: https://github.com/Chen-5510/Role-Defined-Open-Domain-Conversation. Additional information can be found on my personal website at the following link: https://chen5510.github.io/publication/20230420_RDOC.

Researchers have made notable progress in QTP by enhancing search outcomes, but existing approaches often rely on statistical models that are difficult to interpret. To address the lack of transparency, a new QTP approach is proposed, leveraging latent topics to predict terms. By incorporating the predictive analytics capabilities of Naive Bayes and a static knowledge base, this framework achieves impressive results, outperforming state-of-the-art baselines and providing clear explanations for its term predictions. The framework's source code is freely available on GitHub at https://github.com/aleksandar-todorovic/TAPAS-QTP. Evaluation metrics indicate that the proposed framework predicts terms with high precision among similar documents and related terms, ultimately improving search engines' ability to guess unknown queries' intended meaning. The study provides evidence that a hybrid approach incorporating latent topics and static knowledge can surpass state-of-the-art QTP methods, offering a highly interpretable and transparent system. This equilibrium is characterized by the particles moving together in a harmonically oscillating pattern, with the frequency and amplitude dependent on the particles' size and the surrounding fluid's properties. Our numerical model utilizes the "fracture mesh modification" technique to seamlessly integrate fracture pieces into a primary mesh, where we apply the Mimetic Finite Variation method for solution computation. To enhance numerical stability, we employ both conventional and stabilized approaches on both fracture surfaces and bulk regions. Our work also includes comparisons of numerical models with distinct mesh resolutions to quantify the impact of mesh density on modeling outcomes. The Seidel matrix is a popular tool for analyzing social network data, recently expanded to visualize relationships in chain graphs, a type of mathematical model, by applying a matrix representation. Chain graphs are distinct from regular graphs in their circular properties. Researchers have developed methods to calculate the Seidel matrix's eigenvalues and determine its spectrum, yet key aspects of the matrix remain unclear, including its range and energy.

This study aims to resolve two unresolved questions about the Seidel matrix: the extent of its range and its link to network data, specifically the delta-matrix and B-matrix, and a related measure called the Seidel energy. To answer these questions, we develop an iterative approach to break down the Seidel matrix into manageable components, allowing us to derive accurate estimates of its maximum off-diagonal entry and establish a direct connection between the Seidel energy and network data, specifically the trace of the B-matrix. This connection gives rise to the Seidel energy's upper and lower bounds in terms of network parameters. Consequently, our results broaden the Seidel matrix's applicability to modeling cyclic network interactions. Moreover, our findings have implications in information theory, as they relate to the chain graph's capacity and a measure of graph connectivity called the Seidel index. To demonstrate the practical significance of our findings, we present two examples highlighting the differences between the Seidel energy and traditional network measures. Notably, our results show that the Seidel energy can serve as a more sensitive indicator of certain network characteristics. We hope that our work will stimulate further research on the Seidel matrix and its matrix product with vectors of (0,1)-variables. Furthermore, our study may contribute to the development of innovative network data analysis methods.

Therefore, we transform the problem into a fixed-point problem, which requires solving an ordinary differential equation. We then demonstrate the existence and uniqueness of solutions to this problem under certain conditions, which can become arbitrarily complex. The study of band gaps in this elliptic operator is significant because it connects to the transversality of periodic orbits in related Hamiltonian systems, and consequently to the ground states of time-dependent quantum systems described by the Floquet-Bloch theory. In this paper, we explore the nature of band gaps in a Dirac operator with a compact range and establish a theorem relating its band gaps to the graph topology of a related supersymmetric elliptic operator, thereby providing a visible connection between the geometry of the manifold and the band structure. As a consequence, we are able to demonstrate the existence of band gaps under various geometric assumptions and provide examples that illustrate both necessary and sufficient conditions for the band gap property. Moreover, we are able to show that the band gaps in a Dirac operator can be linked to the properties of linked components in a related supersymmetric operator. This connection allows us to devise a general strategy to find energies in the band gaps by incorporating "glued at infinity" techniques and using topological properties like the van-Kampen theorem. This approach provides a visible link between the geometry and the band structure. In a related direction, we are studying periodic Dirac operators with gluing at infinity to explore the related question of Dirac operators with band gaps in compact manifolds. This involves connecting finite-band energies in elliptic operators to the topology of band gaps in quantum systems. Specifically, we are investigating under which geometric conditions a periodic Dirac operator has a band gap, and we are relating this to the linking properties of associated graphs to projective spaces. This inquiry into the connections between geometric properties and quantum system behavior is a key part of our broader research aim to establish a topological framework for the ground states of time-dependent quantum systems described by the Floquet-Bloch theory. Along the way, we are also developing novel techniques to analyze periodic Dirac operators with gluing at infinity and exploring related generalizations to study quantum system behavior. This includes connections to the van-Kampen theorem, the Seifert-fibered spaces, and projective spaces. Those connections are significant because they allow us to establish a topological framework for the ground states of time-dependent quantum systems described by the Floquet-Bloch theory. In the context of Vehicle-to-Vehicle (V2V) communication, a crucial safety feature is relayed by the network service provider to enable drivers in accident prevention scenarios to communicate effectively with each other. Although V2V communication benefits from reduced interference when using high frequency bands by spreading signal, it also has significant drawbacks such as increased interference and signal degradation due to electromagnetic wave absorption by vehicles and environment. To address these limitations, roadside units can be utilized to provide vehicle relays with alternative downlink options, effectively enhancing network diversity and relaying capacity in vehicular networks. To promote reliable communication and accident prevention, vehicle relays can establish a local data relay support network by partnering with nearby Roadside Units (RSUs), which in turn act as RSU relays to provide enhanced network diversity, lower downlink traffic, higher data transfer rates, and improved network reliability. To promote reliable communication and accident prevention, we develop mathematical formulas to demonstrate the advantages of this 2-Tier Diverse Vehicle Relay Assisted Relaying Approach (2-TDRAR) in vehicular networks. Simulation results show that this 2-TDRAR approach offers vehicle users a lower packet error rate, faster data transfer rates, lower latency, and increased reliability compared to traditional vehicular networks. To promote reliable communication and accident prevention, we simulate two Scenarios, investigating the effects of vehicle size, vehicle speed, vehicle density, and RSU density on the 2-TDRAR approach. Simulation results show that this 2-TDRAR approach outperforms traditional vehicular networks in all test scenarios. To promote reliable communication and accident prevention, we examine the computational complexity and reliability of the 2-TDRAR approach, which surpass those of traditional vehicular networks based on computational complexity analysis and reliability metrics. Simulation results confirm that this 2-TDRAR approach offers vehicle users a lower computational complexity and higher reliability compared to traditional vehicular networks. To promote reliable communication and accident prevention, we investigate and compare the effects of different vehicular network protocols, vehicle relay sizes, vehicle speeds, vehicle densities, and RSU densities on the 2-TDRAR approach, which effectively enhances network diversity, relaying capacity, latency, and reliability in vehicular networks. To promote reliable communication and accident prevention, we present a step-by step implementation procedure for the 2-TDRAR approach, which effectively improves the performance of vehicular networks by providing vehicle users with a lower packet error rate, faster data transfer rates, lower latency, and increased reliability compared to traditional vehicular networks

Wikipedia relies heavily on community involvement, but sometimes its reliance on user-generated content leads to low-quality content. The platform has established a system where editors can mark articles as problematic and assign tags to indicate specific issues, such as factual inaccuracies or bias. However, this voluntary system means there's currently no centralized place to track patterns in editing behaviors and their effects on article quality. To address this, we developed a method to analyze data on editing behaviors and use it to predict the likelihood of articles being tagged with specific issues, effectively classifying articles based on editing patterns. By using this approach, we can identify articles that need attention without relying on manual editing and enhance Wikipedia's quality control efforts. Currently, our model can predict article tags with moderate accuracy, but we believe this approach has significant potential for further development and improvement. To facilitate future work, we was made available a pre-trained model and associated training data. 

In terms of contributions, this research brings Wikipedia's quality control processes into a mathematical framework that can be modeled and optimized. By using this approach, we can identify articles that need attention without relying on manual editing and enhance Wikipedia's quality control efforts. To prove this, we conducted several experiments using different machine learning algorithms and evaluated our results by comparing predicted tags with actual tags, effectively quantifying Wikipedia's quality control issues. We found that our method can predict article tags with moderate accuracy and, using a simple neural network, achieved a macro F1 score of 0.97 for predicting the Kitemark quality label and performed better than a random guess for predicting the Trusty label. Additionally, we applied our model to identify articles that require attention from editors, focusing on those that need review by the Wikipedia's Quality Control team and found that it predicted these articles with moderate accuracy. We found that editing behaviors such as frequent contributions and complex edits are indicative of articles that need this particular type of review. We believe that our research brings editing behaviors into a mathematical framework that can be analyzed and optimized. To showcase the potential of this approach, we applied it to articles in Spanish and found that editing behaviors such as page moves and diffs are indicative of articles that need review in that language. We found that our method performed better than a random guess for predicting review needs in Spanish, but could be improved by incorporating more data from that language. We believe that our research brings editing behaviors such as page moves and diffs into a mathematical framework that can be analyzed and optimized. To prove this, we made available a pre-trained model and associated training data.

We examine whether a decision theory-based framework can effectively capture human decision-making behavior when confronted with unknown situations, without requiring knowledge of the decision-maker's underlying choice model. To approach this challenge, we first compare human choices in unknown scenarios to the predictions of a modified Bayesian network framework, which incorporates decision-makers' general knowledge and relies on a utility function that can be learned through reinforcement learning. An experiment involving a study with 20 participants, analyzing their decisions in unknown 10D scenarios, reveals that the proposed framework successfully translates human decision-making patterns into a machine-readable format, while also providing insights into the structure of humans' general knowledge. Furthermore, we find that this framework can effectively predict human decisions in situations where they are unfamiliar, often yielding better results than a decision theory-neutral approach. Notably, the proposed framework achieves an average performance accuracy of 57% in predicting human choices, which significantly surpasses a decision theory-neutral approach with an accuracy accuracy of 44%. Finally, we reflect on the implications of these findings, highlighting both the benefits and limitations of capturing human decision-making behavior through a general knowledge framework. In aerial surveillance, gathering images from various angles can be beneficial 
for identifying targets, but current object detection methods are limited to using 
a single view. Research has been conducted to analyze multi-view aerial images and 
apply learning from one view to another, where each image is transformed into 
a normalized format to account for different orientations. However, this approach 
has its drawbacks, as it disregards unique characteristics in images and relies on 
normalization. A new method, CoOL, utilizes both images in the co-learning pair 
and incorporates key features into a unified model for detection. By integrating 
both detection models and combining their losses, CoOL learns and adapts to both 
images, where each model relies on the other's supervision to avoid relying solely 
on limited labeled data. Since human expertise is required to label aerial images, 
CoOL eliminates the necessity for expert input by utilizing unlabeled multi-view 
pairs instead, where each image is paired with an image from a different angle 
for target selection. This approach not only reduces the load but also makes the 
system more flexible and adaptable to various orientations, where target recognition 
is based on the exchange of information between different views. Experimental 
results show that CoOL surpasses current state-of-the-art methods in single-view 
detection and extends the system's performance to multi-view images with unknown 
orientations, where each image can identify the target without the need for manual 
labels and orientation adjustments. Additionally, the system is designed to 
be model-agnostic, where different object detectors can be integrated into the 
system for varied applications and can even be applied to other domains beyond 
aerial images. With its capacity for model-extended capabilities and unsupervised 
labeling, CoOL provides numerous opportunities for expansion and improvement. 
Overall, CoOL brings about a novel and innovative approach for multi-view extended 
object detection and provides a versatile and efficient method for various aerial 
images with unknown orientations, where each image can identify the target 
without the need for manual labels and orientation adjustments. From the technical 
point of view, CoOL can be applied to various domains beyond aerial images. As such, 
CoOL has numerous unsupervised labeling benefits and provides a versatile and 
efficient method for various aerial images with unknown orientations. For this 
reason, CoOL brings about a novel and innovative approach for multi-view extended 
object detection. As such, the code for this research project is available at 
https://github.com/AlexYangSE/Co-Observ

This paper proposes a metric and an efficient method for calculating the performance of PAC codes, which can be applied to evaluate the polarization of astronomical images and remove it in data analysis. The code is designed to identify polarized components within an image by iteratively calculating the least-squares fit of polarization angles at each pixel, thereby minimizing the residual noise. By using the Levinson-Durbin and Krein-Newton methods, the calculation of PAC codes can be accelerated for larger datasets. The authors also provide a versatile implementation of PAC codes in Python, allowing for adaptation in various astronomical imaging applications. The proposed method is then tested on simulated data and compared with other polarization filtering methods, such as the Saturated Pixel Discrimination (SPD) method, to evaluate its performance. The results show that PAC codes outperform SPD in terms of point source preservation and image quality, demonstrating higher accuracy and a longer polarization scale range. The authors conclude that PAC codes offer an effective and efficient solution for polarization correction in X-ray astronomy. The SExtractor-based code is then further developed to incorporate the PAC algorithms, enabling its public release and integration in astronomical data analysis software. The proposed method is then used to demonstrate its effectiveness on actual Chandra observations, showcasing its ability to remove the gradient tail in the surface brightness distribution and enhance the image quality. The integration of PAC codes in widely used astronomical software marks a significant milestone in utilizing PAC codes for polarization correction in X-ray astronomy. The code implementation and test data are available for public access. The authors suggest future research directions, including the extension of PAC codes to other astronomical imaging techniques and the removal of polarization in phase, which could further improve the method's accuracy and efficiency. The paper concludes by highlighting the distinct features and advantages of PAC codes. The authors note that PAC codes possess certain unique characteristics, such as variable code length and metric types, which set it apart from other filtering codes. The conclusion is followed by a future work section, detailing several areas of research that could be influenced by PAC codes. The authors then provide a summary of the paper, reiterating the main results and outlining the public release of the code implementation. The code must be entered into a public repository with the specified license, allowing other researchers to access and build upon the authors' work. The code must be freely available to all, meeting the requirements of a public license. The authors note that the code is already publicly available, as requested. The paper is then closed with the authors' contact information, enabling readers to access the code through the specified repository

A versatile hand-tracking system is demanded across multiple industries and real-world scenarios, requiring accurate and durable hand pose estimation even in challenging outdoor environments. In this study, we present a novel approach to simultaneously track multiple hand joints and linkages, leveraging point cloud data from depth sensors, even in the tough outdoor conditions where illumination and weather can significantly affect performance. By incorporating a sophisticated network that generates detailed hand models in an implicit form, our system ensures robust and reliable results, including in cases of occlusion, as the underlying structure learning technique employs spatial geometry to reconstruct missing joints. By treating the task as a multi-frame video reconstruction problem, our system is capable of tracking moving hands in the wild, outperforming existing hand-tracking systems that rely on RGB cameras. Our method has been demonstrated to achieve state-of-the-art performance across multiple datasets, including the IncognitoOutdoor-Dataset we created, which features highly challenging outdoor scenarios that simulate real-world conditions with varied lighting, weather, surfaces, and objects, as well as dramatic changes in scale and viewpoint. By achieving a mean PASCAL 3D+ mAP of 44.6%, our system has successfully pushed the limits of hand pose estimation, even outperforming its indoor counterpart in difficult cases while maintaining high accuracy overall. This research introduces a cutting-edge hand-tracking system that can accurately follow individual hand joints in complex real-world environments. Unusual lighting and weather conditions pose significant challenges to conventional hand-tracking technologies, prompting the development of a sophisticated new approach that leverages point cloud data from depth sensors. By capturing high-resolution, detailed hand scans, this system achieves unparalleled accuracy even in the most demanding outdoor settings. A novel structure-learning technique enables the reconstruction of missing joints from point cloud sequences, treating the task as a multi-frame video reconstruction problem. As a result, our system has pushed the limits of hand pose estimation, surpassing existing standards in difficult cases while maintaining exceptional overall accuracy. Specifically, we have achieved a mean PASCAL 3D+ mAP of 44.6% across multiple datasets, featuring real-world scenarios that mimic extreme conditions, including dramatic changes in scale and viewpoint. We are introducing the LAMOST Explorers survey, a new project that utilizes the LAMOST 4-meter telescope to conduct a large-scale photometric sky survey over 800 deg$^2$ in the $u$ $g$ $r$ $i$ and $z$ bands. Leveraging the LAMOST project's catalog of nearly 9 million stars with high precision, our team is refining the LAMOST Explorers' point-of-view, or field of view, over 4 $K$2 plates. These fields are then compared to reference data from the $K$2 catalog, demonstrating that variations with timescales under 40 days can be accurately detected and followed up on in the LAMOST Explorers survey, especially in the $g$ and $r$ bands, with an overall precision of 3.5-4.5%. Furthermore, we are tracking periodic changes in 1,600 variable stars, including 600 new discoveries, in the experiment. Our teams are working to expand the LAMOST Explorers survey, which is now available online at the VLTI database, and plan to use the Xingming-Olympic Iron Pool 2 telescope to conduct in-depth observations of promising candidates. These efforts aim to address critical questions, such as the nature of microlensing events and the occurrence of previously unknown variable stars. We are excited to share our initial findings and look forward to further collaboration. Due to the telescope's limitations, we are unable to conduct our observations independently, but instead choose our fields from past surveys, including the Photo Electric Survey. As a result, our team is now working to optimize the LAMOST Explorers' observing strategy and schedule, and look forward to utilizing the LAMOST telescope's new 60 cm wide field-of-view camera to conduct our next large-scale survey. Random number generation is a critical process in numerous scientific simulations, cryptographic applications, and modeling analyses, yet current methods employing computational algorithms suffer from shortcomings such as lack of entropy, predictability, and vulnerability to reverse engineering. In response to these limitations, we propose utilizing undervolting in SRAM cells to generate truly random numbers, taking advantage of the inherent instability of transistors' behavior in the presence of reduced supply voltage. By harnessing the variability of four distinct transistor types, our design aims to increase deep learning model coverage of uniformly distributed random numbers between 0 and 1 from 81% to 99.97% while maintaining the generation of cryptographically secure random numbers. Lastly, our results demonstrate the feasibility of integrating our method into SRAM manufacturers' design flows to reduce area by replacing traditional SRAM cells with our undervolting cells. With the ability to generate 524 MB of random numbers every second at 0.06 W and 0.02 bit/s power consumption for generating random binary numbers, our design has been verified to be scalable down to 28nm technology nodes. Overall, our approach flexibly addresses diverse application needs for genuine randomness, offering the advantage of integrating undervolting cells into commercial SRAM chips to facilitate random number generation while minimizing effects on nearby circuit performance. Ultimately, our undervolting cells enable the generation of random numbers with minimal latency, high throughput, high entropy, and low power consumption, making it an apt choice for diverse use cases. This research proposes a theoretical model for single-electron resistive switching in molecular devices, consisting of a spherical island connected to two electrodes via insulating shells. It demonstrates that island charges significantly impact the electrode-insulator interaction, thereby influencing resistive switching behavior. Specifically, the model reveals that as the island acquires a charge, it polarizes the surrounding insulator near the electrodes, effectively reducing the insulator gap and thus triggering resistive switching. Furthermore, the study examines how molecule size and island charge affect this phenomenon. To validate the proposed model, a detailed analysis of experimental data on SiO$_2$ and Al$_2$O$_3$ molecules is presented, demonstrating a strong correlation between the results and real-world observations. It is anticipated that a deeper understanding of single-electron resistive switching in molecular devices will contribute to the development of innovative nanoscale memory storage technologies. Additionally, the study lays the groundwork for exploring single-electron resistive switching in a broader range of insulators and environments. Given the general applicability of the model, it is expected that the findings will be relevant to switching behaviors observed in graphene, transition metal dichalcogenides, and other 2D semiconductors. Lastly, the research provides a framework for designing novel nanoscale memory devices based on single-electron resistive switching. To this end, several design concepts, including multi-molecule memory cells and parallel single-electron resistive switch circuits, are proposed. It is anticipated that such designs will pave the way for the creation of robust, scalable single-electron resistive switch memory cells. Crucially, the research emphasizes the need for novel experimental tools that can effectively probe single-electron resistive switching at room temperature, thereby facilitating significant breakthroughs in the field. Ultimately, it is believed that a thorough comprehension of single-electron resistive switching will enable the development of innovative nanoscale memory storage systems and 2D semiconductor devices. Additionally, it is anticipated that the underlying principles will find applications in diverse fields such as biology and medicine where single-electron resistive switching may underpin fundamental cellular processes and their manipulation. Additionally, the study lays the groundwork for exploring single-electron resistive switching in a range of living organisms and their relevance to understanding biological processes and developing novel biomedical therapies. To this end, several speculative examples, including the use of nanoscale memory devices to model synapse behavior and the potential for electromechanical control of cellular processes, are proposed, thereby highlighting the vast potential of single-electron resistive switching

In the initial stages of solvation, water molecules interact strongly with the solute, generating highly excited quantum states. However, the thermal energy quickly erases the high-level excitations, and classical dynamics takes over, or so the common assumption goes. Recent theoretical studies indicate that zero-point motion, a fundamental quantum phenomenon, should not be disregarded in highly excited states of solvation. To further elucidate the significance of zero-point motion, our group utilized path integral molecular dynamics (PIMD) to investigate the solvation shell of sulphuric acid (H2SO4) in water. PIMD calculations were performed at two temperatures, 300K and 900K, using two different potentials that stimulate zero-point motion at the higher temperature. Notably, our results demonstrate that the solvation structure derived from the PIMD approach with the anharmonic potential exhibits a more accurate correlation with experimental neutron scattering data, even at 900K. Conversely, the harmonic potential failed to produce a satisfactory match with experimental data, especially at 900K. which become apparent during matching, to streamline the computation of

This leads to a new, more efficient approach that can be applied within 
next-generation Wilson coefficient analyses, potentially resulting in a 
substantial reduction of computational complexity. Specifically, we 
demonstrate how to obtain accurate Standard Model predictions for four key 
observables - the branching ratio, charge-asymmetry, $q^2$-distributions,

decay modes and incorporating effects from $b\to s$ loop processes within

Automated essay grading has been a persistent challenge in Natural Language Processing.  Despite years of research, it remains an unsolved issue, being considered a particularly difficult task due to essays being broadly diverse in content, language, and format.  In contrast to conventional methods which focus on pinpointing specific words or phrases, more recent studies have utilized deep learning techniques to analyze unstructured data and have achieved notable breakthroughs in this area.  Notably, pre-trained language models such as BERT have greatly improved the efficiency and effectiveness of Automated Essay Grading.  In addition to pre-trained models, data augmentation techniques can also be employed to enhance the quality of the learning dataset.  This research proposes several novel data enhancement strategies for Automated Essay Grading using pre-trained transformer models, specifically BERT and RoBERTa.  Additionally, several popular data augmentation techniques such as BERT-WE and BERT-NMT are also explored and their performance is compared with a model that utilizes BERT fusions with BERT-WE and BERT-NMT on two standard datasets.  The results demonstrate that BERT fusion with BERT-WE and BERT-NMT outperforms the baseline model in both datasets.  More importantly, the best-performing model achieved an F1 score of 0.6246 on the AEGR dataset, breaking the state-of-the-art performance of 0.6240 achieved by a model that utilized BERT-Elasticweightdecay. We introduce an upgraded RingCT protocol that supports quicker and more efficient transactions without revealing user anonymity, achieved through the utilization of a compact proof of knowledge in Schnorr signatures; previously, the standard Schnorr proof was required to verify transaction inputs, comprising signatures and public keys. To facilitate the updated RingCT transactions, we establish a common public parameter known as a Delegated Verification Parameter (DVP), which is created via a trusted process and used to verify both regular and RingCT transactions in a blockchain network. The DVP is comprised of a set of bundled statements that collectively prove the ownership of numerous public keys, thereby enabling the inclusion of RingCT transactions with improved efficiency. These improved transactions can then be included in a blockchain, allowing for faster transaction processing and the preservation of anonymity. The creation of DVP follows a structure similar to that of a proof of capacity in a bounded Schnorr proof system, enabling the verification of RingCT transactions with greater simplicity and reduced complexity. Furthermore, the design of DVP does not restrict the use of standard Schnorr proofs in a blockchain, enabling seamless integration of the upgraded RingCT protocol into existing blockchain systems. We demonstrate the efficacy of our Delegated RingCT protocol through an analysis of specified common parameters in Bitcoin and Dcash, showcasing an overall transaction size reduction from 15KB to 7KB (a 53% decrease) with the DVP method. Additionally, the integration of our Delegated RingCT protocol leads to a noticeable improvement in anonymous transaction processing, resulting in lower fees and faster transaction processing times. Specifically, a standard RingCT transaction is processed in 8 blocks faster, and Dcash transactions are processed 2.7 blocks ahead of those using the traditional RingCT method. We have thoroughly tested our Delegated RingCT protocol through various validation methods, including the use of PySNARK and SNARKFlow in a development environment of Bitcoin and Dcash. We are excited about the potential for Delegated RingCT to contribute to greater efficiency and anonymity protection in blockchain technology. We have made the source code available for public use at https://github.com/kragnos/pyringsct. This analysis explores the impact of singular and ill-conditioned data on linear equation solving algorithms via a detailed examination of each step's arithmetic operations. As a case study, we investigate the Cimmines solver's behavior during Demmel's experiment of adding random components to a previously solved system. Through a space toughness assessment, we demonstrate that this approach can identify the source and severity of instability throughout the solving process, ultimately concluding that ill-conditioning poses a more significant problem than singularities. This new development is enhancing UD-annotated texts previously created for academic projects and creating opportunities for comparative research across various domains. In addition to updating and expanding the existing treebank, efforts are being made to make Hebrew NLP more accessible to others by mirroring the activities of the English community. Recent breakthroughs in neural network based physical models have enabled direct learning from experimental data. However, standard supervised learning techniques often neglect crucial aspects of the measurement process, such as noise. We introduce a new approach, collaborative filtering, which incorporates the challenges of real-world measurements into supervised learning. It utilizes data-driven correlations to separate signal and noise in multiple fields of view, and can handle varying measurement quality and confidence across different sensors. This method was successfully applied to the analysis of experimental flow data in a turbulent jet, and demonstrated the ability to accurately separate and eliminate noise from raw data. It was then used in a forward prediction exercise to generate synthetic data-informed profiles, and compared to standard profiling techniques using raw data. The results show that collaborative filtering enhances the accuracy of inference and downstream downstream tasks, such as turbulence characterization, and reduces the influence of measurement inaccuracies. Furthermore, this method can be adapted for use with single-point measurements, and we propose a modified version that incorporates spatial correlations in thermal-fluids simulations. We verified that this technique yields more accurate results compared to baseline methods using data from an isolated heat source simulation. These advancements can now be integrated into a unified workflow, data-informed modeling, which enables direct learning from experimental data while accounting for noise using collaborative filtering. The accuracy of this approach was validated in a diverse set of experiments, including active control, turbulent jets, and thermal-fluids simulations, and we demonstrate that it can be adapted to a range of applications through detailed user studies. Overall, this research lays the foundation for collaborative data-informed modeling, a general framework that can be applied to a wide range of scientific domains. It leverages the synergies between numerical models and experimental data, and enables direct learning from measurements in highly noisy real-world environments. This study presents a novel low-density parity-check (LDPC) construction method that's easily replicated and allows for the control of codeword density. The proposed design, which features degree-two and degree-three variables, results in a sparse check matrix with a specific structure after further processing. Despite the density of the codewords, caused by the degree-two variables, and the short cyclic nature of the check matrix, which might increase the minimum Hamming distance, our experimental findings indicate that the overall error performance remains satisfactory for the given binary erasure channel. The LDPC code developed here exhibits a significant increase in storage efficiency compared to previous approaches using density evolution and degree-degree or degree-degree-degree scheduling techniques. The proposed LDPC construction method has been tested with various parameter sets and shows excellent overall performance. Additionally, there's a significant reduction in computational requirements associated with density evolution, making the LDPC construction method even more feasible. The overall findings confirm that the proposed LDPC construction method offers an effective solution for balancing storage efficiency and error performance. Furthermore, the degree-degree protocol can be extended to include degree-four messages with the incorporation of a novel and efficient decoding approach for evaluating the Hamming distance. The degree-four protocol exhibits enhanced error performance and flexibility in terms of the degree sequence, which can be tailored to suit specific requirements while still providing satisfactory error performance. The degree-four protocol also enables the use of density evolution for efficient and reliable LDPC code development. A critical flaw in the security of quantum key exchange using partially random phases has been identified. This weakness can be exploited by malicious eavesdroppers who use low-resolution screens, limiting the range of phase randomization. Specifically, if the phases are randomly changed within a certain boundary, an attacker can launch a successful eavesdroption by focusing on a single binary key exchange, significantly reducing the probability of detection. This vulnerability can be mitigated by incorporating a simple yet robust method, such as using multi-bits or a quantum backup system, to ensure the security of quantum key exchange. This threat is not only applicable to current partially quantum key exchange systems but also serves as an important caution for future implementations. Additionally, this discovery has broader implications for the secure applied research in quantum physics. Given the fundamental principles involved, this threat is not confined to partial phase randomization but also extends to other scenarios with limited range of phase randomization. Consequently, this discovery could have far-reaching implications for the field of quantum science. Specifically, this threat could be relevant to recent breakthroughs in quantum key distribution using partial transverse wave functions and could potentially affect other areas of quantum key distribution, including partial linear momentum and other randomization approaches. Furthermore, this discovery could influence the development of quantum key distribution using random moments. Based on these findings, it is clear that phase randomization provides weak, not solid, security for quantum key exchange and other applications. This weakness could be overcome by incorporating more robust methods, such as multi-bits, quantum backup, and other approaches. These alternatives not only enhance the security of quantum key exchange but also open new avenues for its practical implementation. Specifically, multi-bits offer more secure possibilities, while the quantum backup method enables the conversion of partially random phases to fully random ones, significantly enhancing the security of quantum key exchange. These innovative techniques have the potential to revolutionize the applied research in quantum physics, particularly in topics such as quantum key exchange, random phase encryption, and other related applications. Ultimately, this discovery serves as a significant warning to researchers engaged in quantum key exchange and related phenomena. Recent research has shown that large language models can learn to perform tasks in-context with minimal fine-tuning. A critical factor affecting this performance is the size, diversity, and relevance of the training data. To better understand the influence of training data, we compared the performance of a 13B-parameter language model on 13 datasets, including labeled and unlabeled text datasets. We found that training data quantity has a significant impact, with each additional dataset increasing performance by an average of 2.5%. A systematic analysis revealed that unlabeled data contributes more significantly to this improvement, with labeled data only making a difference when the available data is insufficient (below 13 million examples). Notably, the model performed notably better on datasets with diverse writing styles, indicating that training data heterogeneity has a positive effect on the model's general ability to perform in-context learning. Overall, our findings provide valuable insights for creating training datasets that can effectively leverage large language models for in-context learning. Moreover, our research suggests that the effectiveness of a dataset can be accurately predicted by evaluating a simple mask-filling task, thus enabling data labels to be bypassed to accelerate the dataset creation process. The third generation of quarks, consisting of b and c quarks, is of particular interest due to potential issues related to CP symmetry violations observed in related processes. Notably, research has revealed considerable discrepancies between data collected by LHCb and other experiments, such as SAMPHIRE, in Altaru and in FENICE, in Altarede, concerning the rate at which these quarks decay while respecting CP symmetry. In the absence of predicted CP violations rooted in the Standard Model, these discrepancies could be seen as indications of new CP-violating physics. In this review, we will summarize the current knowledge gaps and present various theoretical models capable of explaining these discrepancies, focusing on where they fall short of reproducing experimental results. Lastly, we will outline potential avenues for future research to resolve the remaining ambiguities in the rate at which these quarks decay while respecting CP symmetry. We've derived higher-order vertex operators for a specific $\alpha'$-expansion in superstring theory, which corresponds to a bosonic string with Ramond-Neveu-Schwarz conditions, and then calculated associated scattering amplitudes. By relating these to a fermionic string without $\alpha'$-expansion, we've tested the Gross conjecture, which holds that a specific relationship between bosonic and fermionic string amplitudes remains constant across all orders in $\alpha'$, but rather scales by $1/\alpha'$. The relationship appears to remain constant for lower-order terms but may need further modification for higher-order terms to accurately describe the relationship between bosonic and fermionic string amplitudes. If this modification is accounted for, the Gross conjecture holds that the ratio between bosonic and fermionic string amplitudes remains constant across all orders in $\alpha'$. The derivation of the vertex operators involved a detailed analysis of the Fierz identities in 11D supersymmetry, which was used to demonstrate the decoupling of certain operators as $\alpha'$ tends to zero. Specifically, we showed that certain operators are coupled only by terms involving $\alpha'$ and that their coupling can be eliminated in the $\alpha'$ expansion by using a specific operator that acts as a decoupling operator as $\alpha'$ tends to zero. The analysis demonstrates that certain operators not present in the fermionic string do not contribute to scattering amplitudes for specific states but are present in the bosonic string, where they contribute to tachon poles in scattering amplitudes, which may be related to the mechanism of tachyon removal in the bosonic string through "winding cancellation". This paper explores various tasks necessary for effective central network management in 5G systems and proposes methods to tackle two significant challenges: optimizing network slice availability and balancing cell load. By employing a distributed approach based on swarm intelligence, the research proposes automated solutions to these complex problems, which can be solved through a simple and efficient strategy that requires minimal information exchange within the 5G SLIIC framework. This research explores the possibility of creating a voice model without linguistic inputs, using auditory units extracted directly from speech data. Typically, neural voice models rely on pre-processed text-to-speech data, but this project utilizes a unique transcription method based on human annotation of speech as auditory units, eliminating the need for linguistic annotation. Over 13,000 hours of speech data from multiple languages was used, and it was transcribed into a set of words linked by auditory units, essentially creating a phonological representation. When compared to state-of-the-art voice models, the model developed in this research demonstrated comparable voice quality and intelligibility, despite being constrained by limited data due to the complexity of the auditory units. As the auditory units can be seen as a form of linguistic input, this project raises interesting questions about the minimal requirements for neural language models. Recent advancements in combined convex programming utilizing data-driven McCormick envelope relaxations have shown great potential in applying approximate decomposition to intricate optimization problems. This approach has been effectively applied to single-stage CP models, but its use in multi-stage topological planning is yet to be explored. In this study, we develop a multi-step combined convex programming method that takes into consideration dynamic factors such as sensor measurements, actuator limitations, and collision avoidance, all within the context of topological planning. By incorporating data-driven relaxations, we are able to tackle complex optimization issues with varying levels of uncertainty, including those related to real-world applications such as autonomous driving. Computational results demonstrate that our proposed strategy not only leads to significantly reduced computational times, but also yields practically useful solutions within a feasible time frame. Moreover, the topological structure generated by our approach exhibits a high level of consistency, outperforming existing methods in this domain. This research is backed by extensive simulations using SWIM, an autonomous underwater vehicle testbed. Key findings reveal that the majority of optimal solutions can be obtained within the first few iterations, with a notable 90% of cases reaching near-optimal results. Furthermore, we observed a substantial reduction in processing time of up to 87%, which is directly linked to the degree of uncertainty present. Ultimately, this work presents a novel multi-step combined convex programming paradigm that integrates data-driven relaxations for efficient motion planning in complex, uncertain environments. We investigate the epistemic view of quantum states by examining whether a sequence of quantum states can be transformed into another sequence through a series of operations that don't alter their statistical distributions. Our study reveals two distinct forms of transformability: one where the target states are always reached with certain probability, and another where the target states are always reached without fail. Notably, we demonstrate that certain incoherent operations can serve as a valid measure of the first type of transformability, yet this form of transformability falls short in allowing us to determine the range of achievable statistical distributions in a given scenario. In contrast, the second type of transformability exhibits a more diverse set of achievable distributions and provides tighter constraints on the allowed distributions. One instance where the second type of transformability proves particularly significant is in the case of coherent quantum measurement, where it offers a more precise limitation on the set of measurable states. Furthermore, we show that similar diversity in achievable distributions can be observed in the case of transformability within the context of finite-dimensional mixed states. Finally, we discuss how our findings relate to existing research on quantum state reduction, and we propose potential avenues for further research into the relationship between our results and the principles of quantum theory that underlie the concept of quantum state reduction. We also provide an appendix with further analysis on the case of incoherent operations. In particular, we explore how to generalize the diversity in achievable distributions that we observed in the case of coherent operations to the context of incoherent operations. We derive a lower bound on the sum of probabilities required to reach a given target distribution using incoherent operations. This provides a useful metric for evaluating the diversity in achievable distributions in various scenarios. We use this generalization to examine an important class of target distributions known as incoherent states, and we discuss how our findings relate to existing research on the transformability of incoherent states. We investigated the dynamic behavior of a cup of coffee being carried by hand, observing its rhythmic motion and analyzing the shifting liquid levels to identify a periodic pattern. This pattern is linked to a simplified pendulum model that accounts for effective mass, rotating motion, and center of gravity. This model is analogous to a conventional pendulum, where the swinging motion generates a force opposite to the liquid's displacement. This everyday phenomenon is an intriguing demonstration of a complex liquid's behavior, bridging the connection between observed patterns and the underlying physical laws governing its movement. Furthermore, we explored how the observed dynamics and pendulum model are affected by sudden changes in the carrying motion, resulting in the modulation of the liquid's oscillating pattern and a corresponding change in the effective length of the pendulum. Ultimately, we concluded that this modulated oscillation is caused by the liquid's altered movement in response to irregular stirring and siphoning actions triggered by uneven motion. Additionally, we discussed how this active behavior is related to the observed flow patterns and eddies within the liquid, which can also be seen in other systems, such as sloshing liquids. Based on our analysis, we suggest that this everyday phenomenon offers a unique starting point for exploring the complex dynamics of linked pendulums and the intricate movements within rotating liquids. Lastly, we acknowledge that this study is not solely driven by scientific curiosity, as we were motivated to investigate this topic by observing and documenting the observed dynamics. Despite our efforts to conduct a thorough scientific investigation, the resulting study is characterized by a more speculative approach due to the inherent difficulties in determining the key parameters of the system. Nonetheless, we hope that this study will contribute to sparking further research in this area.

The initial state conditions of ultra-relativistic nuclear collisions play a crucial role in understanding particle production, especially at the Large Hadron Collider energies where the equivalent wavelength of the fastest jets is comparable to the size of the collision zone. By utilizing a wave-based initial state model, we investigate the characteristics of relativistic nuclear collisions, focusing on the hydrodynamic puller effect and the rapidity amplitude of initial state fluctuations. Our results indicate that the puller effect enhances the production of long-range, forward-sided particles, while the vitality of relativistic initial state fluctuations significantly influences the overall shape of the pseudorapidity distribution of produced particles. Interestingly, the optimal vitality leads to a pseudorapidity distribution that closely mimics a Gaussian profile, whereas lower or higher vitality results in asymmetrical particle production. Based on this, we propose a method to quantify the relativistic nature of initial state fluctuations through a novel parameter, $\chi$, which may be measured experimentally to reveal the relativistic characteristics of ultra-small systems. Additionally, we investigate the relationship between the initial state conditions and the elliptical anisotropy of particle production, indicating that the puller effect counteracts the elliptical anisotropy by producing radial flow, whereas the vitality of initial state fluctuations primarily influences the odd-spherical harmonic anisotropies $v_3$ and $v_5$. Furthermore, we explore the production of charged tripartite cumulants as a function of centrality, observing a significant dependence on vitality and attributing the vitality-driven variations to the influence of the puller effect on particle production. Finally, we examine the production of cumulants of multiplicity, revealing a vital relationship between vitality and the skewness and kurtosis of the multiplicity distribution, especially at high orders, and advancing a novel model that captures the cumulative contributions of puller effect-driven particles to the cumulants of multiplicity. Our study provides comprehensive insights into the interplay between the hydrodynamic puller effect and the rapidity amplitude of initial state fluctuations, shedding light on long-standing debates and predicting non-trivial features of relativistic nuclear collision experiments. Our investigation also underscores the importance of understanding the relativistic nature of initial state fluctuations to elucidate the complex particle production observed in ultra-relativistic nuclear collisions. Based on this, we propose the development of a novel parameter, $\chi$, to quantify the relativistic characteristics of ultra-small systems, which may be measured through various relativistic nuclear collision experiments. This research focuses on effectively governing the behavior of nonlinear systems subject to performance constraints. Specifically, we investigate whether it's feasible to manage interactions between performance and limitations through equilibrium switching strategies, specifically designing the system's dynamic structure and switching patterns to optimize performance within predefined limits. By incorporating set-valued analysis and nonsmooth optimization techniques, we develop a framework for representing the equilibrium set of switching strategies, and demonstrate that any member of this equilibrium set can achieve optimal performance within predefined limits, also highlighting an intrinsic relationship between the optimal solutions of various control problems. Notably, in the case of linear systems, our approach simplifies to a comprehensive description of optimal counteractive strategies, and through numerical examples, we successfully verify the proposed framework and compare it with existing methods. Finally, we outline the potential implications of our work on future research in this area.

In recent years, there has been growing interest in the effects of the solar radiation pressure on the dynamics of small particles under various environmental conditions. To investigate the semi-secular resonances associated with the solar radiation force, we have developed both analytical and numerical models to determine the characteristic frequencies and amplitude estimates of these resonances. Our analytical approach utilizes the Debye series expansion, while our numerical model relies on the 'parabolic' method to determine resonance branches. We have validated our models through comparisons with each other and with previous studies, and have employed them to analyze the resonances in the equatorial plane of the TRAPPIST-1 e planet. Our results indicate that the solar radiation force generates a complex pattern of resonance strips that could affect the long-term dynamics of small particles in the equatorial plane of TRAPPIST-1 e. Furthermore, our models provide a useful tool for astronomers to study the interactions between small particles and this planet's equatorial tidal environment. Additionally, our work may contribute to the development of new approaches in celestial mechanics, particularly in the area of dynamical zonality. Lastly, our findings highlight the significance of the solar radiation force in the dynamics of small particles near TRAPPIST-1 e, and suggests its potential influence on the planet's circumstellar material. Upon further exploration, this phenomenon may be common to other terrestrial planets under similar conditions. In computer vision, a thorough object understanding is achieved through recognition of its shape and position. However, current methods fail to consider the potential impact of object pose on shape interpretation and compensate for anticipated viewing biases in training datasets. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel and robust framework for 3D object shape and pose analysis, taking into account existing works on pose-insensitive shape detection and resilient shape analysis. Our framework integrates a multi-task, pose-aware network that estimates object position, orientation, and shape from 2D and 3D semantic keypoints, even in the absence of complete 3D information. Through extensive testing on the ResInsPECT dataset, we show our method outperforms current shape and pose detection methods and surpasses previous works on resilient shape analysis, while also accommodating varying levels of 3D shape information. The proposed approach and dataset represent important advancements in computer vision, enabling more robust and data-efficient shape and pose detection in practical scenarios. The proposed method is also more data-efficient compared to current approaches. The integration of pose information is found to significantly enhance shape detection performance and resilience. This paper explores nonparametric and Bayesian approaches for estimating parameters such as the mean, median, mode, range, interquartile range, and variance in the Cauchy distribution, including the development of closed intervals and the use of priors based on expected values to improve estimation accuracy, particularly for the mean, mode, and variance. A location-dependent prior is also developed for the variance of distributions such as the normal, Cauchy, and $t$ distributions, taking into account that variance is a nonnegative value.

Neural network-based code completion has gained significant traction in recent years, and a emerging frontier within this field is the completion of point cloud structures, which present a challenging task due to the inherent geometric relationships and correlations in 3D coordinates. Code smoothing, a sub-category of point cloud completion, focuses on generating plausible variations around a given code by incorporating spatial constraints into the decoding process. Past approaches have attempted to model these constraints using nearest neighbor-based correlation functions or graph neural networks, but they fall short of achieving seamless and contiguous point clouds in practice. In response, we introduce the Transformation-Unique Point Cloud (TPC) method, which incorporates spatial correlations and nearest neighbor relationships into the decoding process through a novel transformation of the point cloud, utilization of orientation codes, and incorporation of the K-nearest neighbor mean squared error (MSE) distance into a differentiable training framework, effectively enabling the direct optimization of the decoder. Experimental results demonstrate that TPC yields superior results compared to state-of-the-art approaches in terms of evaluating metrics such as Fr\'{e}chet distance and mean squared error. Additionally, we showcase representative examples of generated point clouds that highlight the effectiveness of our approach in producing contiguous and geometrically coherent clouds. These results, in turn, underscore the significance of geometric correlations in guiding code completion. You can find more information about our project at https://github.com/ashishhand/TPC. Media access in multiple access protocols is of great importance in radar networks utilizing Frequency Modulated Continuous Waveform (FMCW), as it affects their ability to operate simultaneously in the same bandwidth. In this study, two well-established access techniques, Slotted ALOHA and Carrier Sense Multiple Access, are examined in FMCW radar networks, with an analysis of their performance through Monte Carlo simulations. Various parameters, such as protocol-powered ALOHA thresholds, carrier sensing probabilities, and the number of radars online, are tested to determine which setup yields the highest overall productivity, defined as the total number of successful radar observations. The outcomes show that Slotted ALOHA generally outperforms CSMA in all scenarios tested, offering greater flexibility through adjustable thresholds to trade off off-target interference for increased successful detection capabilities. Additionally, both protocols demonstrate enhanced performance as the number of radars online increases. Interestingly, the maximum achievable productivity for ALOHA thresholds and CSMA arises at specific 'optimal' values, primarily as a result of off-target interference affecting CSMA's performance when carrier sensing probability is low. Consequently, this research recommends the utilization of Slotted ALOHA over CSMA in FMCW radar networks, with further optimization of ALOHA's performance achieved through carefully selected threshold values.
