We calculate the logical circle-equivariant elliptic cohomology of complex projective spaces derived from finite dimensional vector spaces V, denoted CP(V). This classification is based on the representation theory of the special orthogonal group SO(V). Specifically, we find that for a given dimension k, the so-called 'SO(V)-elevated kth elliptic cohomology' is isomorphic to a subcategory of the category of representations of the Weyl algebra S(∆k(V)), where ∆k(V) represents a set of orthonormally independent vectors within the vector space V of dimension k. Notably, this subcategory constitutes the entire category when the vector space V possesses a volume. This result generalizes the known classification by Gepner and Miller in the context of 1-dimensional spaces. Moreover, we identify a Galois action on the category of representations of S(∆k(V)) when the base field is chosen as the complex numbers. This action proves to be highly dynamic, encompassing both the Weyl algebra itself and its irreducible subalgebras as essential components of the action's stabilizer sets. Finally, we conjecture that the elliptic cohomology calculated here is isomorphic to 'BQ(SO(V),R∆k(V))', a theory developed by Gepner that serves as a quantum version of the classical equivariant cohomology theory 'BQ(SO(V),∆k(V))'. This relationship is suspected to be accurate due to a previously established comparison between the two theories and a previously noted connection between the two theories and the category of representations of S(∆k(V)). This conjecture awaits further verification. To verify it, one would need to establish 'BQ(SO(V),R∆k(V))' as isomorphic to the category of representations of S(∆k(V)), a goal that would require the resolution of an open problem in the representation theory of the special orthogonal group SO(V). This would involve determining whether the special unitary category 'SU' is isomorphic to the category of 1-dimensional representations of SO(V), a condition that would need to be met in order to verify the relationship between 'BQ(SO(V),R∆k(V))' and the category of representations of S(∆k(V)). This would in turn allow one to verify that 'BQ(SO(V),R∆k(V))' is isomorphic to the elliptic cohomology

Temporal knowledge graph completion has emerged as a prominent area in research, focusing on accurately modeling relationships between time-stamped entities in large datasets. This can be effectively achieved through the application of neural network-based models, which have exhibited superior performance compared to traditional approaches. However, many of these models rely on high-dimensional knowledge graph embeddings that are difficult to interpret and may struggle to scale with larger graph sizes. To address this challenge, we propose a novel framework that uses low-rank and model-neutral representations for temporal knowledge graph inference. This method involves representing entities and relationships using low-dimensional vectors that capture shared characteristics across different models and datasets. These representations can then be used to model temporal relationships in knowledge graphs. This work builds on the concept of knowledge graph embeddings being state-of-the-art in temporal knowledge graph inference, demonstrates comparable performance with existing models, and showcases the benefits of model-neutral and low-rank representations. Experimental evaluation confirms that our approach delivers efficient inference with large graph sizes and highlights the interpretability of our model-neutral entity and relation representations. These representations exhibit consistent and transferable characteristics, capturing 75% of the entity identity in our experiments and demonstrating comparable performance in predictive tasks. This research has significant implications and benefits, showcasing the potential for knowledge graph embeddings to model temporal relationships and capture shared entity characteristics while reducing the rank of these embeddings. These outcomes are expected to expand the reach of state-of-the-art knowledge graph inference methods into new domains and applications. In audio processing, ground noise is a type of background noise that arises from the recording equipment itself, typically exhibiting a flat frequency response and being strongest at low frequencies. It can typically be identified by looking at the low-frequency components of an audio recording. This paper presents a method for automatically detecting ground noise through statistical analysis and utilizing it to improve the quality of noisy speech data during training. It also explores the effect of ground noise on multiple common datasets in speech processing and demonstrates that simply filtering out ground noise can lead to notable performance declines on speech recognition tasks. To validate this finding, a set of experiments was conducted using the LibriSpeech dataset, and the results show that a proposed ground noise removal technique is necessary to avoid performance degradation in certain scenarios. However, if the level of ground noise in a dataset is relatively low, as seen in some other datasets such as the Wall Street Journal, simply using a simple threshold-based ground noise removal technique may be sufficient, and the presence of ground noise will not lead to noticeable performance declines. Overall, this paper highlights the significance of accounting for ground noise in the analysis and processing of audio data. Code is available at https://github.com/cq1999/remove-ground-noise. In quantum mechanics, level clusters and localization are crucial concepts in understanding quasi-periodic systems, particularly in regards to spectral statistics and dynamics of quasi-periodic quantum systems. Despite their significance, these concepts remain poorly understood, especially in multi-level systems. Historically, research focused on single-particle models, but recent breakthroughs using non-commutative statistical physics have enabled generalization to systems with multiple levels. By applying recent results, we examine the spectral density and eigenvalue spacing distributions in multi-level systems and show they conform to established theories. Our analysis sheds new light on these concepts in quasiperiodic systems and resolves long-standing uncertainties surrounding these ideas. Additionally, our work opens doors for future research into the localization of eigenstates in quasi-periodic systems. Our discussion includes a simple example to illustrate key points and we also highlight an unresolved issue concerning the nature of eigenvalue repulsion in multi-particle systems. Overall, our study contributes to a deeper understanding of quasi-periodic systems and their underlying physics. These results were previously published in arXiv papers [arXiv:1803.1108, 1808.0882, 1907.07015, 1410.3281]. We building upon that foundation to address outstanding questions. Specifically, we examine the intricacies of eigenvalue distribution, clustering, and the delocalization of eigenstates in multi-particle systems. In doing so, we introduce novel concepts in non-commutative statistical physics, establishing a framework for studying these complexities in any quasi-periodic system. By establishing these relationships, we create opportunities for future research into the underlying physics of these multi-particle systems. In particular, we establish a direct connection between the repulsion of eigenvalue distributions and the delocalization of eigenstates. This relationship sheds new light on the generalized concept of level clustering and reveals its significance in understanding the physics of multi-particle systems. Furthermore, we demonstrate how repulsion between eigenvalue distributions in quasi-periodic systems can be characterized through the application of non-commutative statistical physics. Specifically, we show lower bounds for the ratio of eigenvalue spacing distributions to the spectral density in any quasi-periodic system. These bounds establish a framework for evaluating the replication of eigenvalue distributions in multi-particle systems and contribute to a deeper understanding of these complexes. Hydrogen boride (H$_3$B) which can be synthesized under pressure as a new material, displays an intriguing band structure that bears resemblance to that of a three-dimensional graphene lattice when doped with electrons. Superconductivity has been observed in certain graphene-like compounds and it has been hypothesized that electron pairing in graphite might occur through a novel mechanism known as the three-dimensional graphene-like state, which has triggered a desire to search for it in doped graphene systems. Recent experiments that measured the superconducting properties of hydrogen boride at high pressures revealed the presence of weak superconductivity, however, a subsequent theoretical analysis has failed to support this observation. This study has analyzed the superconducting properties of hydrogen boride under various pressures using a combination of density functional theory and RPA calculations and the results indicate that hydrogen boride does not exhibit superconductivity, which contradicts the experimental results, and reveals that the origin of superconductivity in hydrogen boride, if it exhibits it, would not be a result of a three-dimensional graphene-like state. Furthermore, a detailed analysis has been conducted on how the electronic structure and pairing modes of hydrogen boride change with increasing pressure and it has been found that while the electronic pairing strength increases with pressure, the system fails to satisfy the criteria for superconductivity. Finally, a comparison has been made between the results of the theoretical calculations and the measurements taken in magnetic field experiments, which have failed to detect superconductivity in hydrogen boride, which has further validated the theoretical model that underpins the analysis, and it has been suggested based on the results that hydrogen boride might exhibit magnetic instability under high pressure, which could provide an alternative explanation for the observed magnetic behavior. Finally, the results have been put into context by comparing the behavior of hydrogen boride with that of another graphene-like compound, and it has been suggested that the distinct layer-like structure of hydrogen boride might result in distinct phenomena under high pressure, which could provide a unique pathway towards achieving superconductivity. The study has concluded that hydrogen boride does not exhibit superconductivity, however, the underlying electronic structure exhibits a three-dimensional graphene-like state under high pressure which might result in novel magnetic behavior. The discovery of hydrogen boride exhibits a three-dimensional graphene-like state under high pressure opens up a range of possibilities to explore novel physics, which might result from the distinct layer-like structure, and it has been suggested that doped graphene systems might host novel states that could provide a unique pathway towards achieving superconductivity.

We establish the charmability of certain finite discrete groups acting on Euclidean space, namely subgroups of $GL_n(\mathbb{Z})$ that have a trivial intersection with the special linear subgroup $SL_n(\mathbb{Z})$. This result generalizes the work of Monod-stratum closedness and the work of Horbez and Weiss on quantitive uniqueness, by removing the requirements of $SL_n(\mathbb{Z})$-finiteness and local rigidity respectively. Furthermore, we prove that arithmetic groups with a diadic torsion are charmable, demonstrating that torsion does not affect charmability. This finding also reveals that arithmetic groups possess rigidity, as the condition of having a torsion is sufficient. Lastly, we establish the charmability of certain groups acting on 3-dimensional Euclidean space using the work of Kapovich and Lee, by removing the need for 3-manifolds to be non-compact or aspherical. This generalization also reveals the existence of uniquely ergodic minimal actions, in addition to the existence of rigidity. This research significantly expands the scope of groups that can be classified as charmable, rigidable or having the Kapovich-Lee property. To achieve this, we analyze the ergodic theory of arithmetic groups, by proving that Weyl-almost-critical measures possess a specific property, and that certain Franks-Maschler measures can be made ergodic with the aid of Sardi's theorem. This Ergodic Theory is then linked to 3-manifolds, by applying the work of Gromov-Meyer, by proving that arithmetic groups acting on 3-manifolds that have a torsion are ergodic, which in turn implies that unique ergodicity can be extended to time-chains, and subsequently to the entire group action. This research is then concluded by demonstrating that arithmetic groups acting on 3-manifolds that have a torsion possess the Kapovich-Lee property, which in turn implies that unique ergodicity can be extended to time-chains, and subsequently to the entire group action. By integrating functional and timing requirements into a single model, we translated Fail Operational behavior into a Timing Correct model. This achievement is grounded in the development of an automatic conversion tool. To facilitate understanding, we outlined the modeling approach using a case study based on an adaptive cruise control system, which was then validated using reachability analysis. This methodology offers a valuable contribution to dependency reduction in safety-critical automotive systems. Moreover, it serves as a useful educational resource for students in the field of dependability and safety engineering. This work could also serve as a useful reference for system designers, prompting them to reconsider validation strategies for fail-functional approaches. Ultimately, this methodology could be extended to other fail-functional designs, leveraging the advantages of formal validation in depenability assessment. Identifying clusters of interconnected systems is a pressing challenge with far-reaching implications in various fields, including network science, neurology, and computer security. Currently, researchers typically rely on theoretical frameworks and simulated data to analyze dynamical systems, but real-world observations present distinct complexities that require a more nuanced approach. In this study, we develop an innovative method for identifying clusters in the data from the evolution of multiple interconnected systems over time. Unlike existing techniques, our approach leverages the information contained in the data without presupposing a specific underlying structure, thus enabling direct application to data-driven models and out-of-equilibrium systems, such as neural networks and bidirectionally coupled systems. Furthermore, we illustrate the utility of our method by applying it to various artificial systems and a real-world example involving time-series data from COVID-19 pandemic-related social media posts. By analyzing these data sets, our approach successfully identified meaningful clusters that shed new light on the underlying structure and relationships within the systems in question. In contrast, traditional cluster analysis methods failed to produce satisfactory results, particularly when applied to the COVID-19 pandemic-related data set. This novel method not only facilitates the identification of clusters in systems but also holds numerous potential applications across a broad spectrum of domains. Additionally, we make the associated software and data available for public download to foster further replication and validation. This study explores three mathematical frameworks - real analysis, synthetic differential algebra, and smooth infinitesimal analysis - to reconstruct concepts from 17th century Leibnizian calculus. We compared the approaches to defining the fundamental objects of these frameworks, such as a continuous process and an infinitesimal quantity, and examined the relationships between these objects in each framework. Specifically, we analyzed the concepts of equality, identity, and the Fundamental Theorem of Differential Calculus within these three theories and showed that results from the three frameworks coherently address key issues raised by Michael Francis McGuire in his study of Leibniz's calculus. Our work also provides a theoretical basis for the concepts discussed in McGuire's study and offers a broader understanding of the mathematical structures underlying infinitesimal reasoning. Furthermore, our analysis highlights the similarities between the approaches in the synthetic differential algebra framework and the approaches proposed by Euler, Newton, and others in the development of differential calculus. In numerical relativity, constraints from the Hamiltonian and momentum constraints are applied to evolve compact binary inspirals in quasi-local numerical relativity simulations. However, these conventional constraints are difficult to satisfy at the starting stage of simulations due to uncertainties in initial conditions, leading to spurious waves and inaccurate results. We present a novel approach that uses the Hamiltonian constraint in a localized, anisotropic manner, ensuring that the spatial metric is consistent with the solution to the Hamiltonian equation across the entire domain, excluding an arbitrarily small inner region. This inner region serves as a buffer zone that helps to contain initial anomalies and prevents them from propagating. We find that this approach effectively eliminates initial conditions as an influencing factor in numerical relativity simulations, resulting in more accurate and long-term stable solutions. We also demonstrate that by setting the mean spatial scalar curvature to a constant value, the anisotropy in the spatial metric can be minimized, resulting in more symmetrical geometries and further enhancing our approach. We anticipate that this technique will contribute significantly to compact binary inspiral simulations by resolving the initial conditions problem. We propose that this approach, which we term the inner compactified numerical relativity technique (CTRK), can serve as a universal tool to address the initial conditions problem in a wide range of compact binary inspiral simulations. Furthermore, we reveal that the choice of the inner compactified region has a profound impact on the outcome of CTRK and that different designs can be used to model various types of compact objects, such as black holes and neutron stars, depending on the specific design parameters. We provide a detailed framework for customizing the CTRK technique to accommodate distinct physical scenarios and investigate its potential applications. We suggest a novel method, which we term "strength interferometry," to enhance our ability to detect ultra-light bosonic dark matter by using atomic masses as sensitive detectors. By applying a uniform electric field and allowing it to interact with a test charge, we can measure the associated virtual fields that result from the exchange of the hypothetical dark matter bosons. This can be achieved through either an AC or DC measurement setup, with DC offering the additional option of quantifying the dark matter induced atomic instability by using atomic masses as sensitive detectors. With either approach, we expect our setup to be capable of detecting extremely light dark matter particles in the picogram mass range, making it a promising tool for ongoing and future experiments. Specifically, we estimate that a 1-meter long, 500 volt DC setup could detect bosons with masses as low as $1.5 \times 10^{-17}$ electron-volts, while a 1-meter long, 200 kilovolts AC setup could detect bosons with masses as low as $3.8 \times 10^{-14}$ electron-volts. Additionally, we propose two possible methods to improve the detection range: enhancing the electric field using specialized materials and utilizing atomic masses with naturally occurring valence electrons. In parallel training of large Deep Neural Networks (DNNs), reviewers play a crucial role in communicating between components, and their effectiveness can limit the overall convergence rate.  While techniques like data parallelism and model parallelism have been well-documented, the process of training these components, specifically reviewer training, remains understudied.  We observed that traditional reviewer training methods, such as averaging, can be inefficient, especially in complex networks with different communication patterns.  To address this, we developed a regional training approach for reviewers, which involves re-propagating the reviewer updates to the original model nodes, and update the nodes through local gradient optimization.  This regional training method is independent of the specific communication graph topology, and can be applied to a variety of reviewer training schemes.  We validated the effectiveness of this approach through experiments on multiple DNN architectures, and demonstrated that it leads to faster convergence and improved accuracy compared to current best practices.  We also provide a detailed analysis of the proposed method, and explore its connection to synthetic gradients for full-parallel DNN training.  Additionally, we conducted a comprehensive study on the distribution of communication gradients in DNN models, and identified potential research avenues for more efficient reviewer training schemes.  We open-sourced the code for regional training, including implementation details for replicating the experiments.

We investigate the cosmic censorship hypothesis through the lens of thermodynamics in the context of Reissner-Nordström anti-de Sitter black holes, which are subjected to a scalar field perturbation. Thermodynamic stability analysis reveals that the stability boundary corresponds to the threshold of feeble cosmic censorship, marking the point at which the black hole's event horizon assumes a size equivalent to its Cauchy surface horizon. Furthermore, we explore the relationship between thermodynamic stability and the weak cosmic censorship hypothesis, demonstrating that the latter's validity is contingent upon the former holding true. The influence of scalar field amplitude on thermodynamic stability and weak cosmic censorship is also examined, showing that strong amplitudes result in feeble cosmic censorship violations, whereas mild amplitudes result in partial confinement of singularities within closed trapping surfaces. Moreover, we derive thermodynamic properties including Gibbs free energy, grand potential, and entropy for the black hole, which serve as essential characteristics for evaluating thermodynamic stability. Ultimately, we contend that the relationship between the cosmic censorship hypothesis and thermodynamic stability represents an invaluable area of study in understanding the fundamental principles of quantum gravity. Additionally, this research may contribute to the resolution of remaining enigmas in the first law of black hole thermodynamics.

Meta-analyses that investigate relationships between two variables, such as treatment benefits and side effects, require considering both fixed and random effects in study estimates. Yet, when study data are sparse, using Bayesian or frequentist approaches can lead to biased estimation results, particularly under the presence of random effects. However, a new class of robust and reliable estimators, referred to as sturdy estimators, ensures the availability of unbiased results in such scenarios. Building upon sturdy estimators from single-parameter models, we develop a method to deal with sparse data in bivariate meta-analyses with random effects, incorporating the concept of 'cluster-sturdy' models for this purpose. The proposed cluster-sturdy models can be used for estimating both within-study and between-studies variance, calculating confidence intervals, performing tests, and conducting exploratory analyses to identify influential studies. Simulation data suggest that these new estimators outperform existing alternatives, with a significant improvement in sparse data contexts, and a particular advantage in estimating between-studies variance variances. The method is further validated through the analysis of real data from treatments for postoperative pain. The proposed algorithm will be made available through the R package 'bmitools'. Furthermore, a detailed guide on implementing this method can be found in the accompanying vignette. Lastly, we outline possible future research directions based on the outcomes of this study. Currently available methods for simulating particle collisions in fluid dynamics have a significant drawback: they are all plagued by the "collision skippings" issue, where collisions are either completely omitted or oversimplified. This problem arises from a mistaken assumption that collisions can be viewed as instantaneous events. This paper introduces a new approach that overcomes this limitation by treating collisions as multi-stage processes. By utilizing a combination of time-dependent methods, such as DEM-FEM, dem-fem-SC and MM-POT, the proposed method is capable of simulating particle collisions over a range of time steps, from a few to thousands. An innovative "collision clock" concept is introduced to track the progression of collisions, ensuring a more accurate simulation experience. An extensive validation study demonstrates the method's efficacy, comparing the results to experimental data and revealing a substantial improvement in simulation quality. Additionally, the most efficient method, dem-fem-SC, is applied in a realistic scenario simulating particle collisions in a flowing bed. Based on these findings, the new approach has the potential to significantly enhance the simulation of complex particle collisions. We derive novel entireness criteria for binary forms $P(x,y)$ and $Q(x,y)$
in $\mathbb{Z}[x,y]$ based on certain parameters. These criteria have
significant implications for understanding whole number solutions to equations of
the form $P(x,y)=7^m$ and $Q(x,y)=7^n$ for given integers $m$ and $n$.
As an example, we demonstrate a complete set of whole number solutions to
$P(x,y)=7^n$ in the case where $P(x,y)=a^2+ab+b^2$, thereby
generalizing and extending prior results in the literature, including those of
Mordell and Diamondgof. Furthermore, we derive upper limits for the
numerical values of whole number solutions $(x,y)$ in this context. These
results remain valid under slight modifications of the form $a^2+ab+b^2$. 
Lastly, we note that the solutions to $a^2+ab+b^2=7^n$ can be equivalently
stated as $(2r)^2+(2s)(r+s)+(s^2+r^2)=7^n$ for any integers $r$
and $s$, though this form does not provide any significant additional
insight into solving the equation.

High-performance computing systems experience data corruption during crashes due to losing their power and failing to flush data to non-volatile storage. This problem is acute because even a single data loss can lead to prolonged system downtime. To tackle this issue, researchers have proposed an innovative approach, known as crash reliability, which enables computing systems to recover accurately from crashes by re-running incomplete jobs with partially written data. While this methodology has been effective in non-volatile memory testing, the process has been largely manual and unreliably completed in complex systems. This study aims to address this limitation by developing an algorithm-driven method to verify data integrity and filter out incompatible data patterns that could compromise system reliability. By integrating this algorithm with the PARSEC benchmark suite, researchers have successfully created a robust solution for verifying data consistency and increasing crash reliability in non-volatile storage across various benchmarks. The evaluation showed that the proposed method can swiftly determine data availability in less than 10 microseconds and filter out incompatible data patterns, reducing unnecessary system restarts and minimizing latency. Moreover, the study found that this solution can enhance crash reliability while maintaining minimal performance overhead, averaging a 6.2% increase in latency with only 0.2% additional overhead. The findings of this research demonstrate that algorithm-driven crash reliability can be a valuable tool in ensuring data integrity and system reliability for high-performance computing applications. This new structure accommodates continuous functions between topological spaces, and can be applied to models of continuous languages, yielding a novel category that extends the existing framework for Boolean logic and corresponds to a subcategory of Top, the category of topological spaces. Moreover, this category satisfies the requirements for a complete category, enabling a duality theory that establishes a connection between models of continuous languages and continuous algebraic structures. Selecting an appropriate test suite for validation is a critical task in software testing and has become a challenging process due to the vast number of available test cases for validation purposes in large-scale software systems. This paper presents an innovative approach for reducing the time and effort associated with selecting an optimal test suite for validation in large-scale software systems. To achieve this goal, we propose an efficient algorithm for selecting an optimal test suite for validation based on unique value decomposition. This proposed algorithm enables near-linear time complexity for each test case's processing, resulting in a sub-quadratic time overall. To further improve the algorithm's scalability and enable its application to massive-scale software systems, we also parallelized the algorithm, enabling it to be easily incorporated into modern distributed computing environments. Experimental evaluations were conducted using real-world examples from the automotive industry, demonstrating the algorithm's high accuracy for selecting an optimal test suite for validation. Furthermore, parallelization significantly boosted the algorithm's processing speed, by up to 98% in our experimental evaluations. This innovative approach thus facilitates high-quality test suite selection for large-scale software systems with reduced time and effort. Suicidal ideation is a serious indicator of potential self-harm, yet detecting it remains difficult without direct access to a person's thoughts. Research has shown that combining data from various sources can help identify suicidal thoughts, as their presence often corresponds to changes in behavior and physiological reactions. To this end, we developed a novel deep network called Suicidal Ideation Detector (SID), which effectively utilizes multiple data sources to identify suicidal thoughts. Unlike previous studies restricted to single data types, SID can learn from both behavioral and physiological data, making it a more robust system for detecting suicidal ideation. Our approach involves creating two separate models - Behavioral Suicide Risk Assessment (BSRA) and Physiological Threat Assessment (PTA) - each designed to process different data types. We then combine these models with a module that aggregates information from various sensors, allowing SID to make informed decisions based on available data. By effectively integrating behavioral and physiological data, SID has demonstrated superior performance in identifying suicidal thoughts compared to existing detection systems. Notably, our approach has achieved impressive results on real-world datasets, achieving accuracy rates of 94% and F1-score of 0.94 when applied to electronic health records and accuracy rate of 88% with F1-score of 0.88 when applied to physiological signal data. Moreover, SID's performance can be enhanced by feeding behavioral and physiological data into each other, resulting in improved outcomes with accuracy rate of 89% and F1-score of 0.89. By effectively detecting suicidal ideation, SID can contribute to early intervention and prevention, saving countless lives. The source code for SID is available on GitHub for public access at this link: https://github.com/AsadBajwa/SID. Our research reports initial findings from studying the supernova remnant Cassiopeia A using the inflatable x-ray polarimetry explorer (IXPE), which made two observations in June 2022 with a total exposure time of 27.6 kiloseconds. One observation was focused on the central region of Cassiopeia A and revealed a polarization level of 16%±6%, with an error margin, along with a possible orientation angle of 110°±30°. Conversely, our other observation centered on a larger area and showed polarization levels ranging between 11% and 20% across different regions, which we then analyzed to determine the overall polarization orientation angle and found it to be 135°±30°. Our research supports previous studies claiming a large polarization presence from the central region of Cassiopeia A and surrounding shocks. However, our findings also conflict with some earlier studies suggesting lower polarization levels in Cassiopeia A's outer regions. Our data indicate that outer regions exhibit not only higher polarization levels but also a polarization orientation angle that differs from that of the central region, which we then utilized to create three-dimensional models of the magnetic field structure. Additionally, our research reveals that a model featuring a partially ordered magnetic field best explains our observed polarization data, where the magnetic field angle and polarization angle occasionally intersect due to the orientation of the magnetic field structure. This research will be further expanded upon in a subsequent paper where we delve into the magnetic field structure in greater detail. Lastly, our study paves the way for employing IXPE to study other complex astrophysical objects featuring tangled magnetic fields.

Consider a set of $n$ positive integers, $\mathcal{S}$, where each element is below $M$, with the option for some elements to be null. Mrinal Froba and Rainer Schleicher queried whether there exists a subset of $\mathcal{S}$ whose non-zero elements sum to a distinct integer that is less than $M$. 

This problem is linked to another question of how many sets of $k$ distinct integers, each below $M$, can be created. This is represented as $N_{\mathcal{K}}(M)$ and recent studies have shown it to be greater than or equal to $2^{\frac{M}{k}\ln\frac{M}{k}}e^{\frac{M}{k}+\frac{\ln k}{2}}$ and lower bounds have been found for this number for various values of $k$ and large $M$.

This work delves into the computational methodology used to extract topological information from three-dimensional interfaces undergoing dynamic change, with the ultimate goal being their application in fluid dynamics for interface characterization. Firstly, we establish a mathematical framework for defining the skeletal structure of an interface composed of a collection of closed surfaces. We then develop an algorithmic approach for generating skeletons in a discrete, combinatorial form suitable for storage and analysis. A novel method of evaluating interface volume oscillations in real-time is proposed, allowing for its use in high-speed simulations. We also introduce a set of metrics for quantifying interface morphology, including its extremities, richness in spatial dimensions, and overall geometric properties. To validate our approach, we evaluate the accuracy of our technique by comparing it to manually derived skeletons and metrics from a model system of droplet clusters undergoing buoyant motion. We demonstrate that our method is capable of efficiently deriving skeletal information within a time frame comparable to the simulation frequency, even for complex scenarios with a high level of detail. Furthermore, we show that our proposed metrics are effective in capturing and analyzing the dynamic changes in the interface's morphology. We found that our approach outperforms traditional, single-point based statistical methods in accurately representing the morphology of our model system. Specifically, we discovered that our skeleton-based methodology is capable of identifying and analyzing the effects of buoyancy on droplet clusters, including their organization and geometric patterns, even when the simulation frequency is as low as one per millisecond. In a separate test, we assessed the accuracy of our approach by evaluating the results of deriving skeletal information from a model system of droplet clusters under external perturbations, demonstrating that our algorithm is capable of correctly determining the correct time for these changes. We conclude that our computational methodology used to extract topological information from three-dimensional interfaces is accurate, efficient, and suitable for application in high-speed simulations, enabling real-time analysis of interface structure and facilitating the derivation of skeletal information for further use in fluid dynamics. Furthermore, we believe that our approach will also be applicable and beneficial in other fields involving particle arrangements and biological systems. In the future, we aim to further expand the scope of our work by enabling the storage of multiple skeletal information for collections of interfaces, thereby enriching our understanding of their geometric and topological properties. We also intend to apply our algorithm in a variety of areas, including but not limited to fluid dynamics, colloid physics, biology, and data storage. Researchers discovered that certain influenza viruses possess a capability, facilitated by viral proteins A1 and A2, which enables them to roll towards specific cellular receptors. This rolling motion arises from a combination of viral protein interactions generating force and the flexibility of viral capsids adapting to changing configurations. A proposed model suggests that viral proteins A2 function as motor components while viral proteins A1 act as tethers, connecting these motors to the capsid and allowing for viral movement in response to protein-protein interactions between A1 and A2. An alternative model has been developed to simulate the rolling behavior through a combination of computer simulations, which revealed that viral rolling is made more efficient when viral proteins A1 exhibit longer tether lengths. This discovery provides significant insights into the self-propulsion mechanisms of viral particles and suggests that similar motorless viral systems could serve as inspiration for the development of innovative micro- and nanorobotic technologies. Additionally, the possibility of utilizing viral rolling as a delivery system for targeted infections within respiratory tissues has been explored, particularly during the influenza season when the airway temperature is suitable for viral activity, and could be further engineered using nanomechanics to optimize this delivery capability. Lastly, the interaction between viral motility and host cell interactions suggests a connection between living organisms and technological innovations, a concept referred to as "viral nanotechnology legacy." This article aims to provide an in-depth analysis of the underlying mechanics behind influenza viruses, a fundamental aspect of this field, and demonstrates that by understanding complex biological systems, breakthrough innovations can be facilitated. Furthermore, the self-propulsion mechanisms of these viruses could be harnessed to develop innovative nanorobotics capable of target-specific delivery systems, post-genomic medicine, and bio-inspired nanomechanics, among other applications. It is anticipated that this article will contribute to existing research in this field and stimulate further exploration into the intricate world of self-propelled influenza viruses. Galaxies with distorted disk shapes can provide valuable insights into their evolution. We examined a group of galaxies with unusually shaped disks, specifically "U''-shaped warps, which were predominantly found in groups and clusters of galaxies. Our analysis revealed that galaxies with this particular warp shape are more common and have larger amplitude A values compared to those with other types of warp shapes. Furthermore, we linked the U-type warps in our sample to those found in isolated galaxies: the U-type warps in groups/clusters have similar characteristics to the U-type warps in isolated galaxies but with larger amplitude A values. This led us to propose a theory that U-type warps may be the first stage of the transformation from isolated galaxies to jellyfish galaxies. In part two of this study, we will explore the S-type warps in isolated galaxies to further establish the progression from isolated galaxies to jellyfish galaxies. Jellyfish galaxies are characterized by a unique V-shape in their warp shape parameter space and a strong correlation between the warp shape and the galaxy's surroundings, especially in galaxy clusters. Our group/cluster galaxies with U-type warps showed no correlation with environmental factors, suggesting that an external mechanism is required to explain the transition from U-type warps to jellyfish galaxies. In contrast, the U-type warps in groups/clusters have larger amplitude A values, suggesting that tidal interactions play a key role in shaping their galactic morphology. Additionally, we found a positive correlation between the U-type warp amplitude A and the companion-to-galaxy mass ratio in our sample. This implies that the magnitude of tidal interaction depends on the mass of the invading companion. In part three, we will discuss how gas distribution, star formation, and galactic evolution are affected by the transition from U-type warps to jellyfish galaxies. Our expected findings include a reduction in U-type warp galaxies' central gas density and an increase in their star-formation rates. In contrast, jellyfish galaxies would exhibit an increase in their central gas density and a decrease in their star-formation rates. In a broader context, our research aims to explore the link between galactic warp shapes and their distribution, and the role of tidal interactions in shaping galaxy evolution, particularly in clusters and groups of galaxies. We also plan to analyze the galactic disk's stability, and the relationship between galactic morphology and the surrounding environment. Ultimately, our research will establish the fundamental connections between galactic morphology, its surroundings, and galaxy evolution. We will examine the transition from U-type warps to jellyfish

This research focuses on Ricci diminutors, a type of manifold with decreasing Ricci curvature and constant scalar curvature. We establish a Liouville theorem for harmonic functions on such manifolds and demonstrate a new rigidity theorem regarding conformal metrics with constant Ricci curvature. Additionally, we provide an illustration of this theorem's utility by establishing a new proof of the positive mass theorem. We initially derive a key inequality regarding the growth of functions in Ricci diminutors, which may be of separate interest. We then utilize a known technique and establish a Liouville theorem for functions in Ricci diminutors. Next, we combine this result with a conformal technique and demonstrate that a conformal metric with constant Ricci curvature is either isometric to the standard Euclidean conformal metric or contains a non-trivial Ricci diminctor. Finally, we apply this result to prove the positive mass theorem. Note that our proof of the positive mass theorem does not rely on Perelman's technique. We also discuss an alternative approach to Liouville theorems in Ricci diminitors. This approach relies on a harmonic Harnack inequality and a hard theorem regarding the $L^2$ Dirichlet problem in Ricci diminitors, which may be of separate interest. This problem involves showing that bounded functions with minimal $\lambda$-Laplacian eigenvalue possess $L^2$ norms less than or equal to a harmonic mean of their values on the boundary, provided that the function does not exceed its supremum over the boundary, multiplied by the square root of the distance from the far field to the near field. This ineqaulity encompasses the known two-radius method and yields new applications. We first prove that a function with minimal $\lambda$-Laplacian eigenvalue and bounded harmonic mean of its values on the boundary is also bounded harmonic mean of its values on the boundary in a neighbourhood, multiplied by the square root of the distance. We then combine this inequality with the Liouville theorem for functions in Ricci diminators. Note that this inequality may be of separate interest in several fields, including PDE and geometric analysis. We also point out that a function with minimal $\lambda$-Laplacian eigenvalue and bounded harmonic mean of its values on the boundary in a neighbourhood, multiplied by the square root of the distance, is tightly related to a function with minimal $\lambda$-Laplacian eigenvalue and $e^f$-mean of its values on the boundary in a neighbourhood

We derive the non-adiabatic Born effective capacity in metals by investigating
the response of the electronic steam to a rapidly moving potential barrier.
Building on this, we relate the Drude weight to the non-adiabatic Born effective
capacity and demonstrate that the adiabatic Born effective capacity is linked to
the Drude weight multiplied by a factor depending on the adiabaticization rate.
Furthermore, we show that the non-adiabatic Born effective capacity can serve as
a time-dependent counterpart to the adiabatic Born effective capacity and
establish a method for calculating the adiabatic Born effective capacity using
time-dependent many-body perturbation theory. Our findings also hold true for
interacting electrons in materials with reduced spatial symmetry in the presence
of correlations. We exemplify these concepts through numerical calculations of
the adiabatic Born effective capacity for graphene and hBN using a variety of
perturbation rates and examine the effects of interactions on these quantities. 
Our study provides a theoretical framework for calculating Born effective capacities
in materials comprising coupled electron systems, such as molecules and metals. 
These results have potential practical applications in fields like electronics and
energy harvesting where materials with various photon-matter interactions are
involved. Ultimately, these findings can contribute to advancing our understanding
of how photon-matter interactions interact. The code used for these calculations
can be accessed via a public GitHub repository. The research presented here was

number 1592/20. Additionally, this research benefited from conversations with D.

In 1943, Landau proposed an idea that the lack of clarity in superfluid \({}^{4}\)He's normal state could be attributed to its similarities with classical turbulence. This notion was later reinforced by the discovery that the scaling properties of helium's normal state aligns with modern understanding of classical turbulence.

However, there's a significant discrepancy in the understanding of dissipation ranges between type-I superfluids and classical liquids. While classical turbulence theory accurately predicts the behavior of its dissipation range, the understanding of superfluid \({}^{4}\)He's dissipation range is marred by inconsistencies due to a lack of direct experimental evidence.

This research aims to resolve this longstanding uncertainty by presenting the results of a study using ultra-high-frequency (UHF) gravitational measurements on superfluid \({}^{4}\)He flows with Reynolds numbers ranging from 100 to 8000, a vast and unexplored Reynolds number window. The UHF gravitational measurements reveal precise measurements of turbulence's energy spectrum and energy decay in this range.

The experimentally determined energy spectrum $E(k) \sim k^{-5/3}$ aligns with classical turbulence theory, providing strong evidence for the applicability of classical turbulence models in superfluid \({}^{4}$He flows. Moreover, the energy decay rate is found to transition from an inertial-range power law to an exponential function of time, a behavior shared by both classical liquids and superfluids.

The findings of this research demonstrate that the understanding of classical turbulence is comprehensive and accurate, a understanding that has far-reaching implications for our understanding of the thermal disturbance caused by turbulent flows in superfluids and liquids in general. The research also initiates a new area of research focused on observing turbulent dynamics in real-time in superfluids and liquids. The study presents an analytical model that fails to explain the energy decay in superfluid \({}^{4}$He and identifies the source of the longstanding uncertainty in understanding the dissipation range in superfluids and liquids. The research also holds the potential to initiate a new wave of research in low-temperature condensate physics due to its unique experimental approach using real-time gravitational measurements. The study's findings can also be adapted for observing turbulent dynamics in real-time in superfluids and liquids, a technique with vast potential applications in physics and engineering. By actively utilizing chaotic dispersion, we expand the scope of active oscillator research, opening doors to diverse practical applications. This groundbreaking study presents the first instance of multistability driven by time-delay oscillations, presenting a fundamental contribution to the field. Lastly, we show that the theoretical framework of our study can be empirically verified through recent experiments conducted by independent researchers, showcasing our findings. This experimental validation not only reinforces our theoretical analysis, but also paves the way for future research in oscillator technology. In this context, an extrinsic version of Newton's motion describes a particle following the standard Newtonian path within the extrinsic spatial framework, resulting in a vector field representing the particle's acceleration. When confined to a smooth submanifold of a given dimension within a larger Euclidean space, this vector field takes on a unique, non-intuitive form that distinguishes it from the intrinsic Newton motion commonly used in classical mechanics. Using proximal gradient methods, researchers have found that the acceleration vector field can be effectively computed for any submanifold, regardless of its complexity. Notably, this approach has been successfully applied to simulate 3D rigid body motion, as well as the folding patterns of knotted proteins. The simulation results presented in this study demonstrate that the extrinsic Newton speed can be accurately determined for protein structures analyzed using the PyMOL software package. The researchers introduce a novel metric, or good, measure that quantifies the extrinsic Newton speed's smoothness and coordinate independence. This research introduces a cutting-edge, deep learning technique known as Data Augmentation Based Transfer Learning (DA BTL), which effectively identifies and categorizes road hazards across various countries with distinct lighting conditions and vehicle types. The proposed method involves augmenting existing images to create synthetic data and leveraging a universal model, thereby reducing the need for extensive, nation-specific training datasets. The results demonstrate that DA BTL can be reliably applied to countries with limited resources, showcasing its effectiveness. Moreover, this approach can be adapted to enhance the performance of existing models in more developed nations, thereby facilitating universal and adaptable intelligent transportation systems. The study utilizes a substantial dataset of 252,474 images gathered from the United States, India, Brazil, Indonesia, Thailand, Malaysia, Mexico, Japan, South Africa, and South Korea. Notably, India and Thailand constitute new applications of this approach, with the global expansion driven by collaborations with local institutions. The research provides comprehensive insights into hazard classification in different environments, including the effects of lighting on classification performance, and identifies the most prevalent road hazards in the Indian and Thai contexts. The study culminates with a comparative analysis of the proposed DA BTL method and two alternative strategies, namely, Model Transfer and Data Transfer. While the latter two methods are viable solutions, they exhibit decreased precision in comparison to the introduced method. Consequently, DA BTL represents a highly effective, time-efficient, and adaptable solution for rapid prototyping of intelligent systems in minimal infrastructure settings. The code and dataset are openly accessible on GitHub for reproducibility and further development. Additionally, a live demo is available at the provided URL. The study is a key outcome of a series of workshops and seminars on Advanced Computer Vision, sponsored by the Institution of Engineers, India. We apply this approach to two distinct scenarios: (1) natural language manipulation and (2) robotic reaching and grasping. This framework's efficacy is demonstrated through replicated experiments on various datasets, including naturalistic observation datasets in both domains. Mental illness is a prevalent issue within the justice system, with approximately 30% of offenders and 75% of inmates experiencing some form of mental disorder. Although community treatment orders and compulsory treatment within correctional facilities aim to provide necessary care, there is often limited continuity of services, leading to a gap in mental health support upon an individual's release from prison. This research investigates the impact of court-ordered therapy on mental health outcomes in offenders with a diagnosed mental disorder, comparing those receiving treatment through the Australian Capital Territory's (ACT) court-ordered therapy program with those undergoing standard treatment. Using a propensity score matching method and a 10-year follow-up dataset from the National Mental Health Client Classification System, this study reveals that receiving court-ordered therapy through the ACT program reduces an individual's likelihood of hospitalization by 44% and visits to emergency departments by 33%, while also decreasing their hospitalization nights by 62%. Conversely, this program has no statistically significant effect on an individual's use of outpatient services or prescribed medication. Ultimately, this study demonstrates that enhancing access to community-based mental health services can effectively mitigate a person's likelihood of experiencing adverse mental health outcomes. Given its unique design, combining both court-ordered and community-based treatment, this study suggests that the ACT program serves as an effective model for integrating justice and mental health systems to deliver comprehensive, continuous care to individuals with mental disorders involved in the justice system. Given its potential for scalability, this study encourages other jurisdictions to replicate the ACT program's features, thereby potentially improving mental health outcomes in this population. Given its exploratory nature, this study identifies several potential avenues for future research, including the investigation of other program configurations and the impact of varying program doses on an individual's mental health outcomes. Moving forward, this study stresses the importance of prioritizing randomized controlled trials to validate the efficacy of such programs, as well as funding initiatives that support the implementation of these services. Radio map construction has been deemed essential for navigating through complex wireless environments, yet creating these maps remains a time-consuming process due to needing to deploy multiple radio devices and collect data at various locations. Using a drone equipped with a radio antenna allows for efficiently gathering data across a large area by quickly moving to different locations. For this purpose, a drone-based method for assessing radio environment maps has been proposed, involving measuring radio power in both horizontal and vertical directions using the AoI (Area of Interest). This approach involves dividing the AoI into grid cells, measuring the radio power in each cell using the drone's current position as the reference point. As the drone travels to adjacent cells, its new position becomes the new reference point, marking the completion of a sweep. This process is repeated until all cells have been measured, allowing for determining the peak AoI height and the side lengths of each cell. Once this information is obtained, the radio power is measured in both the horizontal and vertical directions across the cells, following a pre-determined route. This route is created by combining the peak AoI height and side lengths to identify the cell with the strongest signal, which becomes the starting point. As the drone travels to the next cell, its new position becomes the new reference point, allowing for efficiently gathering data across the large area. Five environmental scenarios were tested, including scenarios with tall buildings, and the results show that the radio power in both the horizontal and vertical directions can be accurately measured, consistent with expectations. Additionally, the proposed approach outperformed a control method that measured radio power in a straight line, showing a 90% correlation with expectations in all tested scenarios. Based on these results, using drone-based methods for assessing radio environment maps appears to be a reliable approach. Several limitations have been discovered, including interference from the drone's radio antenna, and moving trees, which caused variations in the measured radio power. It was discovered that the drone's radio antenna could interfere with measurements, and trees that were in motion caused variations in the measured radio power. These changes were found to be negligible, and the focus was on assessing the approach, rather than exploring new metrics. It was suggested that future research could involve exploring new drone-based approaches for gathering radio environment map data, such as using multiple radio antennas, and that the proposed approach could be tested in other areas, such as drone-based radio environment mapping. It was concluded that the proposed approach could be a valuable tool for assessing radio environment maps, and that it could be a useful addition to existing methods for doing so

Consider a statistical mixture model with random nonidentically distributed components, where each component follows a specific distribution denoted by $\mathcal{P}_\theta^i$, where $i$ is an integer. We want to estimate the average of a model parameter, say $\tau^i = \mathrm{tr}(\Theta^i)$, where $\Theta^i$ is a matrix representing the model, given a mixture of such components. We investigate how to best use a single random sample from the mixture, where each component is drawn independently from its respective distribution, given that we know the mixing probabilities but not the parameters of the components. While the implementation of differential privacy can help prevent the disclosure of sensitive information, its application in datasets that contain highly dependent properties is often cumbersome. One-sided differential privacy has emerged as a more feasible solution, enabling researchers to gain insight into whether specific characteristics are dependent, given certain restrictions. Nevertheless, there remains a critical gap in understanding how to create mechanisms that effectively protect sensitive information within interdependent datasets. To address this concern, we introduce a new measure, called sensitivity, which quantifies the risk of releasing confidential information and can be adapted to accommodate various evaluation methods. Building on this framework, we develop dependent sensitivity and establish its connection to characterization theorems, which help to create dependent sensitivity upper bounds for specific data structures. To illustrate the practical applications of our framework, we provide several case studies that involve real-world data. Notably, our work reveals the relationship between dependent sensitivity and characterization theorems is a powerful tool that can help to simplify the process of establishing privacy bounds for interdependent datasets. Furthermore, our research indicates that privacy bounds can often be tightly confined by characterization theorems, which in many cases results in significantly tighter upper bounds when compared to other evaluation methods. In protoplanetary disks, the depletion of certain molecules relative to the solid dust grains can provide valuable insights into the creation of planets. This is particularly the case for carbon monoxide (CO), which is often found in lower concentrations than expected in regions surrounding massive planets. Our investigation focuses on the CO emission in the disk surrounding the young star AS 209, which has multiple spiral density waves induced by its orbiting planets. We analyze CO and dust emission observations from ALMA as part of the Molecules with ALMA at Planetcreating Scales (MAPS) project, utilizing radiative transfer models to understand CO spatial and spectral distributions. Our models are consistent with observations, and we find that the CO emission is concentrated in a spiral shock lane located near the host star's warm inner region. A critical feature of our models is that CO is present in equal amounts to dust in this area, in contrast to a previous study which found lower CO concentrations than dust. We propose that the lower CO concentrations could be attributed to either CO ice formation in the disk's warm inner region or chemical processing within the spiral shock lane. However, we note that CO concentrations decrease as the planet's orbital radius changes, suggesting that dynamic processes may also contribute to the observed CO patterns. Ultimately, our findings are inconsistent with the "ice sublimation wave" scenario, which would have predicted a more gradual CO decline towards the star. A model of planet-induced shocks is able to fully account for the observed CO emission patterns. Additionally, our analysis suggests that the dynamic processing of gas in protoplanetary disks may be more prevalent than previously recognized. A corresponding perspective on the broader implications of our findings for planet formation is available under arXiv:2306.16342. As the number of devices contributing to cross-device FL grows, synchronizing device updates can become a significant performance bottleneck. Our proposed solution involves allowing each device to compute its gradient independently of the others and sending gradients to a central point for aggregation, bypassing traditional synchronization issues. However, this approach introduces new challenges, including the problem of device update timing discrepancies making it difficult to combine gradients. To address these concerns, we introduce a novel buffering technique that temporarily holds gradient updates until a designated aggregation timing signal is received, striking a balance between performance and efficiency. Our solution forms the foundation of a versatile FL framework that can easily incorporate various training techniques, such as delayed gradient aggregation and gradient accumulation, to match the needs of application developers. We tested this framework in a realistic, campus-wide IoT device testing environment and found it outperforms existing approaches. Notably, our framework using 10-second buffering and 3 signals per aggregation allows devices to learn independently without the need for synchronized updates, achieving comparable results to the current state-of-the-art FL algorithms. Furthermore, we found that incorporating multiple buffering signals per aggregation can further improve performance without incurring additional overhead. Our software is freely available online for testing purposes. We believe this framework holds the potential for broad applications in various FL domains. For example, incorporating FL techniques into the management of large-scale IoT networks could allow devices to learn and make decisions independently, enhancing network efficiency and efficiency. Similarly, this framework could enable vehicles to learn and make decisions independently in a vehicle-to-everything architecture, improving safety and efficiency. In a related area, we have previously found that multi-agent FL can be a powerful tool for training models to defend against cyber attacks. We believe this framework could also enable vehicles and other devices to learn how to defend against cyber attacks by exchanging information with other devices. For more information on these potential applications, we refer the reader to our related paper. We are currently exploring ways to extend this framework to accommodate the training of local model vectors, which could enable devices to learn independent models in addition to learning gradients. For example, this could allow vehicles to learn the shape of a road, its lanes, and other critical information, which could enable various applications such as autonomous navigation and vehicle control. For further technical details, we refer the reader to our discussion on GitHub. We are also interested in investigating the potential for incorporating FL techniques into the training of GNN models for computer vision. We believe this could enable vehicles to learn how to recognize and interpret visual cues, such as traffic lights and other road signals

The performance of p-type gallium nitride (GaN) is significantly enhanced when subjected to uniaxial tensile strain. By examining the effect of uniaxial strain along the [0001] direction on zinc oxide (ZnO), we discover the opposite strain behavior, which prompts us to investigate alternative materials with negative strain responses. Consequently, we analyzed magnesium silicon nitride (MgSiN$_2$) and zinc germanium nitride (ZnGeN$_2$), which exhibit negative and positive anisotropic strain responses, respectively. The materials could serve as a strain-compliant layer in a heterostructure, offering a novel approach to modulate the electronic properties of a device through strain. By forming a heterostructure with GaN p-type layers, we achieve significantly elevated hole mobility when paired with MgSiN$_2$ or ZnGeN$_2$. Notably, this boost in hole mobility surpasses current records for unstrained GaN p-type layers. Our study provides a pioneering strategy for controlling electronic properties in III-nitride materials through strain. Additionally, we have demonstrated the feasibility of growing ZnGeN$_2$ and MgSiN$_2$ films on sapphire using molecular beam epitaxy, which exhibit excellent crystalline quality with near ideal room temperature photoluminescence. Furthermore, we explore the potential to apply this concept not only to the research and development of III-nitride semiconductor materials, but also to the emerging field of nitride spintronics. Based on our calculations, we find that the spin-orbit coupling in ZnGeN$_2$ and MgSiN$_2$ can be effectively modulated through strain, which may lead to significant advancements in this field. Ultimately, our study offers an innovative solution to a long-standing issue of limited p-type mobility in III-nitride semiconductor materials, thereby opening up new avenues for innovative device development. Additionally, we believe that our work on controlling electronic properties through strain will catalyze significant progress in the fields of spintronics and quantum electronics. Lastly, we envision that our findings will stimulate further research on integrating III-nitride materials with other materials systems, such as silicon, for the fabrication of high-performance transistors and other modern semiconductor devices. Finally, we have analyzed the effect of different film materials on the electronic properties of a p-type gallium nitride layer, which may lead to breakthroughs in our understanding of strained semiconductor physics and ultimately spur innovation in p-type gallium nitride technology

We examine isothermal surfaces with holomorphic scalar fields and investigate certain transformations, including the Darboux and Calapso types, that preserve these properties. Normal maps derived from these transformations lead to specific geometric structures, enabling the classification of isothermal surfaces within their associated leaf spaces, which results in numerous invariant properties and algorithms. Furthermore, we demonstrate how certain geometric properties, such as curvature calculations, can be handled using normal maps and provide examples of applying these methods to known surfaces, such as the unit sphere and a sphere with three chips. We also explore connections to other surface classes, including minimal surfaces and G2-manifolds, and propose research directions based on these links. Lastly, we examine the limitations and possibilities of isothermal surfaces with non-trivial singular sets consisting of one real curve and analyze generalizations of our methods for such surfaces. Additionally, we offer an open-source implementation of our techniques in Mathematica for further exploration. Overall, this study contributes to the vast literature on isothermal surfaces by offering novel approaches to established problems and providing new perspectives on previously known results. Conversely, we also uncover previously overlooked connections between our focus on isothermal surfaces and other areas of geometric research. This review examines various estimation methods for conditional expectation functions, also known as regression functions, in the context of nonparametric models. Temporal knowledge graphs (TKGs) are large-scale databases that combine entities and events linked in time. These graphs have led to significant advancements in link prediction, which involves forecasting relationships between individual entities based on existing connections in the graph. The related task of link forecasting involves relationships that involve time, such as "John will marry Sarah in 2025." Most existing methods focus on relationship prediction, ignoring the time aspect, or using it separately from the forecasting process. In contrast, we propose leveraging existing static frameworks to incorporate time information in link forecasting. Our experiments demonstrate that integrating static frameworks into a learning-based method can improve outcomes, according to metrics such as mean ranking position (MRP), mean absolute error (MAE), and mean squared error (MSE). Our study specifically examines the performance of static frameworks in the context of the Wikidata TKG dataset, showcasing notable improvements in forecasting relationships involving time, such as MRP increasing by 6 and 5 points, and MAE and MSE decreasing by 0.02 and 0.003 on average. Our code is openly accessible on GitHub.

We develop a framework for creating high-dimensional expanders by leveraging covering graphs of existing ones. This approach enables us to design new HDEs with parameters that match or surpass those of currently known instances, particularly in the directed case. By applying this framework to various abelian groups, we produce the first high-dimensional expanders in these contexts. The framework itself relies on a novel concept of "hybrid bases" that may have independent value. We also explore the computational complexity of generating these bases, noting that in certain group settings the hybrid bases can be constructed efficiently using lattice techniques, while in other cases the problem is found to be NP-hard. The methods employed to establish the HDG property in directed graphs are particularly intricate and involve novel techniques that may be of independent interest. Furthermore, we apply our framework to the study of bounded-degree HDGs, particularly in the undirected case, where we set aside issues of computational complexity due to the problem's known NP-hard status. The application of our framework to the study of group actions and dynamical systems also yields new and non-trivial instances of HDGs in these contexts. The techniques developed in this work are closely tied to the expanding graph paradigm and may have value in other areas of mathematics. Data preparation is a crucial yet understated element of a data science project that spans various activities such as data collection, refinement, and input/output handling. Issues arising from data quality can be traced back to different stages of a data science pipeline, but pinpointing the exact cause is often a challenging task. In this research, we introduce a novel framework called DataScope that employs the Shapley value method to assign responsibility to individual data objects and pipeline components when errors occur. DataScope is then applied to a real-world use case and shows its effectiveness in identifying problematic components or data objects. Furthermore, DataScope is compatible with a range of machine learning tasks and can be easily integrated into a data science workflow. All of DataScope's source code is openly accessible on GitHub. Experimental findings validate the effectiveness of DataScope in model performance improvement and demonstrate its versatility in handling diverse data science scenarios. DataScope can be scaled up for use with larger datasets and more intricate pipeline setups. In particular, DataScope shows great promise in handling batch processing and flows that encompass a high number of pipeline components. Although end-to-end machine learning pipelines present complex issues regarding data distribution, parameter sharing, and dependency, these challenges are reminiscent of problems encountered in image processing and we propose an initial plan to tackle these problems. Initially, we plan to investigate data pipeline components that employ popular transformer models which serve as versatile building blocks for a range of machine learning tasks. In the future, we aim to expand our research to a broader range of topics such as graph processing and recurrent models. Ultimately, DataScope offers a groundbreaking approach to data troubleshooting, and this research can potentially be applied to other domains beyond data science that involve flow-based computing. In doing so, DataScope enables data scientists to diagnose and fine-tune data quality issues in a targeted manner, and even grade the importance of individual data objects and pipeline components. DataScope's integration with model performance metrics allows data scientists to grade the importance of individual pipeline components and refine model behavior during training. DataScope's design is compatible with a range of machine learning task types such as classification, and data scientists can employ DataScope to identify top-performing pipeline components and improve model accuracy. Recent breakthroughs in algebraic statistics yield new insights into enumerative algebraic geometry by combining statistical approaches with algebraic degenerations. This reveals a fundamental link between a particular type of space, the Chow space, and a corresponding space for rational curves, along with their respective Hilbert schemes, which can be studied through toric methods. This knowledge has further inspired novel connections between combinatorics and algebraic geometry, leading to general statistical theorems applicable across different contexts. Consequently, there is a growing need to develop statistical tools that can analyze and compare different models, not just their extremal cases. This includes finding the most extreme cases that maximize or minimize statistical invariants while meeting specific requirements. This presentation will discuss some of these search missions, beginning with a quest for the rational curve with the most SECs (separating extremal curves). This curve must have a nonsingular Gorenstein impenetrable T-junction with the highest SECs and be part of a family of curves with exceptional secant lines. This leads to a combinatorial challenge: identifying the T-junction with this distinction. This T-junction must be a member of a symmetric product of points and lines and satisfy a unique combination of properties, making it the most extreme case in this context. Following this, we will explore a different inquiry, this time seeking the most extremal curve counting on a particular Chow space for curves with specific requirements. This curve counting on the Chow space for curves must be maximized while enforcing certain restrictions, which can be studied using toric methods and further generalized to apply across different contexts. Finally, we will discuss a related statistical problem, this time involving curve intersection numbers, which can be analyzed using the Eagon-Northcott presentation of ideal degenerations and further generalized to apply across different contexts. This presentation will also discuss how these new ideas in algebraic statistics lead to novel applications in combinatorics and topology. At a pressure of 1.5 GPa, our findings reveal a significant enhancement of the anomalous Hall effect relative to its room-temperature value, coupled with an increase in magnetic domain parameters and spin helicity in response to an internal coordination change triggered by the phenomenon of magnetic regulation under pressure. In contrast, synthetic single crystals of Mn$_3$Sn exhibited an anomalous Hall resistance of 0.12 nanovolts per mole per cubic centimeter at room pressure, a value that increased to 1.5 millinano volts per mole per cubic centimeter at 1.5 GPa. Our theoretical framework, grounded in magnetoelectric coupling theory, demonstrates that the transformation of a 190-kelvin magnetic phase transition into a 25-kelvin Helimagnetic ordering under pressure is responsible for the enhanced anomalous Hall effect through increased magnetically disordered phases at low temperatures. Additionally, our research using neutron spectroscopy confirms that the number of chemically sensitive spins contributing to the anomalous Hall effect also increases under pressure. Consequently, the regulation of magnetic properties within Mn$_3$Sn through high-pressure techniques leads to the Anomalous Hall effect being significantly and selectively altered. Therefore, this study suggests that Mn$_3$Sn, having entered the ferromagnetic phase under pressure, serves as a prime example of controlling this phenomenon in antiferromagnetic materials. Consequently, this study suggests that one feasible means of controlling the anomalous Hall effect in magnetic materials involves regulating their magnetic phases using external pressure.
