Recent research has shown that large language models can create high-quality text without input prompts, and with minimal prompts, by leveraging processes like diffusion and discretization. However, current models lack understanding of the text they generate, leading to inconsistent output quality. In this study, we propose the Steady Creator, a structured model that incorporates semantic knowledge into the diffusion process to facilitate guided text generation. The Steady Creator's creator component uses a transformer-based encoder to capture the semantic essence of text sequences, which is then fed into the diffuser component to initiate a sequential generation process. The diffuser applies a structured transformer that incorporates the creator's semantic representation, and uses a specialized adapter to refine each new token based on prior generated tokens and the semantic guide. Experimental results demonstrate that the Steady Creator produces better text with fewer prompts, and with reduced prompt iterations, compared to existing state-of-the-art models. Additionally, the Steady Creator outperforms baselines in targeted text generation tasks like code generation and text completion. The proposed model also surpasses existing models in text completion and code generation with fewer prompts, and shows great potential for other text generation applications with minimal prompts. Predicting climate change has become increasingly important for understanding the ongoing shift in the Earth's climate. Machine learning models have shown potential in this field by using historical climate data to forecast future weather patterns. However, improving the accuracy of these predictions is crucial for precise future climate prediction. Current models rely on recurrent neural networks (RNNs) or Fourier series for temporal and Fourier/Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) or Fourier/Convolutional for spatial encoding, but these combinations have limited effectiveness. In contrast, transformer models have shown superior performance in computer vision and have been successfully applied in climate prediction, but like their RNN/MLP counterparts, they fail to simultaneously encode temporal and spatial information from past climate data. To address this limitation, we propose introducing a new architecture that integrates the power of self-attention with the accuracy of Fourier encoding for both space and time, combining the strengths of previous models. The new Shifted Window Cross-Attention (SWCA) method utilizes the unique characteristics of the Fourier encoding to determine the window size for cross-attention, ultimately resulting in superior climate prediction performance. Experimental evaluations of the SWCA architecture revealed significant improvements over state-of-the-art models, demonstrating its potential as a cutting-edge climate prediction method. The code for this project is available at https://github.com/Chen-chen2022/SWCA_Temporal_Spatial_Encoding. The datasets can be found at https://doi.org/10.6086/M2WS2K.0 and https://doi.org/10.6086/M2WS2K.1. Validation of the approach was performed using numerical analysis on two widely used climate prediction datasets, the CMIP5 and NSRD datasets, utilizing Fourier encoding for temporal and spatial components. The proposed SWCA method demonstrated superior performance, achieving notable improvements over state-of-the-art models, ultimately reaching new heights in climate prediction accuracy. In conclusion, the proposed SWCA architecture has shown remarkable potential in further enhancing the accuracy of climate prediction through the innovative use of Fourier encoding for both space and time in future model development. Additionally, the proposed method has shown potential in other related tasks such as image classification, where it could be applied using image data represented in the Fourier domain. Future work will involve exploring the use of the SWCA architecture in computer vision applications. Furthermore, we aim to expand the use of the Fourier encoding in various domains, including speech, genetics, and protein data, due to its inherent properties that allow for easy integration with other encoders and easy decoding

In neurons, effective regulation of substance transport between a cell's body and its extremities is crucial for communication between different parts of the cell, playing a role in learning and regulation of metabolism, as well as potentially contributing to neurodegenerative diseases when compromised. We develop a mathematical model that incorporates the key processes involved in substance transport, utilizing a novel optimization framework to simulate the behavior of various transport mechanisms. These mechanisms, such as actin dynamics and the movement of substances along microtubules, exhibit characteristics like oscillation, slowing, or reversal - all of which have been observed experimentally. We utilize a constrained optimization approach to model substance transport, formulating it as an optimization problem with specific properties, and rely on the BFGS algorithm to solve it numerically. We are able to demonstrate that our proposed model is capable of accurately replicating the observed oscillatory behavior in oligodendrocytes, as well as the wave-like movements of substances seen in chondrocytes, utilizing essentially no model-specific parameters in the process. Moreover, we are able to utilize our optimization framework to effectively simulate the consequences of alterations in gene expression due to mutations, changes in protein activity, and modifications to the structure of microtubules and other cellular components. These results illustrate the utility of our proposed model structure, effectively bridging the gap between our individual component models and the observed behavior seen with advanced light microscopy techniques. Furthermore, we are able to utilize our optimization framework to simulate various forms of cellular response, effectively modeling the observed computational phenomena seen in the central nervous system and providing a foundation for further research into the regulation of metabolism, learning, and potential links between our model and neurodegenerative diseases. Overall, we view our proposed model as a foundation for a more comprehensive, research-oriented model, one that can be utilized in a wide range of studies examining the role of substance transport in cellular regulation. Researchers are studying a rare astronomical event known as a nova outbreak in the constellation Delphinus, monitoring its development with high-throughput telescopes on the ground and in space.  Typically, a nova occurs when the outer material from a surrounding disk made up of hydrogen gas accretes onto a white dwarf star.  As the accreted material nears the star's surface, it heats up and eventually reaches a critical point triggering a rapid explosion that releases an enormous amount of energy.  Following the explosion, the remaining white dwarf cools, only to begin the process of accreting more material from the disk, eventually restarting the cycle once more.  However, in a specific type of binary star system known as an HEECS (Heating to Emission of Classical Novae in a Soft State), a white dwarf transitions directly into a black hole without first becoming one itself, especially when it weighs less than a certain threshold - two times the mass of our sun.  This unique HEECS system likely produces outflows of plasma when it's in a state of high energy, producing an enormous amount of energy loss - a phenomenon known as mass loss or acceleration of the surrounding gas by magnetic forces, further reducing the available fuel for future explosions.  As the white dwarf transitions into a black hole, it's expected that its surrounding disk of hydrogen gas will change, affecting how much fuel is available for future explosions, while the high energy loss also impacts the overall dynamics of the system.  Therefore, it's hypothesized that nova outbreaks in HEECS systems will exhibit unique characteristics, particularly shorter waiting periods between cycles.  This waiting period, known as the recurrence time, is typically long, but it's expected to be shorter due to the reduced amount of fuel available for future explosions, a phenomenon that has already been observed in other types of systems, such as those with low mass black holes and neutron stars.  This prediction provides further supporting evidence for previous studies indicating that low mass white dwarfs, if they were to become involved in a binary system with a black hole, would also exhibit reduced recurrence times. A parametrized group of diverse Tversky metrics can be established by manipulating the Jaccard distance on a finite set of distinct points. Varying the parameter k affects the metrics' behavior as k changes: when k is between 0 and 1, it expands the metric's distance, when it's greater than 1, it contracts it, and when it equals 1, it transforms into the normalized Hamming distance. By changing the parameter a for 0 ≤ k ≤ 1, it's possible to obtain a family of metrics that connects the Jaccard distance with its counterpart of the information distance, where the parameter a controls this connection just as the parameter k controls the expansion or contraction of the metric. Moreover, the structural stability of the dynamic system based on the Hamming graph with k = 1 can be proven, and it's shown that the stable orbit lies within an equilibrium set that corresponds to the complete links between vertices in the graph. Unlike traditional convolutional networks, GCNNs appear to be an abstract concept with no clear visual representation. In order to shed light on the GCNN mechanism, researchers developed an alternative approach to graph filtering using a matched filtering methodology, which reveals the unique characteristics of GCNNs. By comparing the matched filtering method to GCNNs, researchers gained a deeper understanding of the double circulant matrix and its eigenvalues, which in turn shed light on the hidden group structure within graph data. This new understanding has further led to the creation of an Explainable GCNN (X-GCNN), which uses the matched filtering approach to derive the hidden group structure directly from the graph data, eliminating the need for GCNNs altogether. X-GCNN was then successfully tested on various benchmark datasets and outperformed state-of-the-art methods while providing clear insights into the hidden group structures within the data. Additionally, researchers found that X-GCNN could be applied to multiple tasks, including node classification, link prediction, and graph clustering, using essentially the same algorithm. This innovative approach could potentially be applied to other machine learning models to shed new light on their underlying mechanics. Finally, researchers tested X-GCNN on an artificial dataset and observed that it accurately detected the hidden group structure within the data, confirming the effectiveness of the approach. In summary, this study provided a comprehensive understanding of the GCNN mechanism by comparing the matched filtering method to GCNNs, which led to the creation of an X-GCNN. The benefits of this approach are threefold, as it explains the GCNN mechanism, reduces the computational complexity of GCNNs, and outperforms state-of-the-art methods while providing clear insights into the hidden group structures within graph data. Additionally, researchers found that X-GCNN could be applied to various tasks and even detected hidden group structures in an artificial dataset. With further development, X-GCNN could be applied to real-world applications such as social media, traffic systems, and biological networks to shed new light on the underlying structures within these datasets. Inspired by ranking small objects by size using circular arrangements with unmarked objects, we develop a method to calculate the likelihood of achieving particular rankings with marked objects in any order on a circle. This leads to a nonparametric estimation procedure for ranking items of unknown size based on a single visual observation of the objects in a circular arrangement. We also examine the distribution of the estimated rankings and propose a way to test the equality of several distributions without parametric assumptions, extending a known method to include cases where the distributions may not be equal. Most programming environments use a standard approach to set up their runtime environment, but some systems like native code compilers can optimize this setup for specific use cases during compilation. This study looks at whether a similar optimization is possible in languages with run-time environments that can be customized. Specifically, we examined the run-time loading process of Java classes and successfully reduced the common setup costs to unique patterns specific to the underlying system architecture, allowing for faster load times. This research identifies four distinct loading scenarios and demonstrates that by eliminating unnecessary steps, Java class loading can be significantly accelerated. To achieve this, we employed compile-time specialization, a technique that enables fine-grained control over the optimization of specific code segments at compile time. This involves creating customized load processors for different memory regions, thus eliminating redundant steps in the class loading process. This approach resulted in a notable improvement in loading times, with load times decreasing by 30% and overall system pause times decreasing by 25%. This paper presents a general methodology for applying compile-time specialization to run-time environment setup and provides guidance on extending this approach to other components and mechanisms within run-time environments. While this research focused on Java, the concepts discussed are equally applicable to other languages such as.NET and can potentially be applied to other languages as well. This study opens up new avenues for optimizing systems at compile time and uncovers previously unexplored opportunities for system acceleration. Future work using profiling techniques will be needed to pinpoint the specific system mechanisms that could benefit from further optimization using the compile-time specialization technique. This research is crucial to advancing the domain of high-performance language runtime optimization. Heart rate variability (HRV) or inter-beat interval (IBI) assessment is a crucial process that evaluates cardiac autonomic nervous system (CANX) functioning. Analyzing IBI allows researchers to derive critical parameters from heart rhythms, such as standard deviation of IBI (SDNN), root mean square of successive differences (RMSSD), and heart rate variability index (HRI). Previous studies have employed deep learning techniques, like long short-term memory (LSTM), to forecast IBI and subsequently calculate these parameters. However, existing methods have limitations: they forecast up to five beats ahead, but this is insufficient for parameter calculation since it demands at least ten predictions. Moreover, they rely on beat-based forecasting, but this can be unstable due to noisy ECG signals. To address these issues, we developed a novel deep residual memory network called Tiramisu, which forecasts IBI thirty beats ahead at once. Additionally, we proposed a novel error metric and demonstrated the superiority of Tiramisu over LSTM and traditional methods through simulations using the MIT-BIH arrhythmia database. We found that Tiramisu yields significantly lower error rates compared to other approaches, making it more suitable for real-world heart monitoring applications. Furthermore, we investigated the minimum data required for model training and discovered that as few as twenty data points suffice for accurate IBI forecasting. This research enables the rapid calculation of HRV parameters using only a small training dataset, thereby facilitating more efficient and practical monitoring of CANX functioning in mobile devices. In conclusion, Tiramisu represents a groundbreaking innovation in IBI forecasting, outperforming existing methods while addressing previously unmet challenges. Its exceptional performance will ultimately translate to improved quality-of-life for patients by enhancing mobile electrocardiogram (ECG) assessment. Specifically, it will facilitate more convenient and precise monitoring of CANX functioning using ECG, ECG-to-EEG, ECG-to-EEG, and EEG signals. The Active Ornstein-Uhlenbeck particle (AOUP) model, a simplified self-motivated particle, incorporates an internal force that compensates if it moves too far from a target point. This complex system, influenced by multiple time scales, displays diverse behaviors. By utilizing various analytical methods and numerical simulations, researchers have discovered that its steady-state properties exhibit significant differences when measured in relation to multiple time scales. However, the primary focus of this study lies in the fluctuations surrounding the stable state, particularly the rapid, dynamic movements of the particle. These movements can be attributed to a complex oscillatory pattern, resulting from the interaction between the internal force and external forces such as noise. The presence of noise introduces variability in the system, leading to a complex non-linear response in the fluctuations. By applying a variation of the active Brownian motion model, researchers have developed an analytical approach to understand the full dynamics of the AOUP model. This includes identifying and quantifying the movement patterns of the particle across various time scales and noise levels. Ultimately, this study bridges the gap between measured data and our understanding of the active particle's behavior, providing a crucial framework for interpreting experimental results. Moreover, this study's findings can be generalized to a broader range of active particle models. Key features of this study include the confirmation of a theoretical time-scale separation that affects the labor dynamics, the identification of distinct movement patterns based on internal and external time scales, and the demonstration of noise-induced changes in the particle's movement patterns. This study also reveals that certain movement patterns persist even when the self-motivation force is eliminated. Lastly, this study examines the relationship between internal forces in active particles and proposes a method for dissecting and analyzing these forces based on the steady-state properties of the system. This approach can be applied to a wide range of active particle models and provides a framework for understanding and interpreting experimental data. Additionally, this study confirms that steady-state properties of active particles are robust across various internal force models. Key features of this study include the confirmation of a theoretical time-scale separation in labor dynamics, the identification of distinct movement patterns across different time scales, and the demonstration of noise-induced changes in particle movement. Furthermore, this study examines the relationship between the self-motivation force model and steady-state properties, proposing a novel method for dissecting and analyzing these forces. This study confirms that steady-state properties of active particles are robust across different self-motivation force models. Lastly, this study confirms the wide applicability of our theoretical framework for understanding and interpreting experimental data.

In recent years, human gesture analysis has received significant attention due to its numerous applications across multiple domains. Despite the vast potential of gesture interaction, its application is currently limited by the complexity of accurately interpreting human movement. To accelerate the advancement of human gesture recognition, we have developed HUMBI, a groundbreaking dataset comprising detailed, multiview recordings of human body gestures. Utilizing 192 high-resolution RGB cameras and advanced rendering techniques, HUMBI captures precise, artifact-free data of 200 diverse gestures from 40 participants. Comprising over  20 billion pixels, this comprehensive dataset transcends current benchmarks in resolution, view angles, and semantic annotations. To foster state-of-the-art evaluation and spur innovation, we have integrated a challenging benchmark framework within HUMBI. Leveraging modern deep learning methods for comparison, we have observed significant room for improvement across diverse gesture categories. With its unrivaled scale, richness, and complexity, HUMBI presents an unparalleled opportunity for the advancement of human gesture recognition. This resource is freely accessible to the public at https://humbi.io/. Additionally, a detailed whitepaper outlining the creation and evaluation of HUMBI can be found at https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.04123!.

The widespread availability of neural models has highlighted issues regarding data labeling and domain adaptation across different languages. While pre-trained models can facilitate cross-lingual data transfer with minimal adaptations, they often necessitate substantial labeling costs for tasks like NLP. To address this challenge, our approach aims to make the learning process more efficient by representing task information effectively. By defining Task Represented Supervision (TRS), we propose a framework that enables model-independent task translations with TRS representations, demonstrating the efficacy from several natural language processing tasks including sentiment analysis and question answering. Notably, our method shows promising results in translating tasks across diverse languages, including languages with limited resources, and surpasses the performance of models trained with directly obtained task labels. The code for this project is available at https://github.com/prakharsrivastava/tras. Experimental findings validate the feasibility of TRS in achieving both model-independent task translations and high accuracy performance in sentiment analysis and question-answering tasks. Additionally, models trained with TRS demonstrate a notable reduction in labeling costs while achieving comparable results to models trained with directly obtained task labels. Notably, our approach is versatile and can be applied to both intrinsic and extrinsic transfer scenarios. Furthermore, we analyzed the effectiveness of our task representation method using various evaluation metrics, and our findings suggest that it is influenced by several linguistic and structural factors. Specifically, words that are highly frequent, words with high semantic similarity, and tasks with similar labels facilitate good task representations while reducing labeling costs. Conversely, words with low frequency, words with low semantic similarity, and tasks with distinct labels make it challenging to obtain accurate task representations and are associated with higher labeling costs. In summary, our approach provides feeble supervision by translating task information into a more manageable form while reducing the need for costly data labeling. Furthermore, we have established that words with high frequency, semantic similarity, and task cohesion are essential for obtaining accurate task representations while minimizing labeling expenses. Based on these observations, we propose several potential research directions, including the exploration of other forms of feeble supervision, the development of more robust task representation methods, and the investigation of word semantics in neural IMCT models. Ultimately, our work contributes to advancing the IMCT paradigm with feeble supervision by translating task information into a more manageable form while reducing the need for costly data labeling. Furthermore, we have addressed the issue of word meaning capture in neural IMCT models and observed that words with high frequency, semantic similarity, and task cohesion are essential for obtaining accurate task representations while minimizing labeling expenses. In multi-task reinforcement learning, using a shared representation can be beneficial, allowing tasks to be solved more efficiently. However, the opposite often occurs in model-free learning when separate value functions for individual tasks interfere with each other, a phenomenon known as destructive interference. Destructive interference can be avoided in model-based learning by using a single shared model structure for all tasks, allowing tasks to be solved more efficiently. By decomposing the model into separate modules for predicting action values and state transitions, researchers found that separate modules for individual tasks can outperform a shared model approach, demonstrating that modular structures can prevent destructive interference in model-free multi-task reinforcement learning. Furthermore, a new method was developed that uses a shared policy structure to select the task and action for the maximum expected return in each situation, resulting in superior performance on CartPole and Montezuma's Revenge. Additionally, the Montezuma's Revenge problem was solved using this method, a task that had previously been considered difficult to accomplish. Traditional thermodynamic analyses often overlook the finite duration of heat engines, despite being inherently temporal entities. To address this gap, we'll be investigating a basic model of a heat engine undergoing a quantum transition within a time frame T, influenced by two distinct types of control mechanisms - instantaneous adjustment of system parameters and continuous adjustments facilitated by memory-based quantum strategies. Our analysis will focus on determining optimal engine performance using the thermodynamic figure-of-merit metric for both types of control mechanisms, leading to their respective identification as maximized for the parameter-adjustment model and saturated by memory-based strategies in the continuous-adjustment model. Furthermore, we'll demonstrate that the optimal continuous-control model can exhibit a substantial enhancement in performance, approximately doubling that of its instantaneous counterpart in a quantum system lacking memory. Nonetheless, memory does impart a valuable advantage in this context. To illustrate our theoretical findings, we'll be utilizing a simple yet comprehensive quantum heat engine model featuring two coupled bosonic oscillators. It's worth noting that the optimal instantaneous control strategies can be effectively applied to a wide variety of quantum systems, often simplifying their complex dynamics while yielding results consistent with prior research, including notable generalizations regarding system parameters. Interestingly, our analysis also reveals distinct differences in the optimal continuous-control methods employed in this study and those typically applied in conventional real-time quantum control mechanisms, which may be leveraging cutting-edge innovations in machine learning and other advanced technologies. Finally, we'll be examining the relationship between the optimal continuous-control model and a recently proposed quantum thermodynamic framework focused on long-duration, non-equilibrium processes, revealing both conceptual and formal connections and similarities between these two distinct approaches to thermodynamics. It's our hope that this study will contribute positively to the ongoing development of quantum thermodynamics by integrating the techniques and methods of real-time quantum control into this field. Additionally, we'll be exploring the potential for heat-engine systems with infinite duration to serve as a bridge, facilitating the development of real-world applications using contemporary technologies. In doing so, we may uncover novel insights into the intricate balance between thermodynamic performance and system lifetime in quantum systems. In particular, by applying our analysis to a specific example involving a two-level system, we've identified an unexpected trade-off between thermodynamic performance and system lifetime - a phenomenon we believe to be a widespread phenomenon in quantum systems and may be a fundamental aspect of the underlying thermodynamic structure of these systems. It's our hope that this study will contribute positively to the ongoing development of quantum thermodynamics by integrating the techniques and methods of real-time quantum control into this field

Severe weather conditions like hurricanes and storm surges have devastating effects on power delivery and distribution infrastructure. The accuracy of this method was validated through a comparison with actual damage reports from a severe storm in 2017 in Florida, USA. The results enable utility companies to forecast damage and schedule maintenance in advance, thus reducing costs and ensuring timely service restoration. Furthermore, this research enables policymakers to make informed decisions by providing maps showing areas most prone to line damage and facilitating discussions between utility and government agencies. Under the framework of Clifford analysis, the Dirac operator plays a crucial role in studying partial differential equations. This article explores the maximum principle for eigenfunctions of the Dirac operator in n-dimensional Euclidean space, establishing a three-sphere theorem that extends a prior finding by Jost and Li. Additionally, this article provides local representation formulas for eigenfunctions of the Dirac operator, building upon prior work by Chung, Morin, and Ryan. Notably, this article incorporates recent developments in monotone function theory. For clamped Dirichlet and Neumann problems, the three-sphere theorem leads to solutions and their universal monotonicity in dimensions two and above. Finally, this article examines the extension of the three-sphere theorem to Riemannian manifolds with compact, dimension n+1 or higher.

We examine two iterations of the Heterochaos map, a system exhibiting complex behaviors on the plane, characterized by a mixed phase space of two ergodic components separated by a hyperbolic barrier. This barrier forms a distinctive pattern, dividing the plane into regions that follow the Fibonacci sequence, prompting the adoption of the Fibonacci numbers and sequences to analyze this system's properties. Focusing on two maximal entropy measures, we identify unique properties associated with two distinct sequences, known as the Dyck and Fibonacci sequences. Additionally, we find that these measures can be represented as the limit of two iterative applications of the Heterochaos map on specific initial conditions. Despite one iteration converging towards a stable equilibrium, its entropy cannot be approached by any smaller iteration with the same starting point, illustrating the failure of the entropy approachability hypothesis. This phenomenon is attributed to the system's entrapment in areas defined by specific words of the Dyck sequence. This analysis contributes to existing research on the Heterochaos map while also providing new insights into the properties of the Dyck system. Moreover, it offers a solution to a problem initially posed by Alcalde, answering which Fibonacci numbers are comparable to the entropy of certain stochastic homeomorphisms. Finally, this study provides a numerical tool to determine the entropy of certain stochastic homeomorphisms, relying on the computation of certain critical values, known as "escape rates," on specific areas defined by words of the Dyck sequence. This Computation tool may be applied to other systems, promoting future research on the properties of the Heterochaos map. We have reason to believe that the standard model is not the complete description of particle physics due to unsolved issues like the origin of mass, matter-antimatter imbalance, and certain properties of strongly interacting particles. In this study, we explore how to incorporate hidden scalar sectors, a feature common in many alternative theories, which could provide answers to these outstanding questions. By looking at data from past experiments, Higgs searches, and theoretical predictions about how multiple Higgs bosons interact, we establish model-independent parameters that can be applied to a wide range of scenarios. Specifically, our study focuses on two cases involving two Higgs bosons in different reactions: $pp \to \gamma \gamma \gamma \gamma$ and $pp \to \mu^+\mu^+\mu^-\mu^-$. We calculate the total cross-section for these processes in various models and indicate how to extend them to accommodate complex scalar interactions. Our analysis also includes sensitivity assessments for upcoming experiments: HL-LHC, a future proton collider with 27 TeV energy, and a future lepton collider with 250 GeV energy, to determine how these experiments could further our understanding of hidden scalar interactions that produce high-energy photons or muons. Specifically, our study shows that these experiments could significantly enhance our knowledge of how multiple Higgs bosons interact, particularly in reactions like $pp \to \gamma \gamma \gamma \gamma$ and $pp \to \mu^+\mu^+\mu^-\mu^-$. We find that a future lepton collider has the greatest potential, followed by a future proton collider, and then the current HL-LHC. Our study only considers the sensitivity to one type of scalar interaction and does not account for the sensitivity to other types, a limitation we aim to address in a companion study. This paper presents a generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) to enhance the synthesis of pitch-controlled raw audio waves in the time domain. To overcome the limitations of the standard WaveNet model, which struggles with generating long sequences due to its autoregressive property and is sensitive to speaker identity, QPNet incorporates a Pitch-sensitive Dilated Convolution Neural Network (PCNN). The PCNN learns speaker-independent pitch characteristics and is integrated into WaveNet to enable the generation of longer audio segments (up to 16ms) with improved pitch coherence. Experimental results demonstrate that QPNet yields higher quality audio samples with more pitch accurate results compared to the standard WaveNet model. Additionally, AQPNet outperforms state-of-the-art voice synthesis systems in terms of mean opinion score in subjective evaluations. Furthermore, ablation studies confirm the effectiveness of the proposed PCNN component. The generated audio samples are available on the website: https://lianghao-audiogen.github.io/index.html. The code for this research can be accessed at: https://github.com/lianghaoQQ/Quasi-Periodic-WaveNet. Recommender systems can be divided into two main categories: the hybrid type that addresses data scarcity, and the hybrid type that addresses user information scarcity.  The cooperative filtering (CF) type addresses user information scarcity, and there are two subcategories: global CF and local CF.  The global CF type builds recommendations by combining the global pattern of all users, while local CF builds recommendations by combining the local patterns of specific groups of users.  Biclustering is a type of local pattern finding that considers the preferences of users in a specific group along with the items involved, making it more suitable than other local pattern finding methods like k-nearest neighbors (kNN).  However, traditional biclustering systems have limitations including only considering the global pattern of a specific user without considering item relationships and the scarcity of biclustering systems that use side information such as items' categorization.  This research proposes a novel approach called User-Specific Biclustering (USB), which combines the biclustering of users and items based on user preference in real-time while considering their respective impacts using an fuzzy entropy criterion that avoids over-specialization and over-generalization.  The biclustering approach is then combined with the local CF type's rating prediction mechanism to address the recommendability of recommended items.  Experiments conducted on real-world datasets demonstrate that the proposed USB approach outperforms existing methods in accuracy and diversity while simultaneously addressing user preference subjectivity, item scarcity, and uniqueness.  The proposed USB approach is also shown to be scalable and adaptable, and can be applied in various domains such as movie and document recommendation.  Moreover, the proposed USB approach is shown to be transparent and explainable due to its reliance on user and item biclusters.  Ultimately, the proposed USB approach is shown to be cooperative and human-friendly by addressing user information scarcity through the local CF type's management of user preference locality, sparsity, and subjectivity. In a medium with uniformly distributed and varying density, a plane shock wave initially travels smoothly but starts to develop a sinusoidal perturbation due to the density fluctuations. A growing "finger" of the shock wave forms at the peak of the perturbation, leading to a self-perpetuating and rapidly accelerating structure in a medium where the pressure outside the shock wave is higher than its internal pressure. This type of system is commonly found in nature and not adequately described by previous ideal shock wave models, instead requiring a more realistic analysis that incorporates pressure differences. Three distinct stages of this shock wave evolution have been identified. Firstly, a long, curved structure forms due to the growth of the perturbation, characterized by a growth rate of ~5% per cycle for a specific shock wave strength. The second stage involves the shock wave breaking up into a series of curved rays. The third and final stage is characterized by highly non-linear and highly inelastic shock behavior, where small changes in the system result in dramatic changes to the shock form, ultimately leading to a singular event in a specific system configuration. Additionally, this highly non-linear system exhibits a distinctive property known as 'unpredictive chaos', where tiny variations in the initial conditions result in vastly different outcomes, even within very short timescales. This is in contrast to previous ideal shock models which predict a universal and predictable outcome. Two methods have been employed to analyze this highly non-linear system, including a advanced numerical simulation which provides highly detailed insights into the system behavior and a simplified mathematical approach which accurately identifies key features of the shock wave structure, confirming previous findings and revealing new insights into the system. Notably, the simplified mathematical approach is capable of accurately predicting the system behavior for a specific system strength and provides a precise calculation of the system cycle times. Lastly, further research is recommended to analyze how this collapsing shock wave affects the surrounding medium and how this system compares to other astrophysical systems that exhibit similar shock wave behavior. It is hypothesized that this type of system may play a role in explaining at least one observed phenomenon known as Fast Radio Bursts (FRBs). The growing presence of artificial intelligence systems has led to a significant rise in their use across various domains, spanning healthcare, transportation, and education. As these systems interact with people in critical areas such as healthcare and finance, understanding their decision-making processes is of utmost importance. This study begins to address the gap in research by investigating how AI system developers can meet user-specified needs for clearer reasoning within these systems. Our methodology involves conducting semi-structured interviews with 12 experts from diverse backgrounds, examining current initiatives and challenges related to Explainable AI. Key difficulties in implementing XAI are found to be linked to existing limitations in requirements engineering, particularly in capturing user needs for XAI tailored to specific problem domains. Therefore, this study posits that requirements engineering can play a vital role in addressing these challenges and assist in creating more transparent, user-centric AI systems. Several actionable recommendations for XAI requirements engineering have been identified, centered around user involvement, clear stakeholder roles, and domain knowledge capture. These findings serve as a starting point for further research aimed at developing a more comprehensive approach to capturing explainability needs in AI systems. This approach, inspired by user-centered design, will be explored in greater detail in a subsequent study. In the interim, this study aims to raise awareness among the requirements engineering community about the potential for addressing XAI challenges through their expertise in meeting user needs for explainability.

This paper introduces a novel discovery of sequences based on time-based patterns in data, processed individually at different points in time. A sequence is defined by linking relevant data points together, and researchers use this framework to analyze the behavior of individuals throughout the course of the day. This pattern discovery is analogous to traditional sequence mining, and similar concepts can be applied here, such as discovering continuous patterns within sequences. We examine the implementation of our approach via a case study that focuses on understanding how individuals spend their time, utilizing data collected via mobile devices. Our method is then compared to existing, time-aggregated approaches, and we show that the results can provide insights that would otherwise take human interpretation to reveal. For instance, it is discovered that individuals tend to engage in phone activities about 80% of the time immediately after waking up and roughly 2 hours later, indicating a shift towards other activities. This pattern can be generalized further as $\{phone, other\}$, appearing 80% of the time 2 hours after $\{wake up\}$. We propose enhancing our discovery framework with the ability to identify the cause of these patterns, referred to as explanations, using a novel method that optimizes explanations based on their frequency and relevance to the sequence. It is observed that in the example provided, the use of phones is the common factor linking the initial and latter points in time, serving as an explanation for the discovered pattern. Our work offers a predictive model that can generate potential future patterns in data under current trends, and we demonstrate its effectiveness by applying it to understanding the behavior of individuals throughout the day. Overall, the contribution of this research is three-fold: (1) introducing a pattern discovery framework that takes into account the continuous nature of data collected at varying times, (2) proposing the concept of explanations to provide insight into discovered patterns, and (3) offering a predictive model capable of forecasting future patterns in data. Our findings reveal that this second type of deformation can trigger d-wave superconductivity in certain regions, particularly when it competresses with other ordered states such as d-wave superconductivity, N\'eel antiferromagnetism, stripe antiferromagnetism, and orbital ordering. Accurate vertebral center localization is crucial for analyzing spinal disorders from CT scans, but current methods are limited by low precision and high sensitivity to errors, especially when dealing with variations in CT scan quality and human anatomy. To overcome these challenges, we developed an advanced automated vertebral center localization system, comprising L-shaped structure detection, anatomically-conformed regularization, and a novel L-shaped prior model, to optimize localization with high precision and accuracy. Our method was thoroughly evaluated using 103 CT spinal imaging data sets collected from CT scans of 52 individuals with diverse anatomies and exhibited exceptional performance, achieving a mean distance error of only 0.58 mm with 95.5% precision when manually validated by expert radiologists. Furthermore, we successfully tested and verified the robustness of our method using 24 diverse patient CT scan data sets collected from CT scans of 12 individuals with various spinal disorders, demonstrating high precision and accuracy across a wide range of anatomical variations. To make possible the development of advanced machine learning-based methods for vertebral center localization, we also created a publicly-available dataset consisting of 103 annotated CT spinal imaging data sets collected from CT scans of 52 individuals, providing a valuable resource for advancing the field. Our method represents a significant advancement in automated vertebral center localization, offering high precision and accuracy, anatomical variability robustness, and a publicly-available dataset for further research. It has potential applications in clinical practice for analyzing spinal disorders from CT scans, as well as in machine learning approaches for vertebral center localization and other spinal-related tasks. To facilitate further research, we will make available the code, dataset, and annotated images used in our study at https://github.com/NEU-BIM/VLC. These aggregates form spontaneously due to microscopic interactions among the excitons and the optical field, giving rise to a robust macroscopic quantum state. characterized by long-range and anisotropic optical interactions. As a result, the aggregates exhibit a high degree of symmetry, forming rosetta-like structures that can move around the microcavity due to excess excitonic energy causing them to rotate and contract. Additionally, we demonstrate how these aggregates can be used as optical traps at zero temperature to confine and manipulate excitonic and polaritonic excitons. Given the similarities between the polaritonic and photonic Hamiltonians, we propose the feasibility of experimentally observing the predicted phenomena. The identification of exoplanets orbiting nearby stars offers a chance to analyze their atmospheric and evolutionary characteristics in detail.  The planet K2-22 b, which surrounds the star K2-22 in the Kepler mission dataset, shows remarkable properties such as irregularly shaped grains and temperature fluctuations above 1000K in its atmosphere.  Analyzing transit data from multiple observations, researchers discovered evidence of two key processes that affect the planet's atmosphere: the scattering of starlight and the absorption or scattering of starlight by atmospheric particles.  By using various models and considering factors such as atmospheric grain size, orientation, and temperature effects, scientists estimated the size of dust grains in K2-22 b's atmosphere to be around 0.5-1 micrometer in diameter.  This is larger in size compared to grains found in other planets such as WASP-8 b and HD 189733 b.  According to one particular model used, the amount of dust produced by K2-22 b is significantly higher than previously estimated, indicating a potentially unstable atmosphere and a relationship between this phenomenon and the planet's internal heat source.  This new discovery could aid scientists in understanding the role of planetary internal heat in shaping atmospheric characteristics.

In the case of the Scientific Revolution, I employ a computational technique to identify patterns of 16th-century publishing house networks, both within Italy and across Europe, whose geographic spreadcorresponds to the dissemination of Galileo's scientific ideas through printed works. Galileo's unique position in this network stems from his writing style, which, while conventional in content, exhibited innovative mathematical elements that facilitated its transmission and creation processes, thereby garnering him the support of prominent Medici allies and European mathematicians. However, his failure to fully grasp the philosophical implications of his own work, particularly in terms of heliocentrism and the role of mathematized inquiry, led to miscalculations and mismanagement of the Medici affair, ultimately forcing him to navigate a delicate balance between philosophical skepticism and scientific conviction. We present a novel technique in interactive teaching of programming basics to absolute newcomers, utilizing a human tutor's notes as a framework. This method involves a human tutor taking notes during a coding session with a student, serving as a teaching assistant. As the tutor writes down relevant code and step-by-step explanations, the tutor's trainee, typically an experienced programmer, gains a systematic understanding of the programming fundamentals by observing the tutor's thoughts through their notes. This approach has been effectively implemented in a university setting with positive outcomes. Moreover, a prototype demonstration is available on the web for further exploration. This unique teaching method aims to address the scarcity of quality programming educators by utilizing experienced programmers as interactive learning tools. Key benefits include simplified lesson planning, tutor management, and adaptation to students' skill levels, all while providing comprehensive, searchable knowledge. Furthermore, this technique fosters a deeper understanding of programming concepts among tutors, as they engage in detailed analysis of code to address student queries. Emerging applications also exist in the domain of Open Source Software development, where the tutor's approach can be applied to foster collaborative engagement among contributors by leveraging their collective knowledge via similar note-based interactions. System evaluations through user studies have shown that this method can indeed transfer domain-specific knowledge from human tutors to their trainees and that the latter can effectively demonstrate their understanding by explaining and defending public code repositories. Notably, this technique has received significant attention within the programming community, as evidenced by the submission of 15 high-quality research papers to international conferences and publications. A comprehensive website has been established at bcse.io/programming-education to centralize related resources and research for further discussion and exploration. Key research outcomes include the design and evaluation of collaborative learning graph, a codebase analysis tool, and a study on the optimal size of tutor-student ratios, all of which are openly available on GitHub at https://github.com/programming-education. This novel approach to interactive teaching of programming fundamentals has far-reaching implications and can be further adapted to various subjects, as exemplified by a successful case study in teaching machine learning using similar note-based interactions. As a result, we believe that Scribe presents a promising, data-driven approach to educational learning that can be effectively applied across diverse knowledge domains. Moreover, a prototypical implementation is available on GitHub at https://github.com/education-scribe. To foster a deeper understanding of the underlying educational concepts, we have prepared a publicly accessible knowledge graph at https://bcse.io/education-graph.
